I have seldom known any one who deserted truth in trifles that could be trusted in matters of importance. The life of man consists not in seeing visitors and in dreaming dreams, but in active charity and in willing service.—Lonyfellaw. I look upon indolence as a sort of suicide; for the man is efficiently destroyed, though the appetite of the brute may survive.--Chesterfield. An Irish counsel being questioned by a Judge to know "for whom he was concerned," replied," I am concerned, my lord, for the plaintiff, but I am employed by the defendant." The sweetest word in our language is love. The greatest word in our language is God. Ilia word ex- pressing the shortest time is now. The threomake our greatest and sweetest duties. "Used you pretty rough, didn't he ?" remarked a sym- pathising bystander to a man who had just got an awful licking. "Well, no." replied the subdued one. "I thought he polished me off nicely." "Nature has written henest man' on his face," said a man to Douglas Jerrold, speaking of a person who in Jerrold's faith was not altogether blind. "Humph r replied the wit, Theta the pen must have been a very bad one." A class of boys in Sunday School, studying the lire of Joseph, were asked, "What did Joseph mean when he said to his brethren, `See that ye fall not out by the way'?" And one little fellow replied, "Look out that you don't tumble out of the waggon." A political orator, speaking of a cersain general whom be professed to admire, said that on the field of battle he was always founl where, the bullets were thickest. "Where was that ?" asked one of the auditors. "In the ammunition waggon," said another. A deceased city surgeon adopted an ingenious plan for collecting his fees. He had two bells; when he rang one the servant knew the fee was paid, and bowed the visitor out; when he rang the other, the servant said, "I think, sir, you have forgotten to give Mr. Lock his fee ;" and did not open the door until the fee was paid. A sceptic who was trying to confuse a Christian colotired man by the apparantly contradictory passages in the Bible, asking how it could be that we were in the Spirit and the Spirit in us, received the reply," Oh, dars no posele about dat. It's like dat poker. I put it.in de fire until it gets red hot. Now, de poker's in de fire and de fire's in de poker." , A man visiting London went to church and seated him- self without hesitation in the nearest pew. Soon the awns? came in, eyed the stranger critically, and then ,writing " My pew" on the flyleaf of a prayer-book, handed the book to the intruder. The stranger read the mes- sage, smiled a beautiful smile, and wrote underneath, "Nice pew. What do you pay for it?" - Wee Was ENGLAND CALLED MERRY.—Hundreds of years ago the great delight of the English folk was in music and song. Boys at the public schools had to learn part-singing, net as an "extra," but as a regular por- tion of their lessons. In those times minstrels went about the country singing ballads that often told of the news of the day, and were, in fact, the only means that men had of getting news. Wherever they went the people crowded to listen to them, and to join in the choruses; and it was this love of song and of singing that led to this country being called "Merry England.' You will like to know that this is the meaning of the word, and to think how it came to be given to our own native land.—" Little Folks" Magazine. THE TREATMENT OF A. COLD IN THE .ITEAD.—The hydro- pethic treatment of a cold in the head is more reliable than any other and one which scarcely requires the aid of a physician. It is as follows. In the morning after eks.ing, and at night before retiring, wash the feet and legs as high up as the knees in cola water, and rub them with a rough towel and massage them till the skin is red and glowing. In addition to this, snuff tepid water up the nose frequently during the day, and sip with a tea- spoon a glassful as hot as can be borne an hour before • each meal and at bedtimes. A few days is often quite sufficient for simple cases, and obstinate ones yield if the treatment is prolonged. No medicines are required. If taken in the first stages of the disease a cold is broken up which otherwise become a severe case of bronchitis, lasting many days and weeks. BUILDING A HOUSE IN THREE HOURS.—The Annamese esti put up'a house in three hours—stopping at intervals to smoke a cigar; over-exertion being against their prin- ciples. The posts and sides of their houses are bamboo; the roof is grass-thatched. The door is a bamboo flap like the side of the house, and hinged at the top, so that it can be propped up during daytime and allowed to fall at night. Fowls, dogs, pigs, and ducks enter at pleasure and dispute the comfortable places with the diildren. The appointments of the house are equally primitive. In front of the door le a big low platform or table which *ryes every purpose. A mat spread on it at night turns it into a bed. It is the family dining table, and, when strangers:come, it is the place of honour where they sit and chew betel and smoke spill-like cigars. On one side is the altar to the ancestors of the house. Rich or poor, the appointments are much the same, except that the wealthier have tiled roofs and part of the walls of brick, with beautifully-polished iron-wood posts. Inside there may be a few ponderous benches with pieces of tortoise- shell or mother-of-pearl set into the sides. THE CZAR AND MR, ARCHIBALD FORBES: A RENT- mrsaNcE.—The Schipka Pass had been in Russian pos- session for quite a month, and it was not unreasonable t,o assume that a sketch of the position there was, as a matter of course, in the Imperial Cabinet. I asked for the plan, since with its help my task of explanation would be so greatly simplified. But it seemedthat there was no such document; and I ventured to say that I eculd get along much more satisfactory if I had a sheet of paper on which to jot down some rough explanatory outlines. The Emperor said at once, "Ignatieff, go and fetch paper and pencil." Ignatieff went, and there re- mained the Emperor and myself alone together, standing opposite to each other, with a little green baize table between us. The thought that drifted across my mind as we stood there looking into each others' faces was, that Emperor as he was, no consideration that the world could offer would tempt me to change places with a man so oppressed by ills. And I noticed, or thought that I noticed, what flicker of thought darted into a corner of his mind. As we so stood, he listening to me talking, there came into his face for a fleeting moment a strange, troubled expres- sion, which seemed to reveal the sudden thought— " What a chance for this man to kill The !" It was a mere quick shadow, and had passed away ere Ignatieff came bustling back with a sheet of foolscap on which I rapidly outlined the positions, explaining the details as, I proceeded. It would be superfluous to recapitulate What was almost a purely-technical conversation, which, interspersed by the Emperor's eager questionings, lasted about half-an-hour—considerably longer than' pleased a man who was devoured-by an eager anxiety to be hurrying along the road to Bucharest. Under any other circumstances there would have been no tediousness in the interview; but the Emperor caught up every point with the alertness of a trained military intelligence. I believe that what I told him gave him some comfort. He expressed the same hesitation to accept my: view of the situation as Ignatieff had manifested ; al- though he had been eager enough to know what that Opinion was.—" Interviewed by the Emperor "by ARCM- tam) FORBEE, see The English Illustrated Magazine for April. ernr.s. A certain Nevada judge, who had been a great scamp years before his accession to the Bench, recognised an old acquaintance in a prisoner brought before him, and, supposing himself safe from recognition, asked the pri- soner what had become of the companions of his early life of crime. The reply was, "They are all hanged, your honour, except you and me." At an hotel, a short time since, a girl inquired of a gentleman at the table if his cup was out. "No," said ' be; "but my coffee is !" The poor girl was considerably confused, but determined to pay him in his own coin. While at dinner the stage drove up, and several coming in, the gentleman asked, "Does the stage dine here ?"1 "No, sir," exclaimed the girl in a sarcastic tone; "but the passengers do." A farmer who had engaged the services of a son of the Emerald Isle, sent him out one morning to harrow a piece of ground. He had not worked long 'before nearly all the teeth came out of the harrow. Presently the farmer • went out into the field to take notes of the man's pro- gress, and asked him how he liked harrowing. "Oh," t t-tt replied," it goes a bit smoother now since the pegs

are out." _ With pardonable pride, a lady displayed a very ancient piece of house-linen to her servant, saying, as she held it up for inspection, "Look, Bridget, at this table-cloth; it has been in our family for over two hundred years." Bridget eyed the article in question carefully, and then, stepping close up to her mis' tress, remarked, in a most confidential tone, "Shure, never mind, Mrs. Arthurs, dear. If you just kape quiet about it, and don't let on to anybody, who would know but what it was brought bran'-new out of the shop ?"

IT MATTERS MUCH. It matters little where I was born, If my parents were rich or poor; Whether they shrank at the cold world's scorn, Or walked in the pride of wealth secure; But whether I live an honest man, And hold my integrity firm in my touch, I tell you, my brother, plain as I am,, It matters much!

• In the old coaching days, a sailor was riding to town on the top of a Portsmouth coach, and sitting by the side of a guard, who, according to the mail coach practice, " tootled" loudly on his horn whenever the vehicla passed through a town or village. On one of these occasions the coachman missed the fanfare of the horn, and, turning round on his box, he saw, with dismay, that the guard's seat was vacant. "Why, where is he ?" he asked. Who ?" replied the sailor. 4 Why, the rard to be sure." "If you mean that blowed trumpeter, returned Jack, "I knocked him overboard." DIFFICULTIES OF THE ENGLISH TONGUE.—MarIy funny stories have been told of the difficulties encountered by Frenchmen in trying to master the English language. Here are some new ones i—A Frenchman, M. Dubois, in conversation with Mr. Brown, an Englishman, says, "I am going to leave my hotel. I paid my bill yesterday, and I said to the landlord, Do I owe anything else?' He said, You are square.' 'What am I?' He said again, You are square.' 'That's strange,' said I, lived so long I never knew I was square before.' Then as I was going away he shook me by the hand, saying, !I hope you'll be round soon.' I said, thought you said I was square. Now you hope I'll be round.' •He laughed and said, 'When I tell you you'll be round, I mean you won't be long.' I did not know how many forms he wished me to assume; however, I was glad he did not call me flat." THE Exitausnox or OUR COALFIELDS.—A few years ago my right hon. friend Mr. Gladstone asked me if I would be chairman of a Commission appointed to in- quire int, the important question of the exhaustion of our coalfields. Our commission sat for several years from 1866. The result at which we arrived was very re- markable. We reported there were no less than 146,480,000,000 of tons of coal available in Great Britain without going to a greater depth than 4,000 feet. But our annual consumption last year was 1.63,800,000 tons. I am sorry to say that if we go on expending and Con- suming this great Store of Energy at the rate we are now doing, our supplies will be exhausted in little more than 108 years, and long before that time the approach- ing exhaustion of our, coalfields will be seen and, felt appreciably by the rise in the price of coal That is by no means a very pleasant prospect before us, even though we are told by our friends across the Atlantic that America has an area of coalfields which is 38 times more than that ot the whole of Great Britain.—The Duke of Argyll, in "Good Words." A SO-CALLED FACTORY ON THE WEST COAST.—The name factory as applied to these trading establishments in West Africa is rather a misnomer, and suggests to the English mind a hideous brick building of several storeys, with probably three or four tall chimneys belching forth volumes of black smoke. Nothing could be more unlike the reality. The West African factory consists usually of a one-storeyed house, surrounded by a verandah or piazza, and standing in the midst of an enclosure. No- thing is manufactured in these places; and they are, when all is said, shops, in which cotton-prints, rum, gin, powder, beads, and cheap muskets are bartered for native produce, and sometimes sold. The traders, how- ever, speak of themselves as merchants, and though they will sell anything down to a pennyworth of rum, would consider themselves greatly insulted if called shopkeepers. The ground floor of the building contains the shoo and stock-in-trade, the agent and his clerks live above, and the casks of palm-oil and bags of palm- kernels are stered up in sheds in the yard ready for ship- ment. There is no busy hum of workpeople. Perhaps a native will arrive at the factory with a tanoe full of kegs of palm-oil; he saunters Up to the house, has rum lavished utfoit him to create a generous spirit, and after a time, for he does nothing in a hurry, he mentions that he has got so much oil to dispose of, provided that he can get in exchange so many cutlasses, so much powder, and so on. Then a couple of Kroomen lazily roll the kegs up from the beach, gauge them, examinti the quality of the oil, and in the course of an hour or So re- port progress to their employer, the agent; After this a little haggling, such as the climate has left the trader sufficient energy to indulge jai, takes place; with the result that the native hands over his oil at a nominal price per gallon, which is about half what it is really worth, and gets paid in goods which are rated and ex- changed at about 200 per cent. abovc their value; so that, in one way or another, the trader makes rather a good thing out of it.—" West African Islands," by Major A. B. Ellis. HINTS ON lADIES' DRESS.—" No woman is ugly when I she is dressed," said the gallant .Lord Chesterfield. Nor Is any bird with its plumage. But pluck it! Pluck the bird of paradise itself, and learn a lesson—that renowned fowl owes everything to its dress, and we cannot say that of humanity, however ill-favoured. Our gifts are mani- fold, our chances various, and our hopes endless. It should not be beneath us to attend to ow plumage, and all the other little niceties that add so much to the enjoy- ment of life. A plain woman with any wisdom will make the most of any good point in her physique and as little as she can of her worse points. For instance, if she has a bad, coarse complexion, she will not exhibit more square feet al the material than are needful. Square feet? nay, nor square inches. She will not wear low dresses nor short sleeves. She will carefully select hues in dress that improve, not injure her own natural colouring, and will wear dresses high to the throat !just enough trimmed with lace to give richness without confusion to the lines of her toilet. Nor Will she wear that lace quite white. Only against ivory and skin does white lace tell prettily. A woman with a poor complexion will tint her lace with brown (tea and coffee are good dies), or with the predomi- nant colours in her dress. Thus she will get the soften- ing effect of broken colour at the edges without the risk of calling attention to her blemishes. A very brown woman, hpwever, may make her dark skin" point." Then she will use white lace, and all colours that enhance her own deep colouring. A plain woman with a bad figure can adopt many little harmless devices—at least as harmless as borrowed locks and teeth, which no one now condemns. She can borrow a little enismpoint from the friendly cotton tree; she can swathe in a handsome sleeve the too thin arm or too sharp shoulder which de- tracts from any lingering merit she may have. She can hide her long, ungainly figure with a short, classical waist; or she can mend the churnlike shape with a corset only sufficient to induce a feminine curve., A thin arm may be hidden by a richly-draped sleeve, or improved by thickly lining a close one. A shoulder too low may be mended by a skilful puff, or epaulet; one too high by a trimming so placed as to carry the eye away from the upper part.

Psekets ONE PE2INY and U ward;.—Advt A" pit-set" conference is summoned to be held at Wigan on April 11th, to discuss whether they hall bring out a cuarlidate for one of the West Lancashire Parliamentary THE UNIVERSITY BOAT RACE —For this annual event, which CAM Off 011 Saturday, the weather wee all that could be desired for the onlookers, the sun shining brightly. At half-past ten there was a north-West wind blowing, but an boar later it had calmed down, and the wat-r became com- paratively smooth. The terrace at Barnes' was crowded with carriages, four-in-hands, coachmand vehicles of all descriptions, but the number of sightseers generally scarcely reached the enormous dimensions uSually associated with the race. A start WAS effected at 12 26 precisely, and Ox- ford having wen the toss chose the Surrey station. This fact, combined with the comparative quietude of the stream, h d a marked effect on the betting,•3 to 2, and in some few cases 2to 1, being laid on the Dark Blues. The Oxonians went cif with a slight lead, but Cambridge equalled matters at the bend of the river, and then led slightly. WI en the crews came in sight at Hammersmith they appeared to be level, but upon nearing the Soapworks they began to pill away, and when passing under the bridge was leading by one length. At Mortlake Oxford clearly forged ahead and won by a couple of lengths, but Cambridge pulled well at the close, and gained a trifle as the end was reached.

'RIDTBARB.—This esculent is very accommodating, as it will grow after a fashion in any position or soil. To grow it successfully it should have liberal treatment, and in order to _accomplish this the ground should be trenched 2ft. deep, and the bottom moved as deep as can be with the fork. On this place a layer of manure, and then proceed with the next trench, alternating the layers of soil with manure. On extra clayey soils it would not be wise to go so deep, as it would bring too much clay to the surface. It may, however, be safe to bring ein. to be exposed to the air, and from the covering that is ' usually put round rhubarb, and other causes, it will, before it is turned under again, be converted into a state of fertility. For small gardeners, or those who only wish to plant a few roots, the beet plan is to throw out one single trench, and proceed to deal with it as recom- mended for trenching on a larger scale, by throwing the soil back again and mixing manure with it. Holes may also be made, and the soil and manure mixed as they are filled in. It faust be borne in mind that by either of the three methods the land disturbed will be considerably higher than thatsurrounding it, but there should be no attempt made to bring it to its former state, as in a year or two, by the decomposition of the manure and the process of sinking, it will come to its normal level. The distance between the plants may be from 2ft. to 6ft., but if it succeeds fairly those planted at the former distance should have every other plant taken out the early part of next year for forcing, and if any are required for planting they may be taken from the same source. If planted the greater distance in the first place, a few cauliflowers may the first year be grown between each plant. There is no part of the year more suitable for planting than the present, or just as growth is com- mencing. Before we proceed to plant we turn the warm surface under, and choose a sunny day for the purpose. We also put warm friable soil round the roots, and by so doing they never miss their move. Each crown should also receive a little mulching. For dividing the roots we have not seen anything to supersede a sharp spade. PARSLET.—SO ES to maintain a supply of this, it is as well to make a sowing now. From some cause, no plant in the garden has given us (and some scores of others) so much trouble and anxiety. Not only has this been the case in Lancashire, but in many other parts of the country. It is most unaccountable and provoking to see here and there a patch in perfect health, and appar- ently uncared for. That which has done the best with us was sown on ground that was as firm as human foot could make it, and We have noticed it do well under similar conditions before. The success of one or two patches , may be attributed to fresh land, but neither will account I for the prosperous state of others. RADISHES may be sown broadcast, and slightly covered over with some moderately fine soil. If the seeds are coated with red lead the birds will not interfere with them. MUSTARD AND CRESS may be sown in square patches, and protected with covering at night. Birds are apt to scratch these seeds up, consequently care should be taken of them. TIM FRONT GARDEN.—NOW is a favourable time to repair the grass plot by securing sods producing good kinds of grasses, and, if a little clover, all the better. These should be cut of uniform thickness, and where I much is to be done their width and length also should ' be uniform, so that when they come to be laid down they fit just as evenly as a number of bricks would, providing the ground is made level. If piecing be neces- sary, the pieces should be placed as far from the side of the path as possible, or, at any rate, no nearer than a foot, as they are apt to get moved from their place if anyone should step on the edge. THE Wnroow.—Greenfly will increase rapidly on all plants that court its presence. We have not discovered any more effectual insecticides than tobacco smoke as well as a solution of soft-soap and tobacco. This may be prepared and preserved in a bottle so as to be always ready. The tobacco should be placed in a piece of cloth and steeped in hot water and, after a few minutes soak- ing, drawn out and squeezed till all the juice is out. In another vessel dissolve a piece of soft-soap about the size of a bantam's egg., to every quart of water. Add tobacco juice to this till it is well discoloured. The mixture will be amply strong enough in most instances. Should it fail, more of the juice may be added. Over this the plants may be held in one hand whilst the other is engaged in lifting the mixture and pouring it on the plant. In many instances the shoots may be dipped.

GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— 4 Messrs Greening (chairman), Broadbent, Jolley, Darkyshire, Appleton, Brown, Kilshall, Mackie, Balharry, Ratcliffe, Humphries, Bonnell, Grange W Houghton, Forster, Gibson, ' and the Rev G F Roberts; Grange, Sutton (clerk), and S Sutton (assistant clerk).

THE ACCOTINTS. In seconding a motion to pass the usual accounts, Mr DARBYSHIRE said he was pleased to see the good order in which the accounts were now kept, and he hoped no trades- man or anyone to whom the Union owed anything were behind-hand in sending in their acosunts —The CHAIRMAN quite agreed with Mr Derbyshire that the accounts were now better kept, and they gave very little trouble indeed. He thought from what had been said at that Board they would have no hanging behind in sending in accounts.—The acoounts were then passed. FISH AT THE wortHstorast. The minutes of the House Committee having been read, Dr MACKIE asked if the chairman could tell them anything as to their experience of fish dinners at the Workhouse.— The CHAIRMAN said he could not give any decided answer, but the fish dinner was going on as usual, and the last account he had of it was that it was highly satisfactory.— Mr JOLLEY said the last time he inquired was a short time ago, and he learned then that the dinner was very satisfac- tory and that it was saving something like 30s or £2 a week.—Dr MACKIE said he was glad to bear that.—Mr DARETSHIIIE 'mentioned that although they had had tenders to supply fish from a large fish-dealing firm at Hull, they had been able to get it from a local dealer, who was a rate- payer, lust as cheaply.—Dr MACKIE said that was anether gratifying fact.—The subject then dropped.

THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. THE LA. FLECHE FOWL. It is a well-known fact that French poultry breeders think first of the economic qualities of their fowls, and do not pay the same attention to fancy points that is given on this side the English channel. We do not mean to say there are no poultry keepers who go in for the thing as a hobby, for this is not the case. Many ladies, such as the Duchess° de Monchy, are just as much fanciers as are the Countess of Aberdeen and Lady Brassey. But on the whole the qualities of the birds, rather than their appearance, shape, and feather, are put in the first place. There is every sign in Franco of the growing up of a "fancy." Our neighbours there have copied us in horse racing and sports of that ilk, and there is no reason why they should not do so in the more innocuous pleasure of poultry breeding by ama- teurs. Still we hope they will never lose their hold on the principle that the reason d' 'are of poultry is to lay eggs and to provlde a very valuable food for man. It , is the recognition on their part of this first truth that has advanced their fowls to the high position, from a profitable point of view, which they now occupy. The breeds to be found there are the result of many years of study and thought, and are not the more result of chance. From a table fowl point of view the La Fleche occu- pies almost, if not the, first place amongst the French breeds of poultry. The La Bresse would be perhaps first if quality of flesh were the only consideration. But it is regarded in France as a delicacy rather than a fowl for regular use. Apart from this breed the supremacy of the La, Fleche is unquestioned, No one who has seen the magnificent specimens of this breed at the Paris Show can doubt its right to this position, and we can truly say that we have never seen a dorking equal to some of the best birds at that show for fineness of skin and for whiteness of flesh. It is large in size, and the aptitude for fattening, with the quality of its meat, at once stamps it as a remarkable table fowl. Birds of this breed often weigh 121b5., and this weight is not secured at the expense of quality. The La Fleche fowl obtains its name from the town of that name, in the department of La Sarthe, which is per- haps the most famous poultry district in France. All around there it is very extensively bred, and a large business is done in breeding and rearing for the Paris market. Great credit is due to the breeders of La Fleche, not only for the perfection to which they have brought the fowl, but also that they have preserved the race in all its purity. There has not been the slightest sacrifice of the latter, and we have never heard that any attempt has been made to introduce foreign blood. This example is one that should encourage poultry-breeders elsewhere, and especially in Britain, for there is little doubt but that in several breeds crosses have now and again been introduced with the object of gaining more rapidly some ideal point. Such a cross is often fatal to a special quality, and hence the breed loses favour. It is not a little remarkable that La Fleche fowls have never become really popular in England. The reason for this appears to be twofold. In the first place, the head of the bird has been decidedly against it. The head itself is small. There is a very small rudimentary tuft thereon, and the comb is horned or forked. The beard is rather long, and the ear lobes white and pen- dant. The comb gives it a Satanic look, as they stand not unlike those generally shown on the head of an un- mentionable gentleman. The body is large, deep, and long; the chest wide, and the legs rather long. The plumage is entirely black, with that sheen which is ever so effective. The legs are black also, the unreasonable prejudice against which for table fowls, felt in England, has assisted the objection to the head, and kept in the background one of the best table fowls ever produced. The second reason which has militated against its suc- cess here has been the idea that it is delicate. In France it is hardy, but in Britain it has not generally proved so. This has been shown teebe true only under certain cir- cumstances. As the Dorking—a native bread—cannot thrive in damp, cold places, the same holds good with respect to La Fleche, especially when it is kept in con- finement. Some two or three years ago Mr. Tegetmeier brought over some La Fleche, and put them where they could have full liberty to wander whither they liked in a large wood. This they did, often roosting in the trees, and under those conditions he found them quite hardy. Probably the subjection of them to this treat- ment would in a few generations make a great differ- ence to their ability to withstand both cold and damp. And thus, whilst we can recommend anyone with plenty of ,space at their command to take up La Fleche, wa can scarcely do this at present for those who would be com- pelled to keep the fowls in confinement. In the former case, it would be best to obtain the birds direct from France, and the extra cost of carriage would not be great. The London, Brighton, and South Coast Railway bring birds from Northern France at reasonable rates, and we have known many brought over by them, in all cases satisfactorily. In their native land La Fleche hens are capital layers, of large eggs. One French writer states that the aver- age number of eggs laid by hens of this breed is 140 per annum, knd the Weight 26 ounces per dozen, or 2 1-6 ounces each egg. The hens very rarely sit, and are not regarded as trustworthy mothers. For that reason nearly all the hatching and rearing in La Sarthe is done by turkey. hens. For profitable purposes this indisposi- tion to sit is no detriment. If the hens will lay the eggs, other hens or machines can be obtained to undertake maternal duties. In breeding La Fleche great attention should be paid to size and to shape. A badly-shaped fowl can never be good on the table, and a small one----if it were possible to have it large—is so much waste of opportunity which might have been taken advantage of. Doubtless the dark legs is an objection, but this is dying out, and the sooner it dies the better, for a more unreasonable pre- judice than this was never known. It has been over and over again proved that the colour of the legs has no re- lation to the colour of the flesh. • We have had at last a break in the weather. The east winds have been followed by a snowstorm, and we fear many sitting hens will have been upset during such a time. If hens are set in a warm place they will not be much affected, but, if not, they are very liable to desert their nests. If they do this, a pail of water heated up to 105 deg. should be obtained, and the eggs placed therein for a few minutes until they are thoroughly warmed again. If another hen can be procured they may be put under her, but if not, a couple of wine bottles filled with hot water will serve temporarily. These will require to be wrapped round with flannel and the eggs placed between, with flannel or felt over the whole. Eggs may be kept two or three days in this way, if the water in the bottles is renewed as often as neces- sary, and proper moisture given.

SUNDAY CLOSING.

The CHAIRMAN proposed that a petition to Parliament be sent from that Board in favour of the stoppage of the sale of intoxicating liquors on Sundays. It was one of those things, he said, that they as a Board of Guardians, perhaps more than any other gathering of people, ought to support, beoause they saw a good deal of the effects of drink. log in the workhouse and in various ways. (Hear, hear.) lie was sure the experience he had had in connection with the workhouse and in that room told him that what the petition proposed ought to be done. He did not see why they should not adopt the petition. It had teen said by some that that was not the place and they were not the people to adept suen a petition, and that they emght to have a publie meeting of the town's people. Well, be was glad to say that they had had a public meeting on the pre- vious evening and one that he believed was entirely unani- mous. (Hear, hear.) He had very great pleasure In moving the resolution without saying any- thing further as to the right of publicans to keep open their houses on the Sunday when other tradesmen had to close. They were all aware that that was not a proper state of things for the sake of the well-being of the people at large.—The Rev U F HOBaßva seconded the proposition.—Mr DARBYSHIRE sup- ported the proposal, and he hoped the Board would not go backward in that respect, as they had signed a similar peti- tion before. He noticed that the petition had been signed by the Prescot and Altrincham Boards of Guardians. As the chairman had said, some people had said that Boards of Guardians had nothing to do with the matter, but he thought that Boards of Guardians had everything to do with It, or at least as much as any other body in existence. They should not go backward, but help, in every respect, Parlia- ment to pass a law to enable the country to do its best to keep holy the Sabbath Day. They all knew that they read In the Old Testament of the history of the kings and the very first remarks about the kings generally was that they had done well in ths eight of God, or that they had done evil in the sight of God, and although they were not kings he hoped they should all do well in the sight of God, and try to prevent drunkenness on the Sabbath day.—Mr BROAD- BENT had much pleasure in supporting the resolution. The Subject, he said, was so well thrashed out that they did not need to occupy much limo in talking about it. Of all authorities perhaps Boards of Guardians came facets face with the evils of drinking more than any other. No doubt there were difficulties connected with that matter, as there were with all others, but be noticed that in the petition there was a paragraph which provided for due provision being made for travellers whe rcciaired the use of an inn on Sundays. While he was not a Sabbatarian in the ordinary sense of the word, and did not think that Sunday ought to be made a day of gloom or that people ought to be deprived of all cheerfulness on that day, he still regarded jealously anything which interfered with Sunday being made a day of rest. (Hear, hear.) All of them had no doubt noticed a short time ago that the subject of opening the British Marreum and the South Kensington Museurn.on sun- days creme before the House of Lords, and that there was an equal division on the subject--if he remembered right 64 voted on each side, and in accordance with the rule in that House when there was a tie the proposition was lost. Well, he was not going to enter into the subject of the opening of museums on Sundays, but he did say that if museums and picture galleries, places which would tend to im- prove, and elevate, and refine the minds of the people who visited them, were not to be open on Sunday surely it was desirable that public-houses should not be open on that day. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JOLLEY moved as an amendment that the petition lie on the table and be not signed. In making the motion, he was actuated by as good motives as any gentleman in that room, for he believed the evils which would follow the closing of public-houses on Sundays would be a thousand times worse than they were at proeent He thought that course was undesirable, be- cause it would lead up to private drinking, and all practice kad gone to prove this. They had heard such places as Cardiff !mentioned as instances, and If they remembered some years ago Lord Winmarleigh got a bill passed for Sunday closing, but how many weeks did it last? It was class legislation, and would lead up to revolution sooner than anything else. It was no hardship to those gentlemen who had their wine cellars and beer cellars to legislate to prevent a working man having his glass of beer on a Sun. day. He would like to see the churches and chapels filled on the Sundays as well as those who advocated that scheme; he would like to see morality and sobriety spread in the land, but he was of opinion that this was not the way to achieve it. Working men would begin to take drink home , with them, and their wives and children would be debased by seeing drisking in their houses. He thought they would have the kinclurss and charity to say that his object was a good one; it might be that he was making an error In judgment, but he thought he could bring more to show that he was right then anything they had brought forward that morning. ("Question.")—Mr. ifurannnins seconded I the amendment. He said that so far as Sunday drinking was concerned he had not seen a:drunken person on a Sunday for some years in the neighbourhood where he lived.— Mr Gamow thought that Mr Humphries had spoken more as a publican than a farmer. All the farmers who had any- thing to do with Irishmen said they couldn't get them to their work on Sundays because the public-houses were open. He should think there was not one out of twenty Irishmen who did not wish on Monday morning that all public-houses were closed on Sundays, because they had then spent all their money. (Laughter.)—Dr Memel, in supporting the motion, said that the statement about Lord Winmarleigh's I bill was quite a fallacious one, as that bill applied exclu• eively to- the city of London. He (Dr Machie) thought that any legislation which took place must always except London, as the place was as large that working men had to sleep miles out of the town, while they got their meals there on the week days, and they would expect to do the same on Sundays. The other statement that was made about Car- diff was, he thought, thoroughly exposed at the meeting on the previous evening, and it was a misfortune that Mr Jolley had not been at that meeting. When considering this subject he thought the Guardians should remember that they stood in the position of parents to about three hundred young people, and they ought to do what they could to remove temptation from their way when they left the workhouse. He hoped that Mr Jolley would withdraw his amendment —Mr Jos, tan said it was a fact perhaps not known to all of them that work was being done in their elementary and Sunday schools which was rapidly closing the public-houses. He could tell them that with- in a month there had been more than half-a-dozen licensed victuallers summoned for their rates. He had as great a desire as Dr Mackie to see sobriety promoted, but he felt that the measure they proposed would make things a thousand times worse.—Mr BROADBENT thought that Mr Jolley was utterly incorrect when he said that the evils they now deplored would be increased a thousand-fold if a Sunday Closing Bill be passed, and it was a statement he could not allow to be passed without protest.—Statistics showed undeniably that drunkenness had decreased in Ire- land, Scotland, and Wales through Sunday closing.—The CHAIRMAN was sorry Mr Jolley had thought fit to pro• pose an amendment. He differed from Mr Jolley's state- ments in tots Private drinking had been spoken of, but private drinking was going on at the present day and they had no need to be afraid of that. He also mentioned that it was not the working classes that would be affected, as there were many young men in Warrington not of the working classes who went to the public-houses on Sunday.—Mr. Jolley: And clubs.— The Qumran, continuing, said Mr. Humphries had said that be bad not seen a drunken man on a Sunday for years, but If he would go to his (the chairman's) house he would show him not one but a hundred, and not only men but women, at ten o'clock on Sunday nights. Drunkenness took place not only at Warrington, for he had seen drunhen people turned out of public-houses on the road from The!- wall.—Mr. JOLLEY said he should not be disposed to think that the Chairman could see a hundred drunken people in Warrington on a Sunday. If such a state of things existed it was a disgrace to the police and to the magistratea who controlled them.—The CHAIRMAN said ha spoke in a general way, In Bewsey-road where he lived tkey could

div.head: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTIGULTURF, to.
div.p: NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- GULTURF, to.

HORSES should not be watered for half or three-quar- ters of an hour before eating or two hours afterwards. The Duke of Richmond and Gordon has intimated to his tenants on the Goodwood estate that he has decided to make an abatement of 10 per cent, in their rents for , the next three years, both to leaseholders and yearly tenants. The farm of Hownam Grange, on the Duke of Rox- burghe's estate has been let at a reduction of about 40 per cent. The extensive pastoral farm of Capelgill has been relet at a reduction of 45 per cent, on the present rent. The Earl of Haddington has given his tenants a reduction of from 20 to 30 per cent, on this year's rent. Mr. M‘Leod, of Cadboll, has given his tenants a reduc- tion of 10 per cent. for the year 1884. ; ' There is now alive, and in the possession of Mr. T. Williams, bailiff to the Ludlow county court, a most ex- traordinary bird, being half a fowl and half a duck. The head and neck are those of a cock fowl, and the body and legs those of a duck. The bird crows like a cock, and walks like a duck. It never goes to roost, but squats on the ground. The bird, which is in a healthy state, was hatched at Richards Castle last May. Paorirtc Ews.—Mr. S. D. Pochin, of Croft, near ' Leicester, referring to a report which he sent last year. respecting an ewe which • had had 13 lambs in three years—five, four, four—tells us that this same ewe has four live lambs again this year, making a total of 17 in four years. Two theaves from this ewe in 1883 have each three lambs this year. THR ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY OP IRELAND will hold its annual summer show at Londonderry, on Wed- nesday, the Ist of July, and two following days. The premium schedule has been completed, and should be sufficient to attract to the historical stronghold of the north a large display of stock. The money prizes amount in all to £1,303 10s., thus divided :—Horses, £455; cattle, £414; sheep, £212; swine, £113; poultry, £57; dairy produce, Ix., £62 10s. EXPBRIMENTS IN CarrLa FEEDING.*-SOLDO experiments in cattle feeding have been carried out by a committee on the farm of Colonel Ferguson in Scotland. Eight yearlings, eight two-year-old cattle, and four three-year- old fattening cattle were divided into two lots each, one having silage and the other turnips, with the same extra food. In each case the increase in girth was in favour of the turnips, and the fattening cattle, when slaugh- tered, showed thei same advantage to the turnip-fed animals in increase of weight. In one case, 401bs. of turnips was given as an equivalent to 301bs. of silage; in another, 601ba of turnips to 401135. of silage; i find n a third instance, 901bs. -of turnips to ?Sibs. of silage. Whether these equivalents were fair cannot be told, as the record does not state the quality of the silage, nor even the material from which it was made. Possibly it was made from inferior grass; at any rate, the results of the experiments differ greatly from those previously recorded, which have usually been in favour of silage Exsmaoa port MILK Cows.—A few weeks ago, the Corporation of Crewe instructed the manager of the sewage farm to test the relative value of ensilage and hay in the feeding of milking cattle, and the following statement was issued on Saturday :—Two milking cows, fed with ensilage, consumed in two weeks 1,130 lbs., of ensilage (41 lbs. per day 'each), which at 9d. per cwt. amounted to 7s. 61; 312 'lbs. of hay, at 3s. per cwt., Bs. 4d.; 68 lbs. of turnips, 5d.; 168 lbs. of oats, at 3s. per bushel, 10s. The total yield of ;milk from the two cows for the fortnight was 1,1307 lbs., and the cost of the food £1 es. 3d. Two cattle fed without ensilage con- sumed in the same period of time 656 lbs. of hay, which at 3s. per cwt. came to 178. 6d.; 420 lbs. of turnips, 2s. 10d.; 168 lbs. of oats, 10s. Total yield of milk for the -two weeks, 917 lbs.; cost of food, £1 10s. 4d. It will thus be seen that the cattle fed on ensilage produced 90 lbs. of milk more than those fed mostly on hay and tttralps, and that the difference in cost (about 4s. for the two cows) was also in favour of ensilage. The farm com- mittee regard the result as highly satisfactory. MILKING.—" STRIPPING" AND " NIETELING."—A good milker never confines himself to either of these modes of milking. If a cow has very short teats and her udder is "hogged," as it frequently Is for some days after calving, it is almost, if not, altogether, impossible to milk her except by" stripping." Ifs cow has big teats, and is hard milked as well, it is almost impossible to milk her except by " nieveling," and a milker's common sense will tell him when to milk after one fashion and when the other. When a cowls stripped, or when her teats are sore, the teats ought invariably to be greased with hogs' lard, or some- thing of that kind which has no salt in it. On no account, if it can possibly be helped, ought one man constantly to milk the seam cow. If he does, it often happens that the cow becomes attached to him, and if anything occurs thtit he is away there is frequently quite a scene in con- sequence. If a cow' shows partiality for anyone, he should milk her as little as possible.—John Nodes. THE INDIAN WHEAT HARVEST.—The wheat harvest in India, which begins in February and ends in April, is now in full swing, and we have not heard of any climatic vicissitudes which can have materially affected the latest report on the wheat crop, issued by the Revenue and Agricultural Department of India. The report gene- rally confirms the estimate made on the 20th of January, to the effect that on over eighteen million acres, nine- ' thirteenths of the total wheat area of India, including Native States, the condition and prospects of the crop were, on the whole, up to the average, and that a bumper crop might be expected in the most important province of all—the Punjab; also that the wheat crop in Rajputana and the Central Indian States was quite up to the average, both in area and condition. In some parts of Bombay, however, especially in the Deccan, the crop has suffered from rust; while in the Southern Mahratta country prospects are unsatisfactory, and in i Kaladji the crop s generally reported to be a failure. The report on the condition of the cotton crop, IS de- cidedly unfavourable. The linseed crop appears to be very variable, but moderately good in most parts of the country.

COMMON FARM PESTS. Miss E. A. Ormerod, consulting entomologist to the Royal Agricultural Society, is just issuing her "Report on observations of injurious insects and common farm pests during the year 1884." The report refers to the ravages of all the insect pests of the farm, and describes the best methods of prevention, so far as they are known. The grubs of the daddy longlegs (Tipula oleracea) were extensively prevalent and numerous dur- ing the past year. The mildness of the winter of 1883-84 enabled these mischievous grubs to get to work early, and they did much damage to the winter wheat crops in some districts, especially where wheat followed clover or rye grass. Hand-picking; hoeing, and the ap- plication of nitrate of soda were found most serviceable in reducing the number of the grubs. • Rolling did very little good. The best means of clearing a field infested , with the pests, however, is by cultivating it frequently I previous to sowing, and so exposing them to rooks, i I starlings, and other insectivorous birds. Of course, this treatment is not available in the case ot clover lea, which farmers would be very unwilling to break up in prepar- tion for wheat, which loves a solid furrow. Miss Orme- rod does not refer to the prevalence of the grubs in gardens last year. Where flowers or vegetables are seen to be dwindling, two or more of these grubs may fre- quently be found by drawing the earth away from the roots two or three inches from the surface of the soil. With respect to the corn thrips, which suck away the juices of wheat and oats, causing shrivelled grain, nothing can be done after the attack has commenced; but the insect may be attacked previous to or during its hibernation by deeply ploughing fields infested with it,,by dressing the surface with silt, or by removing waste pieces of wild grass or other means of shelter. Similarly with the wheat midge (Cecidonyies iritici) and its larva, the fed maggot, the most useful preven- tives are methods of treatment which will destroy the grubs in their shelter, such as the collection and burning of stubble roots and infested chaff, deep ploughing, and the removal of grasses from the borders of corn-fields. Whether the sowing of seed infested with red maggot leads to future attacks of the midge is not clearly demonstrated, though it appears to be highly probable. A very curious ex- periment with wire-worm is recorded. As the mustard crop is known to clear off this destructive grub, it was supposed that dressing infested land with Indian rape cake (which is really mustard cake) would prove de- structive to wire-worm. To test the truth of this sup- position, two boxes of earth were sown with oats, and 20 wire-worms were put into each. The soil in one box was well manured with Indian rape cake, while the other had none. The result was that the oats in the former box flourished exceeding, and were scarcely touched by the wire-worms, whereas the oats in the other box were a great deal injured.. It was thought that the grubs in the rape-manured box were dead; but on investigation it was found that they were fat and well, while those in the other box had developed as usual into chick beetles. So the cake prolonged the life of the pest in its larval stage. This peculiar result, Miss Ormerod points out, should be tested by further experiments before it is con- sidered an established fact. During the last few years mangold plants have suffered from wholesale attacks of the maggot of the beet fly (Anthomyia beta) not known to be at all commonly troublesome before 1880. The maggot attacks the leaves, often nearly or quite de,strov- ing the crop. Thorough Autumn cultivation and tfie free use of fertilisers and salt are the best preventives; but when an attack takes place the plants may be sprinkled with a mixture made as follows :—Boil to- gether eight parts of water to one of soft soap, and half fill ordinary wine bottles with the lye thus made. Stand the bottles in boiling water, pour into each two gills of paraffin, fill up with boiling lye, and store away for use. When required a bottle of the mixture is poured into a four-gallon watering-pot, so that the proportion of paraffin to water is half a gill (a wine-glass) to the gal- lon. Greater strength than this would injure the tender leaves of the mangold plant.

div.p: GENERAI NEWS.

The Spanish Senate has approved, by 118 to 18, of the niodus tivendi arranged with Em..7land. • The work of e ploring the Usworth Colliery proceeds slowly. Three bodies.were recovered on Saturday. All bore marks of having been killed by the effects of after-damp. There still remained 20 bodies unrecorered. A LADY VACCINATION OFFICER.—A young lady has been appointed at Fordinabridge, in Hants, to the, post of vac- cination, officer. She commences her clutV.. ehortly. Her appointment;'which has been confirmed bv the Local Go- vernmentlioard, has created quite At stir in the neighbour- hood. WRECK OF A PAi3SENGEII STEratza.-L-SuPPosan 14059 OF SEVENTY LlVES.—Lloyd's agent at Shanghai, under date March 30th, telegraphs that a pative pasienger steamer has been run down and sunk by the Orestes, of Liverpool, and it is reported that 70 of the crew and passengers were .drowned. . . . . .

The Duke of Connaught was selected last week for the command of a division on the North-West Frontier of India. The Queen has been much disappointed by this poepone- ment of his Royal Highness's return to England, but at once sanctioned the appointment of the Duke to this im- portant post. CORPULENCE AND DROWNING:OD Tuesday, William Mills, a butcker, of Blackheath, whilst drunk jumped into a marl hole pool of great depth, and for nearly a quarter of an hour floated in the water, although he could not swim. His escape from drowning is attributed to the fact of his being corpulent. He was rescued by means of ropes, and states that he has no recollection of the occurrence.

• STRIKE AMONG CLERGY.—From Sofia a report comes that the lower clergy all over Bulgaria have begun to strike ' work. They refuse to hold church services, baptise, or solemnise marriages and burials. The strike has been caused! by a withdrawal of the State subsidy of £32,000, which the Sobranje voted for them in 1883 and 1884. This grant had been made because three years ago the Bulgarian peasantry refused to pay tithes. CANDIDATURE OF Mn. J. IL BOTTOMLEIL—Mr J H Bot- tomley, secretary of the Oldham Conservative Working Men's League, the other day received a request from the Conservative Woking Men's Association of Gateshead, ask- ing him to contest that constituency at the next election. He has addressed a large public meeting there, and his pro. posed candidature was well received. Mr Bottomley has formally accepted the position. DEATH OF MR. GEORGE CANDELET. Mr. George Candelet, the well-known and able secretary of the Man- chester and Salford Licensed Victuallers' Association, died at his residence Cheadle Hulme, on Monday. night. Mr. Candelet, who had been suffering for some time past from dropsy and progressive apoplexy, was 64 years of age. The deceased was a native of Staffordshire, and in his early manhood travelled in the brewing business, the connection thus established with the trade never being severed until his death. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—What appears to have been a nar- row escape from a disaster similar to the one which oc- curred near Penistone on New Year's Day happened on Wednesday on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line, near Birdwell, between Sheffield and Barnsley. Some goods wagons which, on being shunted,." fouled" the main line struck against three carriages of a passenger train ap- proaching Birdwell Station- The carriages were badly damaged, but, with the exception of a rather aevere shaking, the passengers escaped unharmed. lionnintE DEATHS —On Sunday, at the spinning fae- tory of Messrs Rust and Co, Leicester, a man named Lewis got caught by a shaft and was thrown round with awful rapidity, his bead, arms, and legs being thrown off by the great velocity before the machinery could be stopped.—On Saturday, in the Manhattan Spinning Mills, Dundee, Gor- don Linton, 14 years sld, Wee lying underneath a machine ,sewing a broken belt, when his clothes were caught by the moving machinery and he was dragged into a machine, and immediately crushed to death, hie body being reduced to an unrecognisable mass. MAN UP THE CHIMNEY: Air ARDENT LOVER.—At Ar- lington, county Kilkenny, a few days ago, the occupants of a house were alarmed by hearing cries issuing from the chimney, and eventually a young man was extricated from it when on the point of suffocation, He confessed that hav- ing been forbidden to make his addressee to the daughter of the house, be determined to get into her bedrconi by means of the chimney. Mounting to the roof, he entered the chimney, but his progress was ,presently 'obstructed by some pieces of timber, and a fail of soot almost suffocated him, lie cried out, and so aroused the inmates of the house. _ _

ATTEMPTED WIFE MURDER AND SCICIDE.-0/3 Wednes- day morning Benjamin Allen, journeyman engineer, of Ban- don, near Bradford, attempted to shoot his wife with a double-barrelled gun, and afterwards cut his throat with a razor. The shot penetrated the woman's neck, but she still lives. Allen was found dead in a cabbage garden about an hour after his attempt. The two have been living apart for several weeks, and Allen had become distressed in mind and somewhat jealous. Before attempting his wife's life he had made a hole for the muzzle of the gun in the wall which she was expected to pass on her way to the well to procure drinking water.

GREAT STRIKE OF COLLIERS.—The demand made by the Yorkshire coalowners for 10 per cent. reduction of wages culminated en Wednesday afternoon in the greatest strike of colliers which has taken place in the country for a number of years, when at every colliery where fortnightly notices had been served the men ceased work. In two or three instances 5 per cent, reduction has been offered and refused. The masters are acting conjointly. The nurnb-J of men on strike is estimated at nearly 25,000. Several thousand men employed at Bab collieries around Barnsley struck work on Wednesday morning, bringing their tools away from the pits. As a result of the accountant's periodi- cal report under the sliding scale the rate of wages for under- ground workmen and banksmen in the Northumberland coal trade will be reduced by 11 per cent STOCK EXCHANGE SCANDAL —FLIGHT OF A IEMBER £lOO,OOO LIABILITIES.—The Tintes,in its city article, says : —Vague rumours of a serious financial difficulty, having occurred were current in the city on Saturday. Although the matter has been the sfibject of general conversation, nothing more can be said at present than that a member of the Stock Exchange is referred to, and that it is understood that he has absconded, to Spain, if is believed, leaving lia- bilities of considerably over £lOO,OOO. The most remark- able feature in the affair is that no member of the Stock Exchange has any claim on the estate of the absconding person, as he had paid all his" differences " previous to his departure. Those who have traosactions open with him for the account of April 15, are in a rather awkward posi- I iion, as under the circumstances be cannot be declared a de- faulter until that date. -

—,„ NATIONAL REFORM UNION.—The annual meeting of the National Reform Union was held on Wednesday night at Manchester. when Lard Rosebery was the principal speaker. A. letter of apology was read from Mr. Gladstone, in which be said he attaches great value to political organisations and to all efforts which have this object in view, especially at a time when serious difficulties have to be confronted. and when everything that conduces to strengthen the hands of the Queen's Government is of national im- ' portirce. Lord Rosebery explained ' the necessity of the operations near Suakin, and laid stress rpen the declaration of Mr. Gladstone denying that their policy was 4: any sense one of butcher and bolt." In Afgt anistan, the policy of the Government was neither a fussy nor a timid one. It was an attitude of absolute deter- mination to fulfil car treaty engagetnents with the Ameer. Their object was not to patch up a mere temporary truce ' which might not be durable, but to arrive at some per- manent modus vivendi for both nations in Central- Asia. Referring to imperial federation, he vindicated the action of the proposers of federation in not presenting a cut-and-dried plan. MRS. S. A. ALLEN'S WORLD'S HAIR' RESTORER is pre- fection for its wonderful life-giving properties to faded or falling lair, quickly changing gray or white hair to its youthful colour, gloss, and beauty.—.ddet.
THE SOTJDAN CAMPAIGN. THE ADVANCE ON TAMAI.-ARRIVAL OF THE AUSTRALIAN CONTIN- GENT.

SIIAXIM. SATIMDAY.—A. convoy was despatched to tho zsreba on the Tama' road at daybreak, escorted by nearly all the infantry and two sqsadrons of cavalry, and reached there safely. A few shots were fired from the guns in the zareba at the enemy, Who was seen in the bash while the coavuy was ap- proaching. Several cases of sunstroke have occurred lately among the troops, who are much overworked in accompinying convoys by day and in performing sentry duty by night. The effects of the hard work are apparent in many of the men, who are tired out. •

The construction of the railway has been suspended for the present, 'owing to the inability of the military to afford Protection to the line farther than the camp, until after the Impending engagement at Tamai. Meanwhile the railway employ6s are engaged in improving the wharfage acconarno• dation, which is much needed. Strextar, SUNDAY, 2-45 roe—The Iberia, with the New South Wales contingent on board, has arrived here. The advance on Tarnsi has been postponed until Wednesday, in order to permit of the colonials taking part in it. SPASM, SUNDAY, 10.45 P.M.—The New South Wales contingent landed this afternoon, and was received by General Ewart. The men, who are in good health and spirits, were enthueiasticallv received by the British regi- ments as they marched into camp. General Graham and staff rode out to meet the contingent, and congratulated them on their appearance, expressing his admiration at the spirit which induced them to come and assist the mother country; adding that he felt proud to have such troops under his command. The cases of sickness among the troops are increasing. The hospital arrangements, however, are excellent.

DESERTIONS FROM O.SMAN DIGNA. SULBIIt, MONDAN, 9-5 P convoy took out w,ster and provisions to the zarela to-day. Nothing whatever was seen of the enemy. A messenger from the enemy's camp came in with a white flag to-day asking on what terms pace could be made. The answer will probably be despatched to- morrow.

It is repotted that the Amara tribe are leaving Osman and retiring into the hills. It is thought probable that Osman Digna will retire from Tamai to Tamanieb. Everything is prepared for our advance on Wednesday. The zareba is being enlarged, and will be finished to-morrow.—Daily

SITAKIM, MOSTEILI —One of the spies sent out by the military authorities earns in from Tamai to-day. Us reports that Osman Digma is almost deserted by Arabs, and now has only about 100 followers at Tamai. A large convoy started this merning to the zsreha on Tamai road, and arrived there without havisg been molested on the way. The portion of the New South Wales contingent which arrived here yesterday has been attached to the Guards' brigade. SITAKII4, 510101AY, 10-45 I' m.—The Australia, with the Colonial Artillery, has arrived here from Sydney. Ills men landed this evening, and were much cheered by the troops. The Italian ironclad Ancona, with 450 troops and six tor- pedo boats, has arrived here, en route for Massowah. RETREAT AND DISPERSION OF OSMAN DIGMA'S FORCES.

SCA)1111, TuEsav,7.l.s P.M.—Tke intended advance by the whole force to Tamai t )-morrow is abandoned, for at all events the preienr. 1 have heard from-undeniable reports brought to us by different spies that Osman Digma's forces are quite broken to. The Amara tribe, it is said, have en- tirely left him. It now appears that in the fighting at the ztreba on Sun- day week Osman Bigots's losses were far greater than was at first supposed, and that since then his followers have been gradually deserting him. Families and herds have I been retiring into the hills towards the west of Sinkat in , small bodies. A white !leg was lately heisted on our now I abandoned Hasheen redoubts. It seems it was placed there merely to cover the enemy's retreat. Any further large gathering of the Arabs isconeidered by authorities to be remote. Osman Drama himself as retired to Erkowit with comparatively few followers, and unless reinforced by the Mandi—which is considered most impro- ' bible, his authority is likely to come to an end. . _ . _ .

A squadron of the sth Lancers skirmished out in the liasheen district this afternoon and discovered small 60 lies of the enemy burying their dead. From the information furnished by our spies, it seems that mac,' of the Arabs ounded during the week have since died is thi hills. In E tatern fiAnrative language, their numbers are described as the sand on the sea shore.
The Mounted Infantry and one troop of Bengal Lancers left for the wirebs this afternoon. Illy will sleep there to- night, and at daybreak will make a reconnaissance towards Tamai.
The railway will now be further advanced in the direc- tion of Barber.
The Australian troops were reviewed by General Graltim this afternoon, aad he was greatly pleased with their appear- ance And bearing.—Daily News
It was • announced by Lord Hartington in the House of Commons on Tuesday night that Sir G Graham had repor- ted that Osman Digma had retreated from Tamai aid Hasbeen.
OSMAN DIGNAAT TAMAL-ANOTIIER BATTLE IMMINENT.

WEDNESD&Y.—The cavalry reconnoitred Tamai this morning, and found the place occupied by a large body of the enemy. The general advance upon Taunt will commence at daybreak to-morrow. The troops will stop the same night at the zareba on the road, and will march upon Tamai on Friday morning. The construction of the railw ty was proceeded with this morning, and some progress was made with the line under the protection of a detachment of the Guards and two guns. Work has, how- ever, been again stopped in consequence of the news from Tarnai.
-GENERAL GRAHAM'S ADVANCE.- OFFICIAL DESPATCH _ _
The Press Association has received the following official cisaatch frcm the War Office:—

TELEGRAM FROM LIEUTENANT-GENERAL SIR G. GRAHAM TO THE SECRETARY OF STATE FOR WAR (CleSpitned from Suakirn six p.m ), April 2, four p.m. : Advanced with entire force in square formation, cavalry scouting, at four a.m. from Suakim. Reached zorebt at nine a.m. ; left at 10-15 a.m. Reconnoitered from balloon. Enemy reported in small numbers. Weather fairly cool ; only a taw men fell oat. Halted at two p.m. for water about three miles from Teselah Hill, near Tamai. Infantry anl ; squadron of Bengal Cavalry reconnoitered front. Advanced at 2-45, and at three p.m. Teselah Hill occupied by Mounted Infantry. Enemy appear to have retired, but BO precaution against attack will be neglected. OSMAN DIGNA'S RETREAT.

SUARIM, TIITIRSDAY, 10 P.M.—The British force marched to Tarnai, but found the place evacuated. The troops then turned towards Tamanieb, and occupied the Teselah A special spy from Sinkat reports that that place is deserted. Several parties of the enemy were seen moving towards the , north.

Information received on Thursday afterncon in London from Su tkirn states that the success of the balloon was un- precedented. The enemy, who were seen in the morning hovering round the hills, retired as the square advanced. When within three miles of Tatnai the troop were halted, and the construction of a zereba commenced. The cavalry,

in the meaatime, scouted within three-quarters ct a mile of Tamal without meeting any opposition. SUBMISSION OF ARAB CHIEFS.

A Daily Telegraph despatch, dated Sualtim, Wednesday, 6-45 p.m., states-1 wo of Osman Digma's most important chiefs daring the recent fighting have just come ino camp with a letter proffering in the humblest terms the immediate submission of the Hassab and Isakarai, both branches of the powerful Nurab tribe. This submission is considered here to be very important, apart altogether from the rank of the chiefs and the character of the tribe, as tendingto show that the sheikhs have at length been brought to recognise British supremacy and England's power and willingness to defend those who may abandon Osman Digma. LORD WOLSELEY'S RETURN TO
CAIRO. - •

DONGOLA., SllNDAY.—LordVolseley, Sir Eedvers Buller, and their staffs arrived here on Friday last. Lord Wolseley to-morrow proceed' to Cairo, accompanied by Lord Charles Beresford, Colonel Grove, and Zohrab Bey. SATURDAY.—The approval of the Egyptian Finan- cial Convention by the House of Commons gives great sods- faction in Ministerial circles, and also among the commercial community. Cam, SUNDAY.—It is reported in military circles that on his arrival bete from Dongola Lord Wolseley will pro- ceed to Su tkim.
REBELLION AGAINST THE MAIIDI. DoNnoLa, MONDAL—The Mudir of Dongola has arrived here from Meraivi.

According to intelligence received here to-day the name of the holy man who is heading the rebellion against the Mandi is El Makki Waled Essaaa, and his influence among his followers ,s stated to be increasing. He has taken pos- session of El Obeid, and great alarm consequently prevails among the MandPe followers. The Kabbabish tribe is reported to have captured a large convoy of provisions intended for the Mandi. General Wolseley left here this afternoon overland for Wady Haifa, where Prince Hassan awaits his arrival. His Lordship ex- pects to leave Wady Haifa on the 7th pros, arriving at Assonan on the following day. He will embark on board the Khedive's yacht at Assioat on the 9th, and is expected to reach Cairo OR the 13th prox. VICTORY FOR THE MUDIR'S TROOPS.

DONGOLA, TIIESDAY.—The Mndir's troops have bad an engagement with the the Hassaneves tribes near Hannak, a mountain south of Merawi, killing 20, and capturing six tribesmen and a number of cattle. The Mudir's troops suffered no loss.
Lady Woleeley will leave London on :Friday night next from Charing Cress to join Lord Wolseley at Cairo, where he is expected to arrive on the 13th inst. ZEBEHR PASHA.

G IBRALTAR, MONDAY.—Zebehr Pasha, his two sons and nephew, and two other Egyptians were landed this morning from Her Majesty's despatch vessel Iris. Accommodation has been provided for them at the residence of the Governor of Gibraltar on Europa Point, where they will be properly guarded. WHY ZEBEHR PASHA WAS ARRESTED.

A Vienna ,newspaper, the 4' Politische Correspendenz," publishes a communication from Constantinople stating that the Porte has received a very different explanation of the arrest of Zthehr Pasha from that which was publishei at the time. It was asserted that a Nubian servant of Zebehr's sucoeeded some time ago in making his was to the Mandi, aml thence reached Khartoum, and it was through this man's agency that Gordon was betrayed and Khartoum given over to the rebels ; and it is further stated that it was this same Nubian who was the actual murderer of Gordon. 'rue whole vile plan is said.to have been concoc- ted by Zebehr in revenge for the execution of his son, which, as will be remembered, was ordered by Gordon. It was on suspicion that he was the instigator and prime or- ganizer of this act that Zebehr was arrested by the English authorities, and not, as has been alleged, lest he should in- cite the Cairenese to create disturbances.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
ENGLAND AND RUSSIA. THE ANIEER AND THE VICEROY.

BERLIN, MONDA.Y BICIIT.—I am able to inform you that Russia has been disappointed at Constantinople. Turkey has rejected all her overtures. The importance of this step on the part of Turkey cannot be underrated. It will certain- ly not be without influence on Russia's future conduct towards England. The firmness: of the British Government evokes admiration in political and diplomatic ercles. The confidence prevailing in financial circles that peace will be maintained was evinced to•day on the Bourse from the fact that larger purchases of Russian stock were again made by the leading banking houses. Itewur. PIERRE, SUNDA.L.—The Viceroy yesterday re. ceivsd visits from various chiefs. His Excallency subse- quently returned the visits, and in the evening held a grand levee.
The Ameer is expected to arrive here on the morning of the 31st inst., and the durbar will be held in the afternoon. After the conference Lord Dufforin will visit Murree and Peshawur.
- The decision of the Council regardinz the number and composition ef the nsheen force is expected to ha announc- ed to-morrow.
.• THE AMEER AT HAKIM PINDI-I\iPOSINCi- PAGEAN P.

RAWCH., Foam, TUESDAY.—The Duke and Duchess of Connaught arrived here last night. The Ameer reached this place at 8 o'clock this morning, and was received at the sta- tion by Sir C Aitchison, Litutenant-Governor of the Pan- janb, and a large number of high officials. An imposing military procession escorted the Ameer from the station to the residence specially prepared for him. All the available troops were massed along the route of proceeesion. The Pageant was, however, greatly marred by the heavy rain which was falling at the time. On reaching his residence the Ameer was met by the Viceroy, who was accompanied by his private secretaries. The Ameer was much impressed by the grandeur of the procession. RAWUL FIND!, THURSDAY, 7-20 PM.—The first sitting of the formal conference between the Ameer and the Viceroy was held to•day. The interview lasted three hours. The weather is now fine, and the grand durbar in honour of the Ameer' s visit is fixed for Monday next.

div.p: PREPARATIONS.' FOR:. WAR.
