PINDEEs MONDAY —The following regim•nts, numbering in all upwards of 25 000 men, have been warned to hold themselves in realiness ,for Odd service :—Cavalry : Bth Hussars 9th and 12th Lancers, Bth, 10tb, 11th, 12th, 14th, and 15th Bengal, 3rd raniab, Central India Horse, and Poonab Horse. Artillery D Battery B Brigate and E and G Batteries A Brigade, Royal Horse Artillery; R Battery 2nd Brigade, L, 0, and P Batteries 3rd Brigade, D and F Batteries 4.h Brigade, Royal Field Artillery ; 9th Battery Ist Brigade, Northern Division; 2nd Battery let Brigade, Southern Division, Royal Garrison Artillery; and the 4tb (Hansa) Mountain Battery;. total 13 batteries. Engineers: Three companies of Bengal and three of Madras rappers. Infantry Ist Battalions Royal %Velar' Fusiliers Oxfordshire Light Inf4ntry, King's own Borderers, Royal Irish Fusiliers, and South Yorkshire Regiments; 2nd Battalions Manchester, Royal Warwickshire, Hampshire, Scottish Rifles, and Derby- shire Regidtents, and 4th Battalions King's Royal Rifle Corps and Elle Brigade, 4th, 6th, 190, 20,h, 24th, and 266 Punjab Native Infantry, 4th, 14th, and 45th Sikhs, 2nd, 4tb, and sth Goorkbas, and 23rd and 32nd Pioneers.
PURCHASE OF AMMUNITION WORKS.-LUNCH
OF A MAN-OF•WAR.
Her Majesty's ship Mersey was launched at Chatham Dockyard on Tuesday. The Mersey is one of the first fast-

protected cruiser class of vessels, and her engines, boilers, magazines, and steering apparatus are enclosed within a steel hexagonal hull. The War Department have purchased the large factory of the National Arms and Ammunition Company, Limited, at Birmingham, from the liquidators. The reports which have been presented from time to time to the shareholders show that the whole concern has been kept in thorough working order, and could be put in operation, if necessary, at a few hours notice. _ _ .

The Conquest, Hyacinth, Hotspur, and Iron Duke were docked on Tuesday. Orders have been received that large numbers of men are to work at Devonport till nine o'clock for four nights. All the launches and pinnaces are to be overhauled and made ready for service at any moment. 'The arvette Ruby has to be in commission by April 16th. An Admiralty order was received at Sheerness on Tues- day directing ten new composite corvettes. The Caro- line (12 guns) and the Pylades (14 guns) are to be im- mediately prepared for active service. The Caroline can be completed for sea in a few days, but the Pylades is not a far advanced. A torpedo boat is also to be fitted for immediate service.

Although a large portion of the First Army Reserve in to be called oat for service with the colours, the authorities have decided that the first Reserves of the Guards batta- lions will not be required. It has also been decided that the Guards will not be further depleted for active service at present, except for supplying necessary drafts for Egypt. An important communication was received from the Ad- miralty at Davenport, on Tuesday, in connection with the armament of 30 feet steam cutters. They are to carry a single outrigger terpedo, on the principle now adopted in 28 and 25 feet boats, with dropping gear for Whitehead tor- pedoes. The gunnery armament of the boats is to consist of one Nordenfelt gun on the stern benches, and a Norden- felt in the bows. The shield arrangements for the 30 feet steam cutters are to be similar to those fitted in 23 and 26 feet boats.

div.head: BILTIC FLEET.
div.p: A BILTIC FLEET.

In connection with the military and naval preparations for a possible conflict with Russia, it is reported from Ports- mouth that a powerful fleet will be despatched to the Bal- tic immediately a rupture occurs. The vessels which would compose the squadron are now lying at Portsmouth and Plymouth, and are undergoing -a thorough overhaul, in pursuance of instructions from the Admiralty. A number of gunboats, torpedo boats, and steam launches are being provisioned and stored at Portsmouth ready for active ser- vice. The engagement of several fast Atlantic " liners" will probably be followed by the chartering of ether large steamers, which will carry guns, and may prove of great vAlue as swift cruisers. The Russian Government, it is said, were negotiating last week for the purchase of fast steamers owned by English firms, and this fact hastened the decision of the Admiralty. Preparations are being made for equipping the reserve men, who are expected to appear in almost their full strength in answer to the pro- clamation, and recruiting for all branches is in active pro- gress. Lord Carnarvon, speaking in Somersetshire on Sat- urday, gave his approval to the military preparations now being made by remarking that the way to ensure peace was by showing ourselves ready for war.

div.head: ARMED CRUISERS FROM LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE ARMED CRUISERS FROM LIVERPOOL.

The National Line steamsr America is to be ready to leave the Mersey in ten days, and a large staff of workmen are now engaged in making the alterations in her fittings neces- sary to adapt her to cruising and transport purposes. The same thing is being done with the Cunard steamer Oregon. It is understood that each vessel will be armed with ten 64-pounder guns, and that they will be put on board at Liverpool, being sent down from Woolwich. Sir Thomas Brassey, who was engaged on Wednesday in inspecting the transports in port, returned to London on Thursday. The Cunard steamship Umbria, 7,000 tons was on Thursday taken up by the Admiralty, and upon her arrival in Liver- pool from America will be docked And fitted for the reception of guns. The Garde Pee, 1,733 tons, and the Alacrity, 1,182 tons, have also been taken up by the Admiralty. REPLY TO THE BRITISH NOTE. The Central News is enabled to state that the reply of the Russian Government to Lord Granville's despatch of March 16th reached London on Wednesday, having been brought by a special Imperial courier, who arrived at Vic- toria Station on Wednesday afternoon by the ordinary mail train. The despatch was delivered at the Foreign Office the same evening, and a printed copy will as soon as pos- sible be placed in the hands of each Cabinet Minister. The Pall Mall Gazette has the following :—" We hove reason to believe that the Russian reply to the English pro- posals of March 14 will be found to be very satisfactory, amounting as it does to a cordial acceptance of Lord Gran- ville's proposition. Russia, we understand, accepts the Eng- lish zone as that of the debateable land, agreeing in princi- ple that the frontier shall nut be drawn further south than Karez Elias arti Chamen-i-Beid, or further north than Shir Tepe and Sari-Yazi. The only point on which it is possible that there may be some further discussion is the Russian suggestion that it would be found more practic LI if the zone of survey were to overlap a little the roughly defined zone of debateable land, in order to allow for the topographical and ethnographical conditions. It is net expected, how- ever, that the suggested extension of the zone of the survey to Os south of M. Lessor's boundary will be serious enough to cause any further difficulty." The Press Association says the Russian Ambassador, M. On Stash, after the receipt on Wednesday night of the answer of his Government to Earl Granville's latest pro- posals, at once made out a copy of the despatch and for- warded it to Earl Grar.ville, into whose hands it was delivered on Thursday morning. Most of the members of the Cabinet were on Thursday informed of the principal points in the reply, which virtually is an acceptance of the more important proposals made by the English Govern- ment.
TFIE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR. FRENCH REVERSES IN TONQUIN. EVACUATION OF LANGSON.

PARIS, FuNDAY.—A te!egrarn from Hanoi da:ted 27th hist, states that during a reconnaissance made by a battalion of French troops to the north of ll3nghoa a large body of pirates were found iatrenched at Phulan Thao. In the course of the fighting which ensued some or the pirates were killed and wounded. General Negrier is at Langson watch- ing the frontier.

The Minister of War has received the following despatch from General Briere de Lisle, dated Hangi, March 28, evening It is with much grief that I have to announce to you that General Negrier has been severely mounded. Be has been obliged to evacuate Langson. Tne Chinese, debouch• log in great numbers and in three columns, attacked our positions before li-Lua with impetuosity. Colonel Her- hinger, in face of the great numerical superiority of the enemy, and having exhausted his supply of ammunition, informs me that he is obliged to fall back on Doug Dang and Than Noi. lam concentrating all the forces at my disposal on the Chu and Kep roads, and should the num- bers of the enemy still increase I shall concentrate them on the Song-Koi. Whatever happens, I hope to be able to de- fend the whole delta. I request the Government to send me out reinforcements as soon as possible." 8,000 TROOPS TO BE SENT TO TONQUIN. FRENCH TRANSPORT DIFFICULTIES.

PARIS, SITHDAY.—Mis morning's papers express the be- lief that the change of Ministry will in no way affect the international relations of France. The Republique Fran• ease considers that all the groups of the kepablican ma- jority :should be represented in the new Cabinet. Eight thousand men will be despatched to reinforce the French troops in Tonquin. This measure was decided upon last Sunday. The Chamber of Deputies to-day unanimously voted the first credit of 50 million francs on acoonnt of the French operations in Tonquin, The Coca. pagnie Transatlantique has offered to transport to Tonquin 10,000 men in 35 days.

PARIS, TUFSDAY, 7 par.—The Temp; publishes a gram from Hanoi, dated Monday, stating that the p-eser• p)eition of the French troops is satisfactory, bat th tt re'n- forcements are urgently needed to atop the Chineee iota eon.

MARSEILLES, TrESDAY.—Great preparations are heio 2 made here and at Toulon for the emblikition of troHpq for Tonquin, but transpcnt difficulties are probable, as only 30 ships remain at the disposition of the Goverr- ment.

CRITICAL POSITION OF THE FRENCH. Pears, WEDNESDAY.—A despatch from Hanoi, dated 7 o'clock this morning, states that the situation continues grave. Large forces of the Chinese, which are supposed to be under ,European leadership, are endeavouting to cut off the French line of retreat. It is added that the Court of Hue is not without responsibility for the recent events in Tonqnin. General Negrier has arrived at Hue. His coEdi- tion is satisfactory. The population is calm. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—II is officially announced to-day that Brigade Generals Jamais and Monier will be despatched to Torquin. The promotion of General Negrier to the rank of general of division is gazetted to-day. The Minister for War received at nine o'clock this morning the following telegram from General Mere de Lisle, dated Hanoi, March 30, 12 p.m.:—" No attack has been made by the enemy upon Than Mol to-day. Oar out-posts at Dong Dog were in sight of those of the enemy at four in the afternoon. We hold in force the Deo Quan Pass." Nine steamers have been chartered by the Government for the transport of the 8,000 troops ordered to Tonquin. They will all have embarked by the 12th inst. PARIS, TRURSDAY.—The Mioister of War has received the following telegram from General Mere de l'lsle, dated Hanoi, yesterday evening :—The second brigade reached Chu at noon to-day, in very good order. It was in contact with the enemy until two o'clock yesterday. The enemy did not pursue actively. Our losses are inconsiderable. The position of Kepis well defended. TERMS OF PEACE WITH CHINA. _ _ _

PARIS, THURSDAY, 9-15 P H.—Persistent rumours were current to-night in the lobbies of the Chamber of Deputies, to the effect that M. Ferry this morning waited upon the President to Sign tbe preliminaries of peace with China. The President, however, declined, saying that M. Ferry should leave that duty t, his successors. It is stated that the preliminary bases of peace are as follows :- 1. Tonquin to be evacuted by the Chinese tro,ps. 2. France to continue to occupy Formosa until the exe- cution of a treaty of peace. 3 France to abandon her demand for a war indemnity. 4. France stipulates for certain industrial and commer- cial advantages being granted to her by China. CAPTURE OF ISLANDS BY THE FRENCH.

600 CHINESE KILLED AND WOUNDED. PARIS, THURSDAY.-A despatch from Hong Kong, of to. day's date, states that the Prescadores Islands, situated be- tween Formosa and the mainland, were attacked by the French on the 30th and 31st ult, and occupied. In the fig' t- ing preceding the occupation the losses of the French were three killed and twelve wounded, and those of the Cninese 600 killed and wounded.
The Minister of Marine has received the following des- patch from Admiral Coorbet, dated Hong Klng to-clay : We took the Prescadores Islands on Sunday. Details will follow.
liowa Kowa, TIMRSDIY.—The French flag was hoisted on the Prescidores Islands on Tuesday.

CRISIS IN FRANCE. RESIGNATION OF THE MINISTRY. PARIS, MONDAY, 2 P.M.—A Cabinet Council WAS held al the Etysee this morning, at which the Ministers decided upon the terms of the bill to be brought forward in the Chambtr of Deputies for authorising the credit of 200 mil- lions of francs on account of the French operations in Ton. quin. PARIS, MONDAY, 4 P.M.—A large crowd aseembled out- side the Chamber of Deputies early this afternoon, but con- trary to the report current on the Bourse, there MO no hostile manifestations. H. Jules Ferry, at the opening of sitting, presented the Ministerial bill for authorising a credit of 200,000,000 f., and demanded priority for a motion that a committee be appointed to examine it. The Premier ' lin his speech introducing the bill commenced by reading to the Chamb.r the despatches telegraphed from Langson yesterday, adding that the French retreat was carried out in, perfect order. M. Ferry's remarks were frequently violently interrupted. M. Clement:l3mi then ascended the tribune and asked leave to interpellate the Government. He exrkessed his approval of the proposed farther credits, but condemned their overthrow. MM. Duval and Ribot declared them- selves willing to vote for any sacrifices as soon as the Ministry had been overthrown, and reproached the Cabinet with having concealed the truth. M. Ferry then demanded priority for the discussion of the appointment of a com- mittee to examine the credits. The proposal was, however, rejected by 305 votes to 161, amid applause, and priority was then granted to the interpellation of M. Clemenceau. M. Ferry thereupon announced the resignation of the Cabinet. M. Laisant, of the Extreme L, ft, and M. Dela- fosse, of the Right, demanded the impeachment of the Ministry. M. Delafosse demanded urgency for the motion, but the demand was rejected by 304 votes to 160. M. Brisson, President of the Chamber, extolled the bravery of the soldiers and sailors in Tonquin, who, he declared, would know bow to repair the recent check to the French arms. (General applause.) The crowd still continued outside the Chamber, and the deputies as they left were greeted with a few cries of "Down with Perry !" "Down with the majority." . . .

. - In the Senate M. Leroyer, the President, called attention to the painful news received from Tonquin. The sitting was suspended, and on the news being received of the rest- nation of the Ministry was finally adjourned. After the sitting of the Chamber the Bureau met and ap• pointed the committee on the credits. All its members are understood to be in favour of voting the sums demanded, but reserve to themselves the right of demanding explana- tions from the new Ministry, while a few recommend a moderate colonial policy after taking revenge upon China. Paws, WEDNESDAY.-31. de Freycinet's Cabinet is ex- pected to be formed to-morrow. It is reported that he will himself take the Ministry of the Interior, assigning the Portfolio for Foreign Affairs to a distinguished diplo- matist.

THE RISING IN CANADA —BO REBELS KILLED. arrawa, FRIDAY.—The mounted police stationed at I Fort Carleton, under the command of Captain Crozier, marched out yeet-rday and engaged the rebels, while the portion under Lieutenant Irvine. numbering 90 men, crossed the river. Captain Croz.er then again withdrew to the fort with ten of his men killed and wounded. A junction was afterwards effected between the two police forces. Eighty of the rebels were killed in the engagement and the rest are now in full retreat towards the west. The battery 1 of artillery has been ordered to be in readiness at Quebec to .proceed by the Canadian Pacific Railway round the north shore of Lake Superior. The railway is completed all but 70 miles, which distance will be traversed in sleighs ivbich are all on the spot. OTIAWA, SUNDAY.—A detachment of volunteers left last night for the north-west by the Canadi en Pacific Railway. They are expected to arrive at Winnipeg on Thursday next. The High Commissioner for Cinada states that be has received a telegram from the Canadian Government respect- ing the engagement between the half breeds and the mounted police that a detachment of 100 police and volunteers were attacked by the half breeds between Carleton and Duck Lake. Two police and ten volunteers were killed, and seven police and four volunteers were woundd. Neither of the police killed were from Engl. tud, but among the wounded are G K Ganda, A M smith, and J J Wood, from Eng- land.

PRINCE BISMARCK'S BIRTHDAY. Wednesday was the seventieth anniversary of the birth of Prince OVO von Bismarck-Scbouhausen, Chancellor of the German Empire, wko was born at Scl iinhansen, in Branden- burg, on April 1. 1814. Prince Bismarck has been Prussian Ministsr of Foreign Affairs and Chief of the Council of Ministers since September 23, 1862 ; he was Chancellor of the North German Confederation from 1867 to 1870, and was appointed Chancellor of the Gorman Empire, after its proclamation at Versailles, on January 18th, 1871. • BERLIN, WEDNESDAY NlGHT.—Berlin has again worn holiday attire to-day, this time in honour of Prince His marck. From atiearly hour the Chancellor has been receiv- ing ovations. At eleven this morning the Emperor and the Royal Princes arriVed at the Palace to congratulate the Prince, who kissed the hand of his King. The Emplror, visibly affected, embraced his faithful servant and kissa him twice. When the Duke ef Ratibor presented the natienal gift he said he was there to interpret the jov of the German nation at its being able to restore to the Chan- cellor his family and ancestral estato, in return for the , Chancellor's restoration of Elsass-Lothriugen to the German empire. THE HANLAN-BEACH SCULLING MATCH. _ .

- . SYDNEY, SATVIDAY —The sculling match for £l,OOO be- tween Hanlan and Beach took place to-dav over the cham- pionship course on the Paramatta river. The event created the greatest interest, and the attendance was enormous, every point of vantage on the river being occupied and the steamers being crowded with spectators. After keeping well together for some distance Beach overhauled his opponent when nearing the winning post, and eventually won by six lengths. The result created intense excitement.
I RECAUTIONS IN AUSTRALIA. lltfm,Borrawr, MONDAY.—Torpecloes have been laid at tbe entrance to Port Philip. Defensive me.szures are also being t tken at the ports of New South Wales and Adelaide.

Gr'WIRRAL GRANI'S ILLNESS. NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY, 11 A.m.—General Grant weak condition this morning is the result of an affeutien of the heart. The patient is mow stated to have lost the power of speech.
NEW YORK, MOND&Y.—General (ifant's illness teak an unfavourable turn on Satarday night, and he is much worse this afternoon. It is stated, however, that there is no immediate danger.

NEW 1-m4 —TUESDAY 11crumwo.—Genera1 Grant passed a quiet night, obtaining sleep at intervals. He is gradnallit growing weaker, and the doctors informed him this morning that he was approaching his end. The General received the intimation very stoically. SOCHI AFRICA.

QAPETOIVII, MO:MlL—Later accounts contradict the report that the British surveying p4rty in Bechuanaland had been made prisoners by the Boers. It appears that they were insulted and their work in,erfered with by some Beers, but they were not detained. The Transvaal border chiefs are applying to be included in the British protectorate. THE ITALIAN RED SEA EXPEDITION. _ _ _ .

ROME, TOESDAL—Several papers declare to•da-y- that the news of the departure of a fourth expedition to the Red Sea, at an early date, is premature. The Italian Government ere, however, aconmulating supplies and war material at several Sicilian ports. The Naval Department has purchased the English steamer Dundee, and appointed an Italian crew, who will bring the vessel from London. THE CENTRAL AMERICAN REVOLUTION.

NEW Yonx, TrESDAY.—lntelligEnce—wlioh has reached here from Aspinwall states that on Monday the revolu- tionists seized the Pacific mail steamship Colon. The vessel was boarded, and all the arms found on board were seiz‘‘al. The captain appealed to the American Consul, who protested against the action of the revolutionists, who retaliated by placing the Consul and the ship's officers under arrest. They were detained for several hours. A despatch has been received in New York from Mexico stating that a battle has been fought between the forces of Gueatemala and San Salvador, in which the former were re- pulsed.
THE DEFENCES OF AUSTRALIA. SrDNEY. TOBSDAY.—The Government of New South Wales are placing the coast line of the Colony in a perfect sUte of defence.
WELLINGTON, TUESDAY.—The New Zealand Government are having heavy guns mounted and torpedoes provided. A. large mosouito &et of torpdo vcssels is in course of organisation.

div.head: EGYPTIAN CONVENTION.
div.p: THE EGYPTIAN CONVENTION.

BERLIIq, SUNDAY.—It is positively stated that Earl Granville on the 25th irtst declared to Musurns Pasha and Hassan Fehmi Pasha that in case the Saltan refused to issue a firman for the Egyptian loin of nine millions he would send them their passports and breily off diplomatic relation with Turkey, and the responsibility for the conse- quences that would result therefi oat for Turkey would rest with them.

VIENNA. SUNDAY.—Telegrams were recently sent by the Porte to the Khedive in regard to the Egyptian Finan- cial Convention. His Highne.s, in reply, said that he had no power in the matter, and that he had vainly protested against an eventual provisional suspension of the Vihate to the Porte.

CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY. In cons-quencl of the de- cision arrived at by the Council of Ministers held at the Palace yesterday, the Porte his sent Last, notions to Mant- ras Pasha and Hassan Fehmi Pasha to sign the Declara- tion and Convention with regard to Egyptian fin tuce, under certain reservations which were accepted by Lord Granville.

ThE SUEZ CANAL COMMISSION. PARIS, MONDAY.—Tht Suez Canal ConuiliSsiOß %YRS far- mally opened to-day. M. Ferry. in his speech on the occa- sion, indicated an intention on the part of France to widen the scope of the Commission. It is understood that the French Government has prepared certain amendments to the British proposals.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR

NEWTON DIVISION. INTERVIEW WITH COL. McCORQUODALE, J.P. Colonel George McCorqusdale, J.P., of Newton-le-Wile lows, having consented to receive a deputation from the Executive Committee of the Liberal Association of the Newton Parliamentary Division, with respect to his pro• posed candidature in the Lib.ral interest for that division, an interview with that gentleman took place on Wednesday evening. The deputation waited upon Col. McCorquedale at hie residence, the Willows, Newton, Where they were courteously received. The denotation was introduced by Councillor Riot). Pdkington, J.e. (St. Helens), and Messrs C Pilkington, JP. (Haydock), W MitcheD (Uolboreeb P Hall (harlestown), S Weeds (Ashton-in- hlakerfield), and 'Thomas Howard, secretary of the Liberal Association, took part in the proceeding% It was explained to Colonel McCorquodale that the Executive Com- mittee of the Liberal Association of the New. too Division were perfectly unanimous in their action in that matter, and he was respectfully asked if he would consent to meet the Council of the Liberal Association with the view of becoming the Liberal candidate for the divieion. In his reply, Colonel McCorqucdale heartily thanked the deputation for the honour they had done him, and expressed his willingnesa to comply with the request of the Executive to meet the Council of the Aosnciation. The deputation then expressed their thanks to Colonel McCorquodiele, and the interview concluded. It is expected that Colonel McCorquodale will meet the Liberal Council at the Co-operative Hall, Earles• town, in the course of a few weeks.

--- CONFESSION OF MIIIIDEIL.—The inquest on the body of Carles flowaro, who was stabbed on the let ult in a quarrel with Henry Alt in the East End of Lotion, was again ad- journed at the hospital on Wednesday. It is stated that Alt has made a statement incriminating himself, and giving the whole account of the matter. , FEARFUL DYNAMITE ExpLosrox.—A shocking aLcident occurred on Wednesday evening at the New Inn public- house, Treherbert, Rhondda Valley. A young man named Morgan, son of the landlady, was holding over thc fire a - saucepan containing dynamite for the purpose of tempering it, when it exploded. shattering his ann and leg and kming his mother, who was standing mar him. The house was completely wrecked. I A TRAIN ON FIRE.—The Midland Scotch express way delayed over two hours and a half on Wednesday morning near Leicester on account of a London and North-Western goods train having caught ffie at Market Harbor,ugh Junc- tion. Two large trucks of leraw became ignited, and burned 1 with such fury that all the traffic was blocked on b oth the 'North-Western and Midland lines. The wagons were isola- ted, and the fire burnt itself out. THE Q m caves Jammu TO Tun CONTINENT.--Her majesfy the Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice and Prince Louis of Battenberg, arrived by special train at Mai- sons Lafitte, just outside 4 Paris, at half-past six on Wednes• day morning. The journey, however, was not broken, and the train proceeded direct to Aix-les•flains. Another tele- gram says the Queen arrived at Aix-lee Bain sat half•past six on Wednesday evening. At tha express desire of Her Majesty, there was no official reception.

Mrainsn OF • SAWYER.-4 travelling pedlar, named Thomas Harrold, alias Ned Billings, was taken into custody at Horncastle, on Wednesday morning, charged with caus- ing the death of a sawyer, named Henry Cooper, of Whittle. sea. Prisoner and the deceased were staying at a lodging. house, and on Tuesday nia ht they quarrelled in consequence, it is stated, of the latt,q m ,king improper obssrvations to prisoner's wife. Deceased was struck by a poker, and died soon after 'rude.

The people of this country will learn with satisfaction that General GRAHAM was suc- cessful yesterday in accomplishing the object of his expedition, and that, too, with little loss. Tamai was occupied, the Arabs making but slight resistance; and the place was burned by the British, who, finding the water unsuitable, did not think it advisable to stay there. OSMAN DIGMA seems to have retreated to Tamanieb, but his power is broken, his troops are desert- ing him and the British may now go into summer quarters without much fear of his doing mischief. The road is now clear, for some distance, for the making of the military railway; but in view of recent events on the Nile, and in the neighbourho)d of Suakim, it becomes necesiary to ask—is it de- sirable to make the railway at all?

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

- NEW COUNTY MAGISTRATES.—We understand that Alder- man John Crosfield and Councillor Broadbent have been communicated with as to their willingness to allow their names to be placed on the Commission of the Peace for Cheshire. Both gentlemen are borough magistrates, and Alderman Crosfield is at the present time a Justice of the Peace for the County of Lancaster. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—In aid of the funds of St Am- brose Church, Widnes a concert was given in the Mission- room on Monday evening by the choir of the Church of. St Thomas, St Helens, assisted by several members of the Widnes Musical Society, and the St Ambrose choir. Thera was only a poor attendance. The first part of the pro- gramme consisted of sacred music including the chorus "0. Father, wnose Almighty power" and the anthem "I will lift mine eyes," whilst the second part consisted of miscel- laneous items. The audience testified to their enjoyment of the concert by frequent applause. CATTLE Dismass.—On Wednesday morning the Clerk of the Peace at Preston received information that plenro•pneu- monia had broken out in a herd of cattle on tbe new Kirk- wall Hall Farm, Culchetb, near Leigh, and that one of the animals had been slaughtered and buried. Swine fever is reported on the Pendleton Farm, near Clitheroe, where three animals have been killed and one died. The Tatum; for Cheshire on Wednesday show that 29 animals were attacked last week with swine disease, of which 4 died and 25 were slaughtered. The disease exists not at Great Budworth, Little Leigh. Ravenscroft, Rushton, and Wartnington. THE GENERAL Erascrtore.— Ile East Anglian Daily Times says :—Tne Attorney-General held a consultation on Saturday at the Law Courts with the revising barristers. The result was that thirty additional revising barristers will be appointed. The revision courts are to commence at the beginning of September, and the work is Ps be concluded by the end of the month. The regis'ers are to be out by the end of October. The Attorney-General stated that it was the Government's intention to go to the country about the 15th of November. A committee of revising barristers, with Mr Curtis Bennett as secretary, was appointed to gather evidence to be placed before the Select Committee of the House of Commons on the registration question. THE HOME IRON Trans.—The tendency of the Eng- lish iron market has not changed much daring the past week. Pig-iron has not been more in demand, and the de- crease in shipments daring March has not helped to impatt to the market the strength of which it is so much in need. The Glasgow warrant market has displayed more firmness this week. Closing quotations on Tuesday were 41s 6icl cash and 418 Bid a month with buyers, sellers asking one halfpenny per ton more. Scotch makers are meeting with a very slack demand, and their prices are a little easier, notwithstanding the firmness of warrants. The pig- iron trade of the North of England has been in a quiet and unsettled condition, with prices not much changed, al- though eellers are scarcely so stiff, especially amongst the makers. The price of No. 3 continues at 31s for early delivery, and 34s 3d for forward account ; no business being done forward owing to political uncertainty.—lron. You WANT Goon CASKS of any description, or tubs, er timber, apply to Mr. Joseph Anderson's Cooperage, Apple- ton-street, Widnes. Cheapest terms in the tewn.—Adet. A MoNsvae PHOTOGRAPH:There is now on view in the window of Messrs. Garnett and Sons, Warrington, a large photograph of the Ammonia and Sods Works of Messrs Brenner. Mond and Co., Winnington, near Northwicb. It has been enlarged from a negative taken by Mr T Birtles, photographer. Warrington, and, apart from the frame, it measures four feet by three feet; with the frame it is five feet by four feet. It is one of the largest photographs, if not the largest, ever taken from a single negative• in this country ; and it makes a magnificent picture. Mr Birtles, after many experiments, has succeeded in getting a view of these large works which is strikingly picturesque. There is a M 389 of foliage in the foreground, with the works and the river Weaver in the middle distance, while the eye is carried • forward over Marbury and on to Marston. The tall chim- neys are finely grouped, and the trailing clouds of smoke are—artistically speaking—quite a relief against the bright sky. The picture is to be sent, along with samples of mannfacture, to thelnyentors' Exhibition to be held in Lon- don. It has been executed at the commission of Messrs Brunner, Mond and Co., of which highly successful com- pany Mr John Crostield, J.P., is chairman, and Mr Edward Milner, J.P., is a managing director. It is handsomely and massively framed in light and dark oak, and will be sure to attract attention at the Exhibition. We congratulate Mr Birtles upon the artistic skill he has displayed and the great . success he has achieved. Soxs or TEMPERANCE.—The friends of the temperance friendly society known as the Sons of Temperance held an important gathering in the Primitive Methodist School- room, Lord-street, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon, when there was formed a Grand Division, to be called the Earles- town Grand Division. The district included in the Division comprises Warrington, St. Helens, Whines, Prescott Barton- town, Rainhill, Newton, Ashton, Golborne, Kenyon Junc- tion, and intermediate places, and the members confidently hope that the uniting of the various branches in.one central Grand Division will considerably strengthen their cause and further their objects. There was a very good attendance of representatives, and the initiatory ceremony was performed by Brother G Beresford, itt W A, of Man- chester, and Brother W Clarke, M W 8, of Manchester. The election of officers for the ensuing year then took place. Brother E Forster, of St. Helens, was appointed 0 W ; Brother William Briscoe, Haydock, G W A; Brother Jehn Prescott, Earlestown, G Ecribe; Brother John Haws, Earlestown, UT; Brother Harrison, Widnes, Grand Con- ductor; Brother William Anderton, St. Helens, Grand Sentinel; Brother J Judson, Earlestown, F 0 WP; Bro- thers Higgins (Earlestown), Briscoe (Elaydock), and William Aocierton (St. Helens), were appointed trustees; Brothers Thomas Hughes (Widnes) and Higgins (Earlestown) were elected auditors; and Brother John Prescott (Earlestown) was appointed to represent the Grand Division at the National Division meeting, to be held at Merthyr Tydvil on the 2nd May. A vets of thanks was tendered to Bros. Beresford and Clarke, of Manchester, for their attendance. The friends and representatives then adjourned, and par- took of a substantial tea in the lower schoolroom. A public meeting was afterwards held, when Brother W Clarke. M W 8, of Manchester, presided, and he was supported by Brother Boreeford. MW A. In an interesting address, the Chairman alluded in eulogistic terms to the objects of the Sons of Temperance Society, and referred to the rapid pro- gress it had made during the last few years. He remarked that they had that day been forming a district to be known henceforward as the Earlestown Grand Division, and went on to state that such societies were greatly superior to other friendly societies, because their meetings were not held in objectionable places.—BrotherJ Judson, Earlestown, gave a financial statement, showing the present position of the Earlestown branch ef the Sons of Temperance Society. He pointed out the funds amounted to about £5 per member; the society being worth over £3OO, although it had been only established a comparatively short time. They had been able to meet all claims for sickness and funeral expenses. (Applause.)—Brother Beresford, MW A, gave an instructive address on temperance questions, and fully explained the objects and advantages of the society.—During the eveaing Brother Allison, of Widnes, sang " No, my friend, no Miss Smith (nine years of age), excellently sang a selection; and Brother George E Warburton effectively gave a recita- tion entitled "A Temperance Speech in Rhyme." Selections on the "fairy bells" by Brother John E Haws, of Liverpool, were efficiently performed and highly appreciated. A pleasing feature of the proceedings was the presentation to Brothers Henry Warburton and Joseph Hughes, of two beautifully-framed emblems of the society, for their faithful ' services as officers of the Earlestown branch. The meeting ' throughout was of a very enjoyable character.

div.head: TITE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1885,
div.p: TITE EXAMINER SATURDAY, APRIL 4, 1885,

IVICTORIA-ROAD IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WlDNES.—.Read- lags and impromptu speakieg formed the programme of the members of this society on Monday evening. The J Hother- sal I presided. The proceedings were very enjoyable. MISSIONARY SERVICES AT FARNWORTH aid of the Church Missionary Society, two sermons were preached at Farnworth Parish Church, on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. C. W. Wooll, vicar of Ditto, and in the evening by the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey. There were good congregations, and the collections amounted to upwards cf £6. A WARNING TO ne.l3 FANCIERS.—Henry Naylor, la- bourer, Travis-row, apeeared before the Widnea magistrates on Wednesday to answer a charge of taking a pigeon, value se, the property of William Rotherham, under circumstances which did not amount to larceny at common law. It ap- peared that the pigeon alighted upon the roof of the defen- dant's house, and the defendant succeeded in enticing it late his pigeon cote. Subsequently he sold the bird to a man named " Jena Perry." Tee prosecutor alleged that he asked for the pigeon, but the defendant refused to give it up. It was stamped on one of its wings with the name of a Widnes Pigeon Society. A fine of 55 and costs was imposed; total 13i 6d. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A SAILOR AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, Jame Duffey, a sea- man, was brought up in custody charged with stealing two Pairs of trousers, value 4s, the property of Thomas Nother. The prisoner bad been an inmate of the lodging-house of Samuel Pegg, Lock-street, but on Saturday he shipped on board the Viola, and left the house on Sunday without paying for his board. Subtsequently two pairs of trousers belonging to Pegg's son-in-law were missed, and P.C. Smith found them secreted in the forecastle of the Viola. The prisoner, whe contended that he 'had purchased tbe trousers in the United States, was remanded until Satur- day. Her/wooer Y.M.C.A. HISTORICAL SOCIE'TY.—On Thursday evening Mr F A Lake read an interesting paper on "some episodes in Dutch history " to the members of this society. The paper having been read, -Dr McDougall, the chairmen, moved a hearty vote of thanks to Mr Lake, and the motion was seconded by Captain Le Couter, and car- ried.—Mr Lake, in replying, spoke of the importance of the study of history, mentioning that the Free Library, con- sidering the period of its existence,was very rich in historical works. He also gave a few valuable hints as to the manner in which the meetings of the Historical Society should be conducted in order to create a deeper and more widespread Interest. T SALVATION ARMY AT WIDNES.—At the beginni HE no' of the week the members of the Widnes branch of the Salvation Army exhibited great activity. On Saauday numerous meet- ings were held in the Drill Hall, and they were well atten- ded. On Monday evening tea was provided and a good number partook of the repast. Afterwards a procession was formed, four men dressed up in a yellow and red costume, and ridiog on horseback, leading the way through the streets. Their appearance created great curiosity, and the principal thoroughfares were crowded with spectators, large numbers of whom followed the procession to the place of meeting, where addresses were delivered by Staff-Captain Weasburg (Liverpool), Captain Greenwood (Runcorn), and Lieutenant Hargreaves (Bolton). IMPUDENT THEFT AT WIDNES —Thomas Moreland, a labourer, livine in al idwood-street, was brought before Mr Gomage and Mr Holbrook Gaskela jun., at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with stealing a bonnet, value 17s 61, the property of Annie Holden, wife of-the landlord of the Albert Hotel. It appeared that on Monday afternoon the prisoner created a disturbance in the hotel, and as he refused to leave Mrs Holden sent for a police officer. The prisoner then kicked her, tore the bonnet from her head, and ran away. The prisoner, who Mrs Holden deposed was not drunk, had the bonnet in his possessien when he arrived at home, and told John Carrell, labourer, of Dickson-street, that he did not know where begot it. In answer to the charge, the prisoner said he supposed he was guilty, and he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. THE REPRESENTATION OF THE NORTIPVICH Dtvistme.— In response to an invitation Mr Robert Verdin and Mr J T Brunner, the gentlemen nominated by the Liberal Council of the Northwich division, and one of whom will be selected as candidate to contest the constituency at the next general election, attended a meeting of the Runcorn repre- sentative in the Bethesda schholroom on Wednesday even- ing. Both the visitors received a cordial welcome. Mr B Kniveton presided. After the transaction of some routine business, Mr Verdin and Mr Brunner gave expression to their views upon the leading topics of the day, and were questioned as to their political faith. It was then decided that the Runcorn delegates should attend the meeting of the General Council at Northwich on Saturday next, when the final selection of a Liberal candidate will be made. THE FAILURE OF A WIDNES Butapea.—The first meeting of the cre Mors of James Walker Carlile. lately a contractor and builder, at Warrington-road, Widnes, took place at the offices of the Official Receiver in Bankruptcy, Victoria- street, Liverpool, on Friday. The atteedence of creditors was small. The Official Receiver, Mr Glans, who pre- sided, said the debtor's statement of affairs placed his lia- bilities at £50,000, but after meeting these and paving the preferential creditors, whose claims amounted to £7Bl, he estimated that his assets would yield a surplus of £9,004 4s 6d. The chief creditors were building societies, to whom most of the debtor's property was pledged. The debtor had no offer to make. Upon the suggestion of the chairman, Mr H P Escheby was appointed trustee, and as there were not mufficlent creditors present to constitute a committee of inspection, the Official 11,-ceiver undertook that office. The debtor having been adjudicated a bankrupt, the meeting adjourned. The I annual distribution of prizes to the children of this school for good attendance, ate, took place OD Friday evening. The Rev J Wright-Williams occupied the chair, and there was a fair attendance. The report read by Mr James Williams showed that during the pest year there were more scholars on the books and a better attendance than formerly. The average attendance for last year was boys 134, girls 139, in- fants 110 ; previous year, boys 141, girls 119, infants 102, total increase 32. There were now three superintendents, and 35 teachers, an increase of three. It was satisfactory to announce that 103 prizes had to be distributed, an in- crease of four upon the last year. Twenty-four children made full attendances. Mr Hughes read a report of St Paul's Sunday school. There were on the books 154 boys and 137 girls, an iscrease of s'x upon the previous year, whilst the total average attendance was 225, being an in- crease of 29 upon the previous year. The number of tea- chers had decreased from 27 to 24, with an average attend- ance in the morning of 15, and 20 in the afternoon. Lest year 63 children obtained the full number of marks, and in the previous year 45, an increase of 18, which spoke well for parents and scholars. Combining the Waterloo-road school and the branch school ,together there were 849 chil- upon the books last year as compared with 773 in 1883, an increase of 76. (Applause.) The average attendance was 651 —Mrs Kilcross then distributed the prize., which con- sisted of handsome bibles, prayer books, ate, to the success- ful scholars, and subsequently a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lady, reference being made to her valuable labours in the Sunday school. RUNCORN Y.M C.A. CONCERT.—On Monday evening a concert, organised with the object of increasing the funds of the Young Men's Christian Association, was given in Bethesda Lecture Hall, and was an unqualified success. The room was crowded, and the finances of the association will be largely augmented as a result. The absence of Cap- tain Haslehurst, who had been announced to preside, caused much disapp dntment, but Mr T Norman, the president, ably occupied the position, and in a short speech pointed out the advantages offered to young men by the institution of which be was the head. He announced that through the kindness of Captain Hazlehurst it was contemplated to es- tablish a gymnasium at the Drill Hall within an early period. The concert opened with a Selection by the band of the 2nd C.R.V., who fully sustained their reputation as a clever body of instrumenteliets. Mr Moulson, who possesees a powerful but cultivated voice, gave an admirable render- ing of "The Vagabond." Miss Poole, of Widnes, sang " The New Kingdom," and later in the evening' Carrier John," and she was loudly applauded on each occasion, the sweet vet full-toned qualities of her voice being beard to advantage. For his capital rendering of the patriotic song "The British Lion," Mr John Davies was awarded an encore, and a still more enthusiastic recall rewarded his song" An old English gentleman," given in the Welsh dia- lect. Miss N Handley sang "The land of rest" with much power and p athos, and she was also highly successful in her interpretation of the song `" Golden love." "He shall feed His flock," from " The Messiah," was given by Miss Wil- liams with great taste and ixpression, and in reEponse to an encore she gave a eherming rendering of "Angels ever bright and fair." The light and cultured tones of Mr C , Pownall's voice were heard to advantage in the song "Made- line," and Mr R Morris Convulsed the audience with a bumourons rendering of" Mrs Jones's musical party." Lieu- tenant Timmins gave a pleasing interpretation of the ballad " Sigh no more ladies." "Heaving the anchor" was sung with great power and expression by Mr A Fox, who pos- sesses a fine well-balanced voice. A cornet solo by Mr J Woods and a euphonium solo by Mr Outhwaite, performed in skilful style, completed the items of an interesting Pro- gramme. Mies Handley, Miss A Pierpoint, Miss A Tim- mins, and Mr John Ravenscroft acted as accompanists.

Ttet, ROBBERY AT RAINHILL.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, qn Wednesday, an elderly man named Archibald Ellison Sutton, a cooper, of Rainhill, was charged with stealing 2a in copper, the property of Mr Peter Foster, land- lord of the Victoria Hotel, Reinhill. Mrs Margaret Foster said that at twenty minutes to font o'clock on Tuesday, afternoon, she heard footsteps in the front bar. She went there, and found the prisoner inside the bar, with some cop- pers in his hand. He was stooping down. Witness seized him by the arm, and he dropped the coppers into the till again. He had about 2s worth in his hand. Prisoner was fined 20s, or 14 days' hard labour. HEARTLESS ROBBERY FROM A CHILD AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Miry Donegan, 17 years of age, was charged with stealing its 61 from Sarah Hunt, aged 12, who lives with her parents at 21, Violet-street. About eight o'clock on Monday morning, the complainant pledged some clothing in Anne-street, West. On leaving the shop with the money in her band, she was followed by the prisoner, who between Oilier-street and Victoria-road, seized hold of her and took a half sovereign from her heed, is 6d falling to the ground. The complainant picked up the is 6d, and pursued the prisoner, several children seeing the chase. Information was given to the police, and P.C. REFRACTORY APPRENTICES AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn , Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mary Thompson, living in Fryer-street, an apprentice in the employ of Mrs Nary and and Mr Fred Orlando Mostyn, fustian cutters, at Lymm and Runcorn,was summoned for having a eented herself from work. One shilling damages was claimed. From a state- ment made by Mr A Browne, solicitor, Warrington, who appeared for the complainant, it appeared that the firm em- ployed upwards of 00 appreneces at Runcorn, but there were only about 42 in attendance at the mill. The loss sustained by the firm through the abeeo.ce of each girl was 3s per week, so that the sum claimed in the present case I did not represent their actual loss by any means. The de- fendant signed indentures of apprenticeship on the 30,11 July last for a term of three years, but since the date men- tioned she had been absent three months. She had also through carelessness broken many knives and spoiled cen- eiderable lengths of material. The father had informed Mr Mostyn that he had done all he could to get the girl to her work, and that he thought 14 days in prison would do her good. The defendant alleged that she had not been to her work in consrquence of the illtreatment she had received from a foreman.—Mr Browne said that this was the first time this complaint had been made. The foreman in ques- tion was not in the employ of the firm more than a fort- night.—The Bench made an order upon the defendant to return to her work and fulfil her terms of apprenticeship. —The alairn was withdrawn.--A similar order WAS made upon Mary Craig, of Ashworth's-row, Mill-brow.
A "HAPPY FAMILY" AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Seseions on Wednesday Mary J Whelan was summoned for using defamatory language respecting Richard Johnson.—Mr J W Knowles, solicitor, defended. He said that the defendant bore the relations of sister-in-law and mother-in-law to the complainant, and he asked the Bench to ask the complainant to be good enough to with- draw the summons, as the matter was a family one.—The complainant said he wanted the CASe to go on, as the defendant had made use of the language too often.—Defendant expreesed a similar wish.— The complainant said the defendant was step-mother to his present wife, and sister-in-law to himself. On th 2Sth tilt defendant came to his house, and walked straight into the front place. His wife and he were getting realy to go out, and defendant said, in a loud voice, " Hallo ! Away you go, out of my mind." Defendant then asked com- plainant what she owed him, and she replied 2a91. She gave him the money, and after she had done so she called him some " awful names," and asked him for the money that be owed her. She then called him a murderer, and said he had poisoned her sister. She subsequently went Into the street, and called him " for everything but a gentleman." Cross-examined by Mr Knowles, the complainant admitted that he struck the defendant.— Thomas Wright said that be he4rd the defendant say that the complainant bad poisoned her sister.—The fatiker of the complainant said he heard the defendant sly that com- plainant has poisoned his wife. Mrs Johnson, wife of complainant, said the defendant was her father's third wife, and she (witness) was her husband's second wife.—Cross- examined by Mr Knowles : I have not gone to my father and tried to make up tales about the defendant. She took up a black sugar basin that! have had for seven years and threw it at my husband, and he then put her out of the house. He did not throw her or shove her out. She wag not knocked down on the floor or in the street by anyone. She lay down herself. —Mr Knowles said the de- fendent entirely denied having laid a finger on the complainant's wife. She went to the com- plainant's house for an account which had been owing for some years. He refused to pay her, and made use of bad language, mad then he struck her across the face and knocked her down. Defendant had told him (Mr Knowles) that she never did sky that complainant had poisoned his wife.—Defendant was then sworn. She said she went to the complainant's house, and he asked her for what he owed her, and she paid it. She then asked him for, what he owed her. She had reared him from the time he was a child. She had no with to say that he poisoned his wife, and she could not say that which she did not know. I The complainant was the means of parting her first husband and herself.—The Bench said they believed the defendant made use of the language imputed to her, and she would have to find sureties of peace for three months, or go to gaol for seven days. They would take her husband'a bail.

WIDNES PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION :—A CON- ] SERVATIVE CANDIDATE WANTED. "Wanted, Parliamentary candidates for the county, in I the Conservative interest, Gentlemen of means and respect- ; ability are asked to kindly forward their names and addresses without delay, as several divisions still remain on offer. Poor Sir Edward Sullivan! This worthy gentleman was approached with a view to becoming a candidate for the 1 Widnes division, but be has declined to come forward, and . 'he is now covered with abuse and ridicule. The party man- agers and wirepullers are very wroth with Sir Edward, and they publish the following nasty paragraph We under- stand that Sir Edward's letter, which was communicated to the committee, in which he declines to become a candidate, intimates that he has 'no politics and no ambition.' That being so, the Conservative party are decidedly better, off without Sir Edward Sullivan. A candidate at any time who has no politics and no ambition' is a very undesirable champion of a political cause. In these times, to have to tight the battle of such a fibreless individual in politics as Sir Edward now declares himself to .be would be a misfor- tune, while to have him placed in the Parliamentary ranks of the party would be an absolute calamity. Toese are days in which there is no place for men of no politics and no ambition in party warfare. Such non-combatants are far better out of the field. Should they be allowed to take any, part in it, they are usually fonnd to interfere with and sometimes demoralise the action of those ache have the courage and are ready to fight.'—Sir Edward Sullivan is a gentleman who is generally understood to have done the Conservative party good service with his pen, but his refusal to stand for the Widnes division is regarded as an unpardon- able offence, and has evoked the publication of the sneering ' remarks above quoted. The next gentleman asked by the wirepullers to come forward will know what he has to ex- ' pect should his modesty get the batter of his ambition. ' There are many ' it's' about the Conservative chances in this ' particular divisioa, and it looks now as though the needful candidate will not be forthcoming."—Liverpool Echo.

RIORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS: I The-monthly meeting Was held at the Beard-room, Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Thursday. Mr R.Shatr presided, and there were present Messrs- Fisher, Taylor, Speakmen, Pritchard, Lightburn, Norman, Dobson, Williams, Whit- taker, D Once, W H Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (sec- retary), and M Barker (surveyor). leleurcee OFFICER'S REPORT.—The Medical Offixter (Dr Mouritz) presented his report for March. It stated that there had been 49 deaths, of which 12 were due to bron- chitis, If to measles, three each to pneumonia convulsions, natural decay, and dropsy, paralysis, kidney disease, laryn- gitis, marasmus accounted for two each. Two inquests were held, making the total deaths 51. Thirty-five. deaths oc- curred amongst children 13 years and under, and of these 25 were one year and under, making a death rate of 392 per 1,000 of the population per annum—ln reply to Mr Mor- man, the Surveyor said the death rate for the corresponding month last year was 30 —Mr Taylor said this state of things ought to be improved new they had a Health Com- mittee and a nuisance inspector.—Mr Dobson You must allow us to get into working order first. THE EPIDEMIC OF MEASLES.—WIDNES- LOCAL BOARD CRITICISED. The Highway and Sanitary Committee had passed a reso- lution to purchase a four-wheel water van to contain 400 gallons, at a cost of £45, and a mud tumbler cart to contain 225 gallons, at a cost of £2B, less flee per cent. disconnt, from the Bristol Wagon Works Company. The surveyor reported that a.death had occurred in Masculestreer from fever. He had.had the locality disinfected and the Meuse fumigated. The Medical Officer presentedia report on the prevalence of.measles in the urban sanitary district of Run- corn, and also as to the probable accuracy of a statement made by a member if the Widnes Local Board at a meeting held on the 10:11 inst. On reference to the death returns he found that the first fatal Case of measles. occurred early in January in Bridge-street. In that month, there were five fatal oases-of measles recorded in the following places, via.: —Bridee-street, Waterloo-road,, Loch,street, Pennington's- row, and Canal Bank. In February there were eight fatal oases, which occurred in the following places: Robert-street, Suffolk-street, Union-street, Cambridge-street, Loch-street, Regent-et., Heath-road, Irwell-lane, Cooper-se, Rutland-st , Ellesmere-street, and Frederick-street. Measles had been very prevalent in all parts of the town daring the present year, but with the means of information,at his disposal he was not without hope that the worst stage of the epidemic was past. It was impossible te ascertain with any degree of accuracy, the actual number of children that had suffered or were suffering from measles, as he had no returns te which he could refer to enable him to make a complete re- port, and he could only speak of the present epidemic ap- proximately. With reference to a statement made by a member of the Widnes Local Board that he was" strongly of opinion that considering the great intercourse there was between the inhabitants of Widnes and Runcorn . . . the disease might have been brought into Widnes from Runcorn," ills possible, bat not very probable, that such an assertion could be verified by facts. In the first place, it was op-n to doubt whether it could be possible for a per- son residing in Runcorn, and having children in his house infected with measles to carry infection to a chemical works and thereby communicate the disease to a fellow-workman wbo may reside in Widnee, and who in bis turn communi- cated it to his children. He thought that themrobability was that such was not likely to take place, more especially as the Local Board of Widnes and others seemed to take great credit for, and place mach confidence in, the disinfect- ing powers of the gases which were allowed to escape so freely in Widnes. lie could not conceive that there were any serious risks of parents conveying the disease in the manner sugeested, even if they were not to believe in the disinfecting potency of those gases ; and he must express his deep regret that these aseertions, unsupported by facts, should have gained such currency ; for although they had a prevailing epidemio cJ measles, it wee impossible to stet, with perfect accuracy that 800 children wem suff-ring from measles at one and the same time, although that num- ber might have been absent from school. Lie believed that where one child was ill in the house the custom*had pre- vailed to keep the other children at horns for fear of carry- ing the infection to healthy children in school. This might account in a great measure for the large number of absen- tees. Measles were now prevalent in the rural sanitary district of the Runcorn Union, bat be had no means of ascertaining whether the infection was imported from those disteicts to Rencorn or vice versa. As he had no specific ieformation as to the exact number of children who had had measles, he was unable to state the percentage of deaths, but he had reason to believe that the mortality rate was higher than in any ordinary epidemic of measles. It seemed te him that so long as there was free intercourse allowed between infected and non-infected children it would be a matter of great difficulty to stem the epidemic until it naturally exhausted itself as epidemics of this kind nsuelly did. This committee had coasidered the application for the appointment of inspector of nuisances, and selected James Bossons, James Wiidon, Richard Killcross, Samuel Spann, James Percival, and Robert Wilson. It was recommended that Mr James Percival, Church-street, be appointed to the position.—Mr Norman moved and Mr Taylor seconded the adoption of the tninutes.—Mr Lightbare said the report of the Medical Officer proved that the measles had not been so bad as they had been represented. (Hear, hear.) There WAS an evidently strong difference of opinion between Dr O'Ketffe and the Medical Officer—At this point the Chair- man asked if it were well to raise this discussion between two public bodies. He was of opinion it would not improve matters.—Mr Lightburn was strongly of opinion that they should not allow aversions of this kind to pass without some reference. (Hear, hear.) He should be sorry to say anything which would hurt the feelings of any correspond- ing authority or any individual member of that authority, but there was one thing clear that there was a bare possi- hil ty of Widnes being affected by measles in Rancern. It was simply a bore possibility, but the area of possibility had never yet been solved. As an illustration of what might be possible he need only refer them to the dle,..usetvu on the matter at Widnes Local Board. Some of the mem- bers actually saw a connection between empty houses and measles. All they (the commissioners) could do was to bow their heals humbly and marvel at the wonderful pen- etration of some men. But to become serious he did think that no body would have attempted to dictate te the working-man how and where he should spend his wages. This was an age of progression, bat he hoped they had not yet reached that point when a working-man could not have control over the wages he had fairly earned—The Chairman said he happened to be one of the manufacturers at Widnes, and he thought Mr Lighthurn should know that the recommendation of an individual member of Wid- nes Local Board could not be charged upon the Board itself. (Hear, bear.) He might say that no member of any firm, and no firm, bad listened, or would listen to any such re- cemmendation—(hear, hear)—and the manufacturers of Widnes were as muds incensed at such an interference with the way in which they should manage their business as any gentleman present could be. He thought, seeing that the only persons who could take action in thie matter, would never dream of tilting the action suggested, the Commissioners might have let it lie where it was.—Mr Lighthurn pointed out that the resolu- tion was passed by the Widnes Local Board.—Mr P Speak. man said this question of measles was raised by Dr 0 Keeffe and widely circulated in Widnes and Runcorn and through- out the district, and he thought it was only just and right that the representatives of Runcorn should give a denial to the statement of Dr O'Keeffe, who might not have made them wilfully, but have been misguided, or heard something which was not true. It was not wise to allow the assertions to go tinchallengeri.—The Chairman asked who could prove which side the disease came from. It was only a question of Opinion. It was just as likely that the measles were carried from Widnes to Runcorn as from Runcorn to Widnes, but no man in his senses would attempt to prove which way tho infection was carried. It was utterly out of the ques- tion, because people were passing to and from the twe towns in hundreds or thousands.—The Law Clerk said the Board would have another opportunity of discussing this question upon a report presented to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority by the medic arofficar, who had made a statement to the effect that Runcorn was the means of die- sensinating, disease into the rural townships —The minutes were then adopted. THE SHIP CANAL SCHEmE.—THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE COMMITTEE —The minutes of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee contained the following items :—Letter from Mr R B Toft, forwarding copy of a resolution passed at a meet- ing of shipowners, approving in general of the clauses submitted by the Commissioners for insertion in the Ship

I Canal Bill, and expressing their willingness to render what- ever support may be deemed necessary. Resolution, that a letter be sent to Mr Toft, to ask the shipowners to consider what evidence they are prepared te furnish ; . that the law clerk be instructed to prepare draft brief with a view to the oroes-examination of Mr E.L Williams. Letter from Mr Phillips, North Staffordshire Railway, pointing out that the Ship Canal will occupy the present "fairway "channel of the Merrey. Letter from Messrs Grundy, Kershaw and Co, etating they cannot accept the clauses in the form sent, and that the committee will be glad to meet a deputation from the Commissioners- in London. It was resolved that the Nerth Staffordshire Railway CO, the Rochdale Canal Co, the Weaver Trustees,.and the Widnes Local Board, be invited to co-operate with the Commissioners, with a view to obtain the necessary. protecting clauses, and to avoid un- necessary expense and.Mr Pritchard and Mr Liohtburn were empowered to wait upon the several authorities named in the preceding resolution.. London daring the progress of the Ship, Canal Bill, and to empower them to take such steps as they consider advisable to protect the interests of the town. The committee, however, could not see their way to accept the same, and instructions were given to the law clerk to amend the Com- missioners' draft clauses as far as possible to meet the views of the promoters, and that the clauses as amended be spin submitted. A letter, dated March 18th, was received from London agents, stating that as they had had to instruct counsel they asked for £lOO on account of fees and outlays. The London agents also suggested that the Commissioners Should, if postable,, take the opportunity of meeting the promoters in Manchester during the Easter recess. At a meeting held oa the 26th ult, the secretary was instructed to write to Messrs-Grundy, Kershaw and Co, suggesting an interview with the Ship Canal Company when in Runcorn; and also to Mr Lioaker with reference to the application of his Landon agents for a cheque for £loo.—Mr Pritchard moved the adoption of the minutes. He was about to make some observations with regard to the Ship Canal Bill, but it was deemed impolitic for him to do so in the present state of the negotiations.—Mr Fisher seconded the motion. BEACON BOCK.IN DINGER.—The Legal and Parliamen- tary Committee recommended that a letter be sent to the representatives of the Marquis of Cholmondeley asking that instructions may be given as would prevent the destruction of Beacon. Rock, Runcorn.—Mr Pritchard explained that this letter was to be sent owing to the fact that stone was being quarried immediately under Beacon Hill. Mauer ratepayers. had expressed their apprehensions of the re- moval of thie prominent and historical landmark. (Hear, hear.) They bid been told it was not the intention of Years Gmest and Son to interfere with Beacon Rock, bee cause they well knew that the public regarded its mainten- ance with particular pride and pleasure. (Hear, hear.) In order to allay any anxiety it was recommended that a corn. 1 munication should be sent to the Marquis of Cholmondeley., —The. recommendation was adopted, and at the suggestion V the Law Clerk it was also decided to communicate with Messrs Guest upon the subject. Treu VACANT SEAT.—The Chairman announced that he had received a letter from Mr W El Rogerson declining the vacant seat.—Mr Taylor thought the Board lead better let the year run our, and he would more a resolution if neces- serve—The Chairman said it was not necessary to do so, and the matter dropped. PROPOSED PUBLIC DRINKING FOUNTAINS.—Mr Dobson, in accordance with notice he had given, moved that a com- ae:tee consisting of Messrs Norman, Taylor, White, and himself should be appointed to consider the advisability of providing several drinking fountains. He argued that they would only be following the example of other towns, men- tioning that at Warrington there were nine, of which seven were erected by private individuals, whilst in. Chester there were 14, of which ten were gifts. The water at each place was provided free of cost. He thought there would be sufficient in Runcorn, one at each end of the town and one in the centre of the town. The present fountain might be utilized by means of a pipe from the MAID. They would have to ask the Water Company's favourable consideration of the water supply. The advantage and benefit the public would derive from the fountains would quite counterbalance the cost.—Mr Lightburn seconded the motion.—Mr Pritchard observed that last year he brought this subject , before the Board, and a committee was appointed to consider IL—Mr Barker seid he was deputed by that com- mittee to wait upon Mr Selkeld with regard to tbe water supply. Mr Salkeld said they could only supply water by meter. It would not be safe to drink the fountain water even though the glycerine works were stopped.—After sere e observations from the chairman upon the importance of committees bringing to an issue matters entrusted to their GOOD FRIDAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. charge, the motion was adopted. THE SALVATION ARMY, RUNCORN.—The members of this religious orgaeisation sat down to a good tea in the Fores- ters' Hall, Devonshire, and afterwards their numbers swelled by a contingent from Widnes, paraded the main thoroughfares to the strains of music discoursed by tha bend of the Army. An open air demonstration followed, and, an adjournment being made to the Foresters' Hall, ad- dresses were delivered by the officers. " Startling revela- tions" were made in an "avalanche of glory." PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, HUNCORN.—The members of this society held the last tea party and enter- tainment of the season. A good number sat down to tea, which was dispensed by Mesdames Aston, and James and Jabez Stubbs ; and Misses Midwood, Gitteus, Lunt, Agnes Joynson, and Pickwell. Mr T Stringfellow presided over the entertainment which followed, and delivered an address on temperance topics. An address was also delivered by Mr Ashley. The children went through a programme of songs, recitations, dzc, and afterwards took part in various games and'amusements. OAKLAND-STREET WESLEYAN SCHOOL, WIDNES.—WiII the object of reducing the debt upon 3loss Bank Wesleyan Chapel, a tea party toolaplace in the above school, about 100 persons being present. Subsequently a concert was given under the presidency of Mr B Brown. An attractive programme of vocal and instrumental music was gone through in a creditable style, Misi Halton ably accompany- ing on the piano. Pniarrrive METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.—The annual large number of persons bitting tea party took place, a down to the tables. Afterwards the children gave an enter- tainment, consisting of songs and recitations. Mr Marshall presided and delivered an address, as did also Mr Elijah Seddon and Mr Shuttleworth. WELSH WESLAVAN CHURCH, WIDNES —The annual tea party took place yesterday in the Lacey-street schoolroom. There was a very good attendance, and the tables were pre- sided over by several ladies of the cotngregation. Subse— quentlywas given under Iv Roberts, of Liverpool. As the vocalists were all favourites with the Widnes public, the various it Iles in the programme were thoroughly enjoyed, especially tense in the language of the Cyrnri. A number of the members of I the Widnes Choral Society, under the leadership of Mr 3 C Crawford. rendered several glees in good stile. Mr A R Jones (Runcorn) and Mr T Sherratt (Liverpool) ably officiated as accompanists.

These applicants ap- peared before the Board, and were qyestioned as to their respective qualifications for the position. Etch name was afterwards voted upon, and eventually Mr Ward was unanimously appointed to the position. Mr Ward has been in the employ of the Runcorn Gas Company. for 28 years. _ .. . _
