RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting was held in the Committee's Board Room, Town Hall, on Wednesday, Mr W Handley in the chair. There were also present Messrs Simpson, Lake, and Jones (librarian). The Librarian's report showed that du- ring the month of March 1,453 books had been issued, be- ing a decrease of 81 on the corresponding month last year. The receipts for fines,sale of tickets, ecc, amounted to II 103 sd. Books had bebn presented during the month by Messrs T Riley, J Simpson, J Handley, dl'., the trustees of the British Museum, and an anonymous donor. . Accounts amounting to ole lclivere passed for payment. The Li- brarian presented a balance sheet for the past year, which showed that at the beginning of the year there was a balance in hand of £3O 16a 3d, the rate had produced .£173 Is 2d, fines £ll 13s Si, catalogues £4 7s, borrowers tickets £4 17s 21, sale;of papers and magaziees £3 4s 101, received for lost and damaged books 7s 7d, contributions in box at en- trance 7d, total £228 IN Si. The total expenditure was £2OO is 3d, and there was a balance in hand of £2B 65104. —A short conversation took place with regard to the ar- rangement for rent to be paid by ties Committee to the Commissioners. It was resolved to call the attention of the Board to the fact that an underetaneling was arrived at that upon the overseers entering upon the occupation of their offices the rent of the Library Committee should be reduced £5 per year, and asking whether the sum of £2. IN ahould not be repaid, as the overseers began paying rent in Jane last.—The balance sheet and estirnatee were then compared, and the Chairman pointed out that the Committee had only exceeded the estimates by £2. The library had been worked for the comparatively small sum of £2OO, which was the educational grant for Rancorn.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the °Meta, Bridge- water-street, on Wednesday. Mr J Pritchard presided, and there Were presekt Messrs T Norman, R,Lea, and F Rigby (clerk). THE PRECEPr.—The Board passed a resolution to issue a precept upon the overseers for £230 for the half-year ending the 29th September.
S4Z7NDAX CLOSING.—The chairman was empowered to sign a petition in favour of closing public-houses on Sunday._

Tun SCHOOL FEE CONTROVERSY.—Tbe Clerk read the following letter, dated 12th February, from Mr John Simp. son:—" Dear Sir,—ln the copy of your letter to the Educa- tion Department given in the report of the School Board meeting on the 7th inst., you state that the Board 'have indisputable evidence to prove that not only the boy Wright but other children have been refused, admission at the three schools in question when they were by so means full. I must request you to be good enough to give me a list of the names of the children referred to so far as the Wesleyan schools are concerned."—The Clerk said he had acknow- ledged the letter.—Mr Norman: Can boys be pointed out that have been refused /—The Clerk: Yes. There was the case of the bey Wright, the bay Humphreys was another, where the teacher admitted on oath that the child had been refused admission. These would cover the statement if there were no others, but there were other cases.—The Chairman did not think it would be wise to re-open the question, as the Education Department had declinei to in. quire into it.—Mr Norman: They may do yet.—The Chair- ' man : Of course if they do we shall be able to prove our position.—The Clerk : Wo have our evidence if it is neces- sary.—The Clerk was directed to reply to the effect that there would be no public advantage in producing evidence which was still at the disposal of the Education Department should they wish it laid before them. THE COST OF TIM NswBcnoot —The Public Works Loan Commissioners, in answer to the application for a loan of £4,675, forwarded a list of questions to be answered, amongst them being one relative to the rates necessary to carry on the work of the Board.—The Clerk explained that on October 6th, 1884, the rateable value of the town was £51,029 17s, and a penny in the £ produc2d £216. The loan of £4,675 at £5 Ils 8d per cent would amount to £260 , per annum, which would be equivalent to a rate of lid in ! the £. The present rate was 10 in the £, and a rate of ,Icl for interest on loan would make a total rate of 2id re- quired. The Clerk observed that they had to make allow- ances for such losses as might accrue under the maintenance of the school, and this they might estimate at £5O a year, so that a rate of 3il would be the outside maximum. There was no other business of public interest.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Present—Lient.-Colonel Ashton (iu the chair), Revs J W N Tanner, .1 Lockwood; Messrs W Hand- ley, T Norman, R Ashton, Highfield, Aaron, Lewis, Stokes, Hall, W Whitlow, W Whittaker, W Fisher, C Rigby, Mid. wood, P Speakman, Smith, Jackson, Weir, Pickering, Acton, II Linaker (clerk), W H Linaker (deputy clerk). TRE Scuoot ArrENriarrce Coustrrree.—On the motion of the Rev J W N Tanner a recommendation of the School Attendance Committee that the clerk's salary for the past year be £35 was unanimously adopted. The estimate of expenditure for the ensuing year was £75. FINANCIL—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to .£733 Os 7d. Carried on the motion of Mr W Handley. Tars New BASIS or Coutrry RATE.—Mr W Handley reported the result of the interview he and the clerk had with the county justices at Chester, on Friday, with respect to the county rate. He thought the result would be that the Runcorn Union would get a very substantial reduction in the amount of the assessment. THE SrPERANNITATION OF ME. WIIIGET.—The cammittee appointed to consider the amount of superannuation to be allowed to Mr Peter Wright, late relieving officer for Run- corn, recommended that be be allowed £65 per annum.—Mr Aaron moved the adoption of the recommendation, paying a tribute to Mr Wright's character and length of service.— Mr Norman seconded the motion. Be said the total amount the Board could allow by law was £7l 13s 4d.-Mr Midwood Why didn't you give it to me then -Mr Norman: There wage difference of opinion in the committee and we wished to be unanimous.—Mr Midwood : You ought to give the whole amount due to him.—Mr Aaron : If tbe Board wishes to give him the full two-thirds of his salary, the committee wou't objrct.—Mr Smith, after some complimentary allusions to Mr Wright, moved that he be allowed £7l 13s 4d.—filr P Speakman seconded.—Mr Ashton thought Mr Wright would be amply satisded with the amount mentioned in the committee's recommendation, which ought to be ad- opted.—Mr W Handley said there were several on the committee who had not the slightest objection to the superannuation being increased to the full two-thirds. He pointed out that had Mr. Wright, like other relieving officers in the union, been also regigtrar of births and deaths, he would have received about £2,000 more money, and probably the Board would not have received any application for superannuation. Mr. Wright was entitled to the most genercus consideration of the Guardians. (Hear, bear. For a camber of years be had been doing his utmost to dispense relief carefully and justly. The amount of relief given in individual eases was more liberal thee it was ten years ago, but the amount of relief given in the aggregate was something like .£l,OOO, and he could remember it baring risen to over £1,500. This was due to the careful way in which Mr. Wright performed his duties; and if they increased the superannuation to £7l the Board would not be misusing the ratepayers money. Mr. Lockwood strongly supported the amendment. —The amendment was then put and there voted for it the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs Smith, Speakman, Midwood, Fisher, . Whittaker, Aaron, and Handley-9. For the original motion there voted 11, and it was therefore declared carried. Mr. Norman abstained from voting. APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICER.—For the posi- tion of relieving officer of the Runcorn district, 10.9 appli- cations had been received, and the committee appointed. to consider them had reduced the competition to the following ,five applicants :—Mesers George Ward, Thomas Faulkner,

ST. HELENS LAIDIIis AND TEE SOLDIERS IN. TUE SOUPAN.—In connection with the Frincessof Wales' Branch of the Red Cross Aid Society, a committee of ladies has been formed at St. Helens. They are the Mayore.es (Mrs Thomas Cook), Mrs Bishop, Mrs J C Bishop, Mrs Gamble, Mrs J C Ganble, Mrs W Gamble, Mrs Jamieson, Mis Pile kington, Mrs Twyford, and Mrs Richard Pilkington, of Rainford Hall, as bon. secretary and treasurer. The obloct of the society is to provide for the comfort of the sick and wounded British soldiers in the Soudan. Surgeons, flied'- ems, and a certain number of nurses are provided by the Army Medical Department, but the climate and intimse beat causes great suffering, and extra nurses, hospital tents, and comforts of many kinds are much needed. It is proposed to i place collecting boxes n works and public places in St. Helens, and a special and an urgent appeal is made for sub. aoriptions.

POLICE_ INTELLIG WARRTNGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY—There was no business. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Messrs John Fairclough, John Greening, and E J Guest. MISCELLANEOUS —The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with :—Michael Graham, labourer, in Butter- market-street, fined Sc and costs, and for assaulting Martin Noon at the slate time and place, fined 103 and costs; Mar- garet Fleming, in ti lass-house-yard, on Saturday evening, dismissed; Thomas Jackson, in Buttermarket-street, on the 20th tilt, dismissed on payment of costs; Edward Fenton and William Yates, in Buttermarket-street, on the 25th tilt, fined 5s and creels each.--Linaeles Greening wah fined 2s 6d for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire.—Thomas Woods, for obstructing the footpath in Froghall-lame, by wheeling a barrow thereon, was fined 2s 6i, including costs.—Wi.liam Wright, fish hawker, for being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart and driving furiously in Winwick-street on the 20th ult, was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.—David Woods, for committing a breach of the peace in Cockhedge- lane, by fighting, on the 22nd ult, was bound over in his own recognisance of £lO to be of good behaviour for six months. FOOTBALL IN TES STREETS.—Eight boys were charged with obstructing Bose and Crown-street on the 23rd ult by playing at football with a bladden—They were only fined is each, but the Chief Constable (Mr Hunt) said that if there was another similar case he should ask for the full penalty to be imt esetrnamely, 40s and costs. Ths prac- tice was becoming common and most be suppressed. PILFERING BOYS.—Two boys named Thomas Wigan and Albert Kirke were brought before the magistrates to be re- primanded. The one was aged 11 years and the other 8 years. The two raised a window of Mr Mynekyne's shop in Priestley-street and stole a polonie. The Bench severely cautioned the youngsters, who were then allowed to go. CHARGE or THEFT —Mary Garritty. a young woman, was ordered to be handed over to the Cheshire police on a charge of stealing articles of clothing at Northwich,a charge preferred against her in this court having been with- drawn. - TUESDAY—Before Mr C Broadbent and Mr F Monks. MISCELLANEGCS.—James Finn was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge"; treet the previous after- noon. He was a stranger in the town, and was allowed to leave on payment of the lock-up fee.--Arthur Willett, charged on a warrant with neelecting to send his child Elizabeth to school, was fined 7s 61, and Sarah Mooney, similarly charged, WAS dismissed on her promise to send the child regularly to school. THURSDAY—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. MISCELLANEOI73.—WiIIiarn Broadhurst, for being drunk in Buttermarket-street on the previous evening, was fined 5s and coats.--John Samnel was charged with being a deserter from H.M.S. Superb, stationed at Malta. On Wed- nesday evening Inspector Spinks saw the prisoner in Butter- market-street, wearing a coat over his uniform. He had no pass and said that he had lost his discharge. He was re- manded for inquiries to be made.—Martin Cassidy, for being drunk in Church-street the previous evening, was fined 5s and costs.--John Butterworth was charged with being guilty of a similar offence in Thelwall-lane on the 28th ult. Ile was dismissed—Joseph Cartledge, who did not appear, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Turner-street on the 29th ult. A fine of Sc and costa was imposed.—Sarah Webb was summoned by Edmend Mills for absenting herself from work as an apprentice fustian cutter, the sum of £2 being put down as damages. She was ordered to return to work and pay the claim at is a week. —The sum of £2 was similarly claimed by Edmond Mills from Clara Benford. Ordered to pay 6.1 a week and return to work.--David Bate was charged with committing a breach ef the peace in Cockhedge-lane. He was ordered to pay the costs and to be bound over for six months in his own recognisances of £lO. WARRINGTON COUNLY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs E Greenall and J Marmon. MescErzeereous --The following cases of drunkenness Were dealt wit:—John Carney at Pa'clgate, on the 16th tilt., 5s and costs; Emma Harris, at Antrobus-street, Orford, on the 26th ult., fined Sc and costs.--Charles Longshaer was uned IS anu lwisL• s.• ,a 2 •1.. ...pm .1.. c.f. Great Sankey, on the 18th March. ALLEGED ASSAULTS.—Thomas Mercer was summoned for assaulting James Chamberlain at Collins Green, on the 281 h ult. Complainant alleged that Mercer struck him without provocation. Chamberlain was summoned for having, at the same time and place, assaulted Catherine Mercer, wife of Thomas Mercer. Mr P Davies appeared for the Me-cers. After a lengthy hearing both Thomas Mercer and Cnamber- lain were bound over to keep the peace. DARESBURY PE LIFY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.-13efOIS Messrs li Greenall, W. Long, James Marsan, and R. Pierpoint. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF Plo9.—James Whitlow,eof Crow- ley, was charged with having allowed 10 pigs to be removed from Warrington to an infected circle without a license ; and Robert Whittaker was charged with being the d iver of these pigs. It was elated by Sergeant Booth that on the 25th March he saw Whittaker driving these pis in the township of Appleton. ,On being questioned, Whittaker sain that he was directed to take the pigs to Mr. Whitlow's place, but he had no certificate. Whitlow was fined 20s and coste, and Whittaker, who had simply been engaged by. Mr. Williams, of Chester, to drive the pigs, was discharged. DRUNKENNESS —John Bennett was charged with having been drunk on the 28t'i ult, at Stratton, and WAS fined 5s and Costs; James Vevey was charged with having com- mitted a similar offence at Halton, on the 17th ult, and was fined 5s and costs. ILLEGAL DELi VERY OF BRIAD.• —Arthur Woods, a baker, was charged with having delivered bread fer sale at Grap- penhall, on the 19th March, without having weights and scales with him. He pleaded guilty, but in extenuation he put in a note from the inspector of weights and measures to show that he bad sent his scales, abc. to be adjusted on the day in question. In consideration of this circumstance, de- fendant was ordered to pay the costs only. ALLEGED DRINKING OE LICENSED PREMISES.—Patrick Duffey was charged with having been drunk on the licen• sed premises of Eliza Cook, at Appleton, en the 28th Feb- ruary, but owing to the contradictory evidence given, the case was dismiseed.—A charge against the landlady of the public-house for selling drink to a drunken man was consee quently withdrawn. Samel Houghton, farmer, Little Leigh, was charged with not having given notice to the authorities of swine fever ex- isting on his farm. It was stated by an officer that on the 28th February he visited the defendant's premises and there found one pig dead and other three suffering from swine fever. He had on the morning of the 28th received notice from the defendant that the pigs were suffering from dis- ease but, it was stated by a -veterinary surgeon that they had probably been sufferiag for several days. The defendant said that he bought the pigs on the 170, and the reason why he did not send notice sooner was that he was not Sure that they were stiff .ring from swine fever until one of them died. He was fired Sc and costs. A SCHOOL CASE.—John Halton was fined 5s for not send- ing his child regularly to school. CRUELTY TO A HORSE —SAMUSI Appleton was charged with having cruelly illtreeted a horse at Acton Bridge, on the 19th March. A fine of 53 sad costs was imposed, or in default seven days. APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS —The following overseers were appointed for the ensuing year :—Acton Grange, Messrs Thomas Hewitt and John Basnett ; Antrobus, Messrs James Egertnn and Joseigh W Boardman; Appleton, Messrs John Derbyshire and Huila Derbyshire ; Partington, Messrs James Lowe and W it Clarke ' • Daresbury, Messrs R T Lowe and C W Phillips ; Dott°l:l' Messrs John Campkin and John Smith ; Grappenball; Messrs W Bradford and W Thrhyshire • Hatton, Messrs T Robinson and T Littlemore; Eeckwick, 'lllessrs J Bennett and S Done; Latchford, Messrs W Dutton and W Pierpoint • Little Leigh, Messrs Horton and J H Seeley; Moore, Mess' s 1:1 Hayes and W Jackson ; New:on-by-Daresbnry, Messrs P Derbyshire and T Dutton ; Preston-o'gle-Hill, Messrs J Spruce and H T Whitlow ; Sevenoaks, Messrs J Frith and W Clarke ; Stret- ton, Messrs J Smith and T Hewitt ; Walton Inferior, Messrs J Muskett and P Shearer; Whitley Inferior, Messrs P N Rutter and C Moontfield ; Whitley Superior, Messrs R Fairhurst and J Owen. WIDNES POLICE COURT. Moue:PAL—Before Mr J Brock. DeataexzeneEss —The following persons were fined for this offence :—Thomas Evans, James Fitzgerald, Ann Bell, Woo Burns (18th appearance), Patrick Lennon (16th ap- pearance), John Brophy, and Mary Tyson. WEDSlEsphol.—Before Mr Holbrook Ciaskell, sen., Mr H Craekell, jun., and Mr J Brock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Edward Roberts, John Ball, and Pat- rick Satter were each fined for drunkenness.—Margaret Roberts, for committing a breach of the peace in Terrace- street. and Patrick Murphy, in Vine-street, were each bound bound over lobe or - gone.. behviour.—Charles Howard, for allowing the chimney of Ids dwelling-house in Lee-street to be on fire, was fined ss.—Michael Ford. Richard Park-Moths, and James Howard were ech fined 2s 61 and costs for throwing stones in Walmsley-street and Wareine,-street re- spectively:

FUDIOIIS DRIVING —James Pemberton, mineral water manufacturer, was charged with furious driving.—P.C. Guineas stated that on the 23rd ult the defendant was gal- loping a horse at a furious rate along Albert-road.—P.C. Oldrnan corroborated.—Walter Pemberton said the animal took fright at some rags on a donkey cart. The defendatt did not use the whip.—The defendant alleged that the horse " shied "at anything, and on the occasion in question only galloped 25 yards.—The defendant was ordered to pay costs 756. WIDNES Scrroot BOARD AT Wortz.—For neglecting to send their children regularly to school the following persons were each fined 5s :—Samuel Booth, Hy Burgess, Michael Mare, Archibald Sullivan, James Kelly, Thomas Roach, John Treacy, James Simpson, Mathew Connor, Michael Wallace, Robert Hoey, Patrick Caine, Peter McLoughlin, Win Fallow, and John Keenceghan.—Mr U H Danby prose- cuted on behalf of the School Board. SLEEPING O.—James McCormick. a lad, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for sleeping in Hutchinson's chemical works on the previous night.

MONDAY.—Before Captain C W Hazlehurst and Mr James Handley.

hirscEstiosEous.-;-:Arnold Unsworth was lined 61 and costs 9s 6J, for having the chimney of his dwelling-house in High-street on fire on the 25th March.—William Light- foot and Thomas Roberts were each fined Sc on a summons by the Aston United District for neglecting to send their children regularly to school.----Gilbert Ball, a seaman, was charged ,vith being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Finney. On Saturday night the prisoner was arrested in Church-street for drunkenness and disorderly behaviour, and whilst in custody he kicked the officer in a most violent manner.—He was ordered to pay a 6s 4d, or go to gaol for

14 days. TTIESDAY.—Before CAptain C W Hazleburst. DISORDERLY CONDI:XT.—Wm Brown, a seaman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly In Bridge-street on the previous night. In company with another sailor the prisoner had created a disturbance, during which the large shop window of Mr Dobson, butcker, Church-street, was smashed. The prisoner's companion escaped.—A fine of 5s and costs 5s 44 was imposed.

THE ODDFELLOWS' SOCIETY AND us BENEFITS. IMPORTANT CASE. A case of considerable importance to members of lodges in connection with the Independent Order of Oddfellows was heard at Newton Petty Sessions, held at the Town Hall on Saturday, when a Mrs Ann Unsworth sought to recover the sum of £3 12s from James Hankicson, secretary of the Earl of Wilton Lodge of the Independent Order of Odd- fellows, held at the Joiners' Arms Inn, Southworth-with- Croft, an amount alleged to be due under the rules of the society. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs R Houghton (in the ;hair), T J Gillespie, C Pilkington, and A C McCorquodale. The defendant was represented by Mr Jenkins. solicitor, Warrington, and Mr J C Sutton, clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians, watched the case on behalf of that body.—On the case being called Mr Sutton rose and said he had an application to make in reference to that case —Mr Jenkins objected to the appearance of Mr Sutton in any capacity whatever. Mr Sutton was net en- titled to make any remark in the case.—Mr Sutton said he was not proposing to do so. His application was, if the Bench would be good enough to hear him, that in a matter in which the Board of Guardians were concerned—Mr Jenkins (interposing): I object to Mr Sutton making any remarks which may tend to prejudice my case. He has no right whatever in this prosecution to utter one word.—Mr Sutton said he appeared to make an application on behalf of the Guardians for a summons or an order, as the clerk of the court might direct ; and he maintained that the appli- cation must be listened to.—Mr Jenkins : Why can't Mr Sutton wait until this case is heard before making his ap- plication ? I say he has no right to address the court until this case has been gone into.—Mr Sutton said it was import- ant that the Court should hear what he had got to say be- fore the case was heard.—The Clerk remarked that accord- ing to the statute only a solicitor was entitled to appear there. —Mr Sutton replied that the law did not say anything of the kind. The Clerk said the proper course was to appear by solicitor.— The complainant, Ann Unsworth, was then called. She said she lived at Southworth-with-Croft. She was the wife of Cornelius Unsworth.—Mr Jenkins : I admit everything except the liability of the society.—After some conversation it was decided that as the facts were admitted Mr Jenkins should address the court on behalf of the defendant.—Mr Jenkins said the society relied for their defence upon sec- tion 5 of the Friendly Society's Act, 1875. It appeared that Cornelius Unsworth become a member of that society so far back as the year 1865, when he was 20 years of age. He appeared to have remained a member for .several years' and a printed copy of rules was handed to him. Rule 22 read as follows :—" Members becoming chargeable to the parish. If any member beloneeng to this lodge becomes chargeable to the parish, and be sent to the workhouse, his benefit and contributions shall cease until he leaves the workhouse; he must give notice in the space of six days to the secretary of the lodge he belongs to of his intention to commence his contributions, or he will not be considered a member any longee. Such contributions to commence from the day he leaves the workhouse." It had nothing to do with him (Mr Jenkins) whether or not the rule was a hardship. It was a rule, and all the members were bound by it. When the rule was framed it was intended to be ayr ise deterrent against members becoming paupers, but whether it had worked well or not was nothing to do with the court. He submitted that every member was bound by it as a rule. After being a member for some years Unsworth ceased for a short time. In the year 1871 he was again admitted a member. Down to the time when he became unfortunately eie e NV,..“.l.aLuu melon tie remained a member of the society, kept up his contribu- tions, and participated in its benefit. It seemed to have been conceived at some occasion that the rules were drawn samewhat harshly, and in the year 1879 the society took seriously into consideration whether it was not desirable that some amendment should be made in the construction of the rules. A meeting was accordingly called, and in keep- ing with the rules it was held on the 15th March, 1879, at which, according to the minute book, it was unani- mously agreed that a new code of rules should be adopted, printed, and registered. The rules were drawn up, but two copies only were printed. 150 copies were ordered, but on the rules being sent to the Registrar of Friendly Societies, the authorities had some objJction to the constructios of some of the rules, and he declined to regis- ter them. They had consequently never been registered op to the present time, so that the old rules were still ia exist- ence and force. Cornelius Unsworth became a member of the society under them, and it was the practice of the lodge when a new member was elected to band to him a copy of the old rules, which were used in their integrity. He cue- tended that when Unsworth joined the society he became bound by the 22nd rule, which, as he had read, debarred him or anyone else recovering any of the benefits if they had become paupers or pauper lunatics, which was included in the term.—James Hankinson, the defendant, was then called. He said he was the secretary of the Earl of Wilton lodge of Oddfellows. He had been a member for over 20 years, and had been the secretary for 15 or 16 years past. He produced the minute book, from which it appeared that Mr Unsworth was a member for seven years, when he ceased to be a member. Ile again joined the lodge. The present rules were then in existence, and he was supplied with a copy. They contemplated having new rules, and they were sent to London, but the Registrar refused to re- gister:them. He bad recently received communications from Mr J C Sutton, clerk to the Board of Guardians, and Mr Caldwell, relieving officer, Newton, stating that Corne- lius Unsworth had been removed to Rainhill Asylum, and claiming for his maintenance four weeks' club money, £1 12s, leas sulycriptions. The Clerk: Lid he go to the Workhouse ? Mrs. Unsworth (complain- ant) : No, sir. —Mr Sutton : He has never been there.—The Clerk : The objects of the society are stated to be, to render assistance to members who are sick and not able to follow their employment. This man is really not able to follow his employment.— Mr Jenkins mid that was the primary object, but it was qealified by rules 22. As a matter of fact he was told that every lunatic pissed through the workhouse.—Mr Sut- toa : Oh no, no.—Mr Jenkins asked the magistrates to take a common sense view of the case. He asked what had been the rule with regard to persons who had become pau- pers, or who had been in receipt of relief. Had the society stopped off their benefits ?—James Hankinson (secretary) : We never had a case like this. This is the first case and it i 3 a test case.—Mr Jenkins : What would be the effect in your society if you were bound to carry out the rules for the benefit of persons who became paupers P—Mr Hankin- son said they would have to stop the society as the money would cease.—James Dickson, one of the trustees, and an old member of the lodge gave corroborative evidence.—The Chairman : Was there a resolution passed to go on with the oil rules after the registrar refused to register the pro- posed new rules P—Mr. Jenkins : That would not be necessary. The very fact of the new rules not being regis- terred was sufficient—Mr Jenkins then stated that that concluded the case, and Mr Sutton asked the Bench to hear his application bet ore giving their decision.-Mr Jenkins opposed the application, and the Bench stated that accord- ing to the rule they could not make an order for the pay- ment of the money.—Mr Jenkins said the case had not been defended with any unkindness towards Mrs Unsworth. the members personally were wishful to do all they could for her, but if the Bench had decided that ths rule was worthless the society could not have been carried on.—The Clerk:. Than it must have been wound tp.—The Chair. man , It is to be hoped the membeys will show their kind. uses and sympathy for Mrs Unsworth.—Mr './enkinson : I cm assure you they will. Mr Sutton then made his application for a summons against the society for the recovery of £ll2e, towards the cost of maintaining Cornelius Uniiworth in Rainhill Lunatic Asylum. In a lengthy address be urged that the old rules of the society had been revoked by resolutiOn and that new rules were adopted. It was not necessary that thg rules should be submitted and registered; and it had recently been decided in the superior courts that it did not matter whether they were registered or not. In the 22nd rule of the society it was stated that members should cease to re- ceive any of the benefits if they were admitted to the Work- house, but a lunatic asylum was a hospital and not a work- house. It was a place provided by law for the cure of sick- ness, where medical men and nerses were kept.—The Chair- man here interposed, and remarked that the Bench were willing to grant a summons and the case could be better argued when it came on for hearing.—Mr Sutton: Lam quite content.—Mr Jenkins : I am willing to meet .Mr Sutton that the thing may be argued out in any possible way.

wards. Newton—a Lane (captain), back; S Rimmer, Aga, and J Boardman, three-quarter backs; W Lane and T Egan, jun., half backs; P 'Thompson, J Naylor, U Willis, T Egan, sen., T Fairclougb, H Liptrott, It Hitchens, A Latimer, and A Lane, forwards. RUNCORN OLD BOYS V. MOSS BANK WHITE STAR (Winnss).—This return engagement took place on the ground of the former club on Saturday afternoon. The game was both a pleasant and a fast one. During the first half nothing was scored by either side, but in the second the home team succeeded in making one try (by A.hrams) and six minor points to the visitors nil. The conduct and play of the visitors cannot be spoken of too highly. The teams were as follows :—Old Boys : Full back, W Wish- lade •, three-quarter backs, W Knight, F Harvey, and W Tickle ; half backs, S Abrams and B Williamson ; forwards, W Stubbs, D Knight, W E C Harvey, T Knight, J Prince, J Layland, J Steele, W Catterall, and E Howard. Umpire, J Shaw. Moss Bank : Full back, Bethlows ; three-quarter backs, Flinn, BoylS, and Minton ; half backs, Devitt and Barker; forwards, Murty, Lomax, Crosby, Hoyle, McKeowis, Atherton, Eastwood, Wailing and Collins. Umpire, H Bennett. WIDNES V WEIINETH (2ND TEAM.)—The return match between the above-named clubs was played at Werneth, on Saturday. Widnes turned up with only 13 men, but they were assisted by Robinson, of,tts Warrington F.C. Wer- neth was successful in obtaining the lead, and Wright kicked off against a strong wind. The visitors were de- clared the victors by one goal one try to Werneth one try and one minor point. For the winners Johnson and Brazen- dale behind, and Robinson, Cowfield, and Sampson forward, showed grand form, and the best for Werneth were Mills and Crompton behind, and Shortridge and Gardner forward. The teams were composed as follows :—Widnes : Penning- ton, full back ; Brazendale, Oakden, and Stirrup, three- quarter-backs; Johnson and Chrimes, half-backs ; Rob- inson, Wright, Davies, Cowfield, Hartley, Sampson, Currie. and Begdvrood, forwards. Werneth : Buckley, full back ; Crompton. Palmer, and Mayers, three-quarter backs ; Mills and Wilson, half-backs ; Hankinson, McLeod, J Andrews, Shortridge, Ripley, Gardner, W Andrews, Stockwell, and Winnurst, forwards.

.11r-wcons V. Asistru. (SxcoNn TEAMS).—These second teams met at Runcorn on Saturday, when a large gathering of spectators watched a capital game and as both teams possess some very promising players, the match was as good as was anticipated. A quick game resulted in a W)Il for Runcorn by one goal, two tries, two minor points to ene touch in goal. On the Runcorn side P Riley played a safe back game. At three-quarters, W Riley and Lunt played a good game, and Ford, Cox, Raffe, and Dunbavand did a lot of hard work in the pack, being well backed by Andrews and Clarke. For Aspull, Johnson, Freeman and Fudge behind, Grundy, Seddon, Lindsay, and Barns in Le forwards did a lot of work. Teams :—Runcorn : Riley, back; W Riley, E Lunt, and 11 Cawley, three-quarter backs; G Whitby and Antrobus, half-backs ; J B Clarke, W Dun- i bavand, J Gittens, E Andrews, J Ford, Raffe, J Snowball, T Abrams, and T Cox, forwards. Aspull: R Johnson, back; A Johnson, .1 Freeman, and Tudge' three-quarter backs Hulme and Taylor. half-backs; B Seddon, J Lindsay, G Lindsay, G Bond, J Bond, J Burns, 1' Marsh, J Westhead, and J Grundy, forwards. Limn v. SALE.,—Two "A " teams of these clubs met at Lymm on Saturday, in the presence of 200 spectators. The game was not commenced until four o'clock, when Kirk, having lost the toss, put the ball in motion. The forwards, following well up, prevented the return being made. The play in the first half was principally carried OR in the Sale quarters, the home team scoring one try (got by Chantler) and four minor points to nil'. After the usual interval, Lingo kicked off for Sale. The home team in this half outplayed their opponents at every point of the game, scoring three tries, one each by the Brothers Kirk and J Holt. At the call of no side the home team were found to be the winners of a very one-sided game by four tries and eight minors to one try (Hargreaves). For the home team Bolt at full back only touched the ball once. P Holt was the best of the three-quarters, although Clarke played well ; the fa- mous wingman, Gleave, put in Borne good runs and kicks. The two halves, Chantler and S Holt, dribbled and tackled splendidly. The passing of the former was also very good. bolt's weakest point is his passing. If they would pass more the Lymm team would have in Chantler and Holt two fine half backs, both being very young, Chantler only 18 years of age. The play of the home team forwards was a treat to witness, their dribbling and tackling being very good. Hargreaves, Allen, and Walters played well for the losers.

EARLESTONVIT V. NEV7TON 11FATEL—This match was played at Newton Heath on Saturday, before 1,000 specta- tors. The visitors baying won the toss took advantage of a slight wind, and started off at a fast rate. Toe Liverpool cupholders pressed Newton Heath, their left wing being par- ticularly busy, Mitchell, however, relieved and sent the leather back to centre. The home players then bore down on their opponents citadel, S. Gotheridge sent in a warm shot, which unfortunately struck the crossthar. From the scrimmage which ensued, Newton Heath obtained a corner, but nothing came of it. Eearlestewn replied with the right wing, who eluded the home back division, and shot for goal but Fulton stopped the leather. From the scrimmage which followed, the visitors scored their first goal. At half time the score was En.letdown one goal to Newton Heath nil. On resuming, the home team commenced to press the visitors, and for a time experienced hard lines. Eventually a corner fell to Newton Heath, which, although beautifully placed, was of no good result, as Earlestown gradually worked the ball up the field. Dagnall and Ogden especially became prominent by a splen- didly executed run, which appeared likely to bear good re- sults. but Black interposed iota at the right moment, and Earp receiving the leather made off to mid-field Sims, for the visitors, was not to be denied, and made a very fine run, and having passed well to Dagnell, the latter sent in a rapid shot, which although Fulton stopped, he could not hold the ball, which fell in front of the goal, and Ogden rushing up sent the leather under. Newton Heath after this played up and strove hard to score. Eventually Davies, for the home team, after a short run, shot through ; but the visi- tors protested against the point on the plea of off side, and the referee decided against the point. At the call of time the game stood in favour of E trlestown by two goals to Newton Heath nil. Teams :—Newton Heath : Fulton, goat; Black and Mitchell, backs ; Moran, Kiy, and Howles, half backs ; Gotheridge, M'Gregor. Esrp, Davies, and Blears, forwards. Eirlestown : Appleton, goal ; R Green and 3 Green, backs ; Clayton, Bswker, and Duxbury, halt backs ; Rich, Ellison, Sims, Ogden, and Dagnall, for- wards.

A. new candidate for the favour of patrons of periodical literature is the English edition of the "Golden Argosy," a weekly paper whose American edition has for some time past been enormously popular on the other side of the Atlantic. Its contents are interesting, wholesome, and good, without being goody, and the paper seems to have class enought to run upon Its own merits. The voprietors, however, announce their in- tention of giving a way among their subscribers, under certain conditions, prizes to the value of £6,000 sterling.—The Referee, London.

We have received the early numbers of the English edition of the "Golden Argosy." a weekly journa containing much that is interesting. The serial stories are ably written, and the paper abounds with matter of a highly entertaining descrip- tion, while the illustrations, which are numerous, are char- acterised by refinement and finish. WS exceedingly well printed on rolled paper.—lforning Advertiser, London. The Golden Argosy," as a publication, has everything in its favour. It is well and clearly printed on good psper, beautifully Illustrated, and nct the least of its recommenda- tions is the fact that the literary matter is of a high order, and makes it fit to circulate in any home The Liverpool Wieldy

The "Golden Argosy."—As the subscription Is only two shillings per quarter for an excellent illustrated weekly budget of literature, it is not Improbable that the number of their subscribers will soon be enormous.—The Lancaster Guardian.

We think the paper ought to become popular. There are three good reasons why it should de so, these being—it is well printed and Illustrated, the subscription is only eight shillings a year, and the whole space is oectspled with reading matter, there being no advertisements. Happy newspaper property, not to require them !—Whitehatl Review, London. . . .

The paper abounds with excellent stories, elevating and pure In tone. and with funniosities "of evety imaginable kind, which cannot fall to be productive of mirth and good humour. —Belfut News-Letter.

div.head: FOOTBALL.'
div.p: FOOTBALL.'

Secretaries of Football Clubs are recinested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to thehead office, Bewaey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
Lawn v. VIILCAN.—PIayed at Leigh on Saturday. Score : Leigh, one goal, three tries, and four minor points to nil.

, TILDESLEY V. Sr. HELENS.—On the grouted of the former on Saturday Tyldesltv winning by two goals, five tries, and ten minor points to one goal and two miner points. Rutecons v. ASPULL.—PIayed at Aspnll on Saturday, when an exceedingly fast and stubbornly contested game ended in favour of the Aripull players by one dropped goal, one try, three minor points, to Runcorn one try and three minor points. EARLBSTOWN (21AD) v. NEWTON HEATH.—These teams met on the ground oi the first named at Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. The visitors had only ten men. The Earlestonians had the best of the game, but the result was a draw of four goals each. WARRINGTON EXCELSIOR Y. RELANDS' MILLS EMPLOYES. —This match was played on the ground of the former, and after a one-sided game, resulted in a victory for the Excel- sior!' by one goal, 4 tries and 10 minor points to nil. Black- ledge obtained 3 trios, whilst Barton kicked a neat goal for the home team. This was the last match of the season. The Excelsiors have played 20 matches, winning ifi, drawn 2, and lost 2.

- PRBSCOT V. LIVERPOOL GYSINASIISM.—ThiS match WAS played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and after a very pleasant game resulted in a win for the home team by three goals to nil. The visiting forwards made several determined efforts to score, but were frustrated by the splendid play of Welsh, Richards, and Milroy. For the visitors, Wilkinson at back and the goalkeeper deserved the greatest credit. •

WARRINGTON TRUE BLUR v. WHITE STAR.—This match was elayed on the ground of the former on Saturday. The borne team were not properly represented, several of their best men being absent. A very rough and noisy game en- sued, and after many disputes the game ended in a draw. Score: True Blues, three minors ; White Star, one disputed , try and three minors. For the True Blues the best men were Stockton' Mather, Acton, and Taylor; and for the visitors Daniels, Knight (captain), and Hill. WARRINGTON 2ND (14 MEN) E. ECCLES 2ND. This match was played at Eccles on Saturday. The visitors were minus the services of Hewitt and Lightfoot, and played a man short during the game, which, however, was very well contested throughout, neither side having much the advan- tage, and at the call of time the game stood a draw, only minors being scored. For Warrington, Rigby, Summers, and Tones were the pick of the forwards, and of the backs Buxton played a good game.

. - NEWTON V. FATAL A"CC7I;ENV IN A COALPIT.—A gate weighrnan named Thomas Tinsley was working in the Maudlin seamn of the Wearmouth Colliery, Sunderland, on Wednesday mwning, when a large stone fell from the roof, killing him instantaneously. Deceased was thirty-one years of age, and leaves a wife and two children.

div.head: SUNDAY CLOSING OF PUBLIC HOUSES.
div.p: SUNDAY CLOSING OF PUBLIC HOUSES.

PUBLIC MEETING AT WARRINGTON. On Tuesday evening a largely attended meeting was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, for the purpose of advocat- ing the necessity of closing public houses on Sunday. The chair was occupied by Mr Beamont, and among those pre- sent were :—Sir Llevrelys Turner, Bart (Chairman of Visit- ing Justices of Her Majesty's Prisons for three counties in North Wales), Mr E Wkitwell, of Kendal (both of whom attended as a deputation); the Mayor (Alderman Harrison); the Revs Samuel Wilkinsos, Morley Stevenson, Father I Scannell, J Phillips, J Warnock, J H Jones, E Moore, John Yonge, J G Richarde, E C E Carleton; and Messrs Charles Broadbent, W Long; Fred Monks, E J Guest, John Green- ing, C .1 Holmes, W J Burgess, John Brown, Robert Gar- nett, C Sawkins Burgess, Dr Mackie, Joseph Shaw Green, D W Finney, H Thornton, E Twiss, R Siddall, Charles Plinston, W Darbvshire, David Houghton, J Titchett, Geo Bayley, and W Roberts (local sec). The Rev S WILKINSON having engaged in prayer' The SECRETARY (Mr William Roberts) said he had re- ceived letters of apology for non-attendance from the follow- ing gentlemen :—Mr McMinnies, M.P., the Revs R Pilcher. G E Cutting, W Mules, Father Browne, and Francis Slater; and Messrs John Rylands, William Crosfield (Liverpool), John Crosfield, Julian Winser, R A Naylor, John Naylor, C E Parker, Thomas Hall, S M Webster. S Chandley, Thomas Birchen, and J Calvert. Mr iticMinnies wrote :—" I regret I am unable to be out after sunset or I should have had pleasure in attending your meeting." Mr William Crosfield wrote as follows :—" I am sorry to find that you are having a Sunday closing meeting on a day when I shall be in Italy. This is a question in which I have taken a very deep in- terest, and I should have made a point of being present if I had been within reacts to add my voice to the testimony of those who are announced."

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the pr ,ceedings, said they were met on a most important occasion. (Applause.) He thought they would, by the resolutions which would be sub- mitted to the meeting, help forward a great movement, a movement which had long hung over them in suspense, and they all hoped that the privilege which had been granted to Ireland and Scotland and Wales would not be wanting in in England. When the great Author of the world had formed it he was disposed to hallow one day out of the seven for the spectal good of men's souls. And, again, when Moses on Mount Sinai showed the Lord's commands, they had a blessing bestowed on the Sabbath day. He was sorry to say that owing to some bad custom which had grown up in England, a large class of their fellow-subjects were de- barred from enjoying the privileges of that holy day by beiog almost compelled, certainly allowed, for many hours of the day to carry on the ordinary business of the week. That was a great evil in itself, and they must deplore it, be- cause it deprived thoso men of the opportunity of attending their places of worship, and also disabled them, as he con- tended they bad not the name energy to carry on their business on the following clay. (Hear, hear.) It was a merciful provision that men should not always be employed about earthly things. When their late excellent neighbour, Lord Winmarleigh—(applause)—was in that neighbourhood, beset on foot a movement like the present for closing public houses entirely on the Sunday. It was his (the chairman's) privilege Jo visit every public house in Warrington on that occasion, and he believed that every man he called upon was actually in favour of public houses being so closed. (Cheers.) Lord Winnaarleigh, in the service of his country, went to Gibraltar, and was absent in the next Parliament, and somehow or other a party was got up, and the Act was repealed, and on the next occasion when he called upon the publicans he found that the vintners, and those who had to deal in alcoholic liquors, were all against him, not because it was their will, but because, they said, they were governed by a body in London. He thought that that was a great incentive to them to en- deavour to get those people who were redly compelled to open their houses to hays liberty like other people to make the best use they cou'd of the Sunday. (Ap- plause.) One of the worthy clergymen present had cpened the meeting with prayer. That was an occasion on which they might ask God's blessing OR their labours. (Cheers.) He remembered that the great poet Milton did not appeal to the muses for inspiration when he was about to commence his great work, but to the Great Spirit, the Third Person in the blessed Trinity, for he said And chiefly Thou, 0 Spirit, that dust prefer Before all temples th' upright heart and pure; Instruct me for Thou knowest : Thou from the first Wa t present, and with mighty wings outspre^.d Dove-like sleet brooding on the vast abyss And macrst it pregnant; what in me is dark Illumine; what is law raise and support." (Cheers.) They might justly appeal to that Holy Spirit to help them in the undertaking in which they were engaged that night, and with his aid they would undoubtedly succeed in accomplishing a great work, for which the country shall be thankful. (Cheers.) The Rev. Father SCANNELL moved the following resolu- tion :—"That this meeting considers that the sale of intoxi- cating liquors on the Lord's day is unfair and injurious, and ought not to be sanctioned by the law of this country." (Applause.) He was present not only as a member of an association for the promotion of temperance in that town, but he bad the honour and privilege of being the chaplain of the Warrington Total Abstinence League of the Cross. (Cheers.) And, therefore, it afforded him the greatest pleasure to stand upon that platform, that platform of temperance, which admitted the representatives of all shades of religious opinions and convictions. (Hear, hear.) It afforded him the greatest pleasure to stand before them to raise his voice, feeble though it might be, and to give his support for the promotion of the elevating and regenerating cause of temperance ; and amongst the many factors which at the present were being brought forward for the promotion of that cause, they had many statistics to Prove that one of the greatest would be the closing of public-house on Sunday —the prohibition of the sale of intoxicating liquors. It had been often said that they could not make men sober by Act of Parliament. He agreed with the statement to a cer- tain extent. It was partially true; but what was wanted was education. They must prepare the country; they must ripen the minds of the people for Sunday closing. (Ap- plause.) How were they to de this? By Bands of Hope, National Alliances, Leagues of the Cross, and by that grand army which was marching wader its blue banner to the triumph of the cause of temperance. (Cheers.) Let them enter into this matter in a united as well as a hearty manner. This was the social question of the day. Let them enrol I themselves under the banner of temperance and success would be theirs. He had much pleasu-e in moving the re- solution he bad read to them. (Applause. Mr. W. I. Unearths seconded the motion, and said he was much plealsed to have made the acquaintance of tbe rev. gentleman who had just addressed them. He had previ- oesly heard of the good work he was doing in Warrington, and be was sure that his work in aid of temperance would be a very great alvantage to the people over whom he ministered. lie was glad to be presentto show how entirely he agreed with those who were anxious that the sale of in- Oxicating drinks on Sunday should be speedily made a thing of the past in this country. He was somewhat dis- appointed with the result of the motion proposed in the Town Cauncil of Warrington a few days ago, as the Cor- poration declined to do what the cities of Liverpool and Manchester and more than a benched other corporations had dons; but he thought be might venture to say that the refusal of their local autherity to support the movement would not in any way affect its ultimate and, he believed, its speedy success. (Applause.) It would effect it speedy success no more than Mrs. Partington's celebrated attempt to stern the progress of the Atlantic with a stable broom. (Leuehter and applause.) The majority of the people of this country were in favour of Sunday closing. (Cheers.). He supported the motion for many reasons. He supported it especially for two reasons, first of all because he was convinced that Sunday closing would diminish drunken- ness, and in the second place because, as the resolution said, Sunday opening and trading was unfair to other trades- people. (Cheers.) He was convinced that Sunday closing would diminish drunkenness. That had been denied in Warrington recently, but there were some people who would deny anything. (Laughter.) They actually told them that Sunday closing had not been productive of a diminution of drunkenness in Scotland. But those who made that assertion he would like to answer in this way. Public houses had not been opened in Scotland for many years, and he bad never heard that the Scotch people them- selves were dissatisfied with the result. If the result had not been satisfactory, there would have been an agitation in favour of opening them, but he had yet to learn that Scotchmen were dissatisfied with the Forbes-Mac- kenzie Act in any way, or that they desired to I see public houses opened on Sunday. (Applause.) The yearly average ef drunkenness in Edinburgh in 1852-3. before the Mackenzie Act was passed, was 6,047. Edin- burgh since then had greatly increased in population, but he found from the year 1871 to 1883 that the yearly aver- age of c thes was 2,362, or a decrease of 3,686. considerably more than one half of the whole. With regard to Wales, it was not true that there had not been a diminution in Wales since the Sunday Closing Act came into operation, but in all towns in Wales there had not been a diminution. and the town pointed out the other day in the Warrington Town Council was Cardiff. That was not three miles out of England. (A voice : " One and a bal.") But, not- withstanding the reference to Cardiff, the Sunday Closing Act in Wales prove I. as Sir William Harcourt slid in the House of Commons theeother day, not an argument against Sunday Closing in Wales but an argument against Sunday opening in England. (Cheers.) Sir LLEWELLYN TURNER supported the resolution. He said if he were to choose a text for his address that evening he could not select a better one than that sentence from the Lord's prayer, " Thy will be done on earth." (Hear' hear.) He might almost say that there never was a period in the history of their country when it was more ine. portant that the people should be a strong, sober, religious people, and a united people than at 'resent. They were threatened with complications right and left, and they knew and believed, otherwise they were deceiving them- selves in building their churches and chapels and in the re- ligious profession they made, that righteousness exalteth a nation, and that sin was a reproach to any people. He said they were stultifying themselves unless they did every thing that lay in their power to hasten God's kingdom on earth, and to make His will better and more clearly known than it was by vast numbers of the people of this land. (Cheers.) It was a most painful revelation to think upon the astounding amount of sin and wickedness due to he drinking habits of this country. He did not ask for an

--....,. Act of Parliament to be forced on the people, but by ap- pealing to the infelligence and commonsense of Englishmr n they would o'glin Acts of Parliament with the sanction and support of the people, and emanating from the people themselves. (Hear, hear.) For many years he had been d justice of the peace, but he said it deliberately that the Act

of Parliament that put into the hands of magistrates the power of deciding whether a public-house should exist or not was a failure. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then carried by acclamation. Dr. MACKIE next moved, "That this meetino demands for England the same prohibition of the traffic in intoxicat- ing liquors during the whole of the Lord's Day as, in other parts of the United Kingdom and many of our colonies, has been attended with most beneficial results; and that a peti- tion to Parliament to this effect be adopted, and signed by the chairman." In speaking to this resolution, he said that probably something like 200 young women would at present be kept at work in public-houses in Warrington on Sun- days, and that meeting wished to set them free on that day. They wanted the publicans to join with them in demanding Sunday closing for themselves and also for every club, whether political or non-political. (Hear, hear.) He con- cluded by expressing the hope that Warrington would set an example in Sunday closing, even without the assistance of the law. (Cheers.) Mr. E. WHITWELL seconded the resolution. He said the present system was breaking God's commandmept as to the Sabbath. The workmen of England had found out that continuous hours of labour were most dangerous to them- selves both as men and citizens. By the passing of the Factory Acts the working-man could return home without having his system tired out by lengthened labours. They wanted the Englishman's home to be to him the happiest spot on earth. (Applause.) The publican did not know the meaning of home, he being too busy with his custo- mers. As to the working-man not being able to enjoy his Sunday dinner without his glass of frothing ale, he (the speaker) was informed that if he would tend his bottle to the barrel on Saturday night it could be filled, securely corked, and kept fresh until the Sunday dinner•time. (Laughter.) It had been said that if this Bill was passed it would be a piece of class legis'ation, as the gentleman had his club while the working-man had none. But he had been told that working-men's clubs were very plentiful in England, and especially in the north, so that obj-ction was done away with. If England were to have its Sonday rest land no trade was dore in the public-house, would they not be the gainers? The publican and his family and servants would not suffer, for they would have the privile4e of en- joying a peaceful Sabbath-day. The working-min would go to his work on Mondry morning not feeling so wretched and miserable as he did now. He would give them a few encouraging features in their movement. In 1882 for the first time in the last quarter of a century a millon signa- tures were attached to petitions in favour of Sunday clos- ing. (Applause.) In 1883 they did better ;till, they had one million eight hundred thousand sign stares. (Applause.) It had been said that the majority of these signatures were those of women and Sunday school children. But that was not true, and if it were who felt the hardship entailed by I drink more than the mothers and wives ? And there was mealy a ragged starving boy and girl who could send:forth a good cry to our legislators to tell them that they knew no- thing of the enormity of the suffering Lod woe caused by the drinking habits of the land. (Applause.) One hun- dred Town Ccuncils and three hundred Boards of Guar- dians had also petitioned. (Applause.) In Warrington 2,824 voted in favour of the Bill and 317 against it. (Loud applause.) In Bootle he had asked the meeting who was in favour of public-houses being open on a Sunday for an hour at noon and an hour in the evening, and ocly three held up their hands. (Applause.) He would new put the same question to them. No hands were held lap in favour of the public-houses being opened for two hours on the Sunday, but a large show was made against the proposi- tion ] The speaker then referred to Scotland, and said that 50 years ago it was the most educated and the most drun- ken country in the world ; 30 years ago they closed their public-houses on Sunday, and now the drunkenness of Edin- burgh and Glasgow was not half what it used to be. In Ire- land Sunday closing had been in operation since 1878 and there were 20,000 fewer cases of drunkenness, and the cen- sumption of spirits was 800,000 gallons less. (Applause.) Canada, New South Wales, and our other colonies also showed good reports. . In Wales Anglesey with a pooula- tion of 51,000, had only one case of Sunday drunkenness dur- ing the oast year. Warrington, with a population of 41,000, had 43 cases, so they found that Anglesey was 50 times better than Warrington. (Laughter and applause. Would they not like Warrington to be 50 times as good as it was ? He wanted them to encourage their member to vote for Sunday closing. Those of them that bad votes in the county must endeavour toinfluencs the county members. They were expecting their troops in the Soudan to do their duty, and they must make their members of Parliament feel that that they were expected to do theirs too. He hoped no feeling of party epirit would prevent any man from doing his duty in this great matter. He was a Liberal in politics, but if the Conservative candidate promised to support Sun- day closing and the Liberal candidate refused to, he should support the Conservative. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was carried by acclamation. The Rev. S. WILICINSOg proposed the following resolu- tion :—That the Chairman be requested to sign, on behalf of the meeting, a memorial in favour of Sunday Closing, and to forward the same to the Prime Minister, the Home Secre- tary, and the members of Parliament for South-West Lanca- shire and Warrington ; and also that the thanks of this meeting be presented to William Beamont, E q., for presiding upon this occasion." Any one, Mr. Wilkinson said, who could answer the arguments in favour of that movement which were contained in the papers that had been circulated by the promoters of it, must be a very clever fellow indeed, for to his mind they were al- most, if not altogether, beyond contradiction. (Hear, hear.) No one, he thought, could for one moment doubt that the closing of public-houses on Sundays would be attended with great blessing to the country. Indeed, he be- lieved that as a rule there was no class of people who were more in favour of that closing than the publicans them- selves would be if the closing were by Act of Parliament made compulsory and general. Many of them would be glad to close on that day, so as to have the rest that ought properly to be theirs on the Lord's Day. (Hear, hear.) Even in a large town, where there were 200 or 300 licensed victuallers, if some of them would persist in keeping open on the Sunday, it caused extreme difficulty to others in closing, and if the country could induce the Legislature to pass an Act that should do away with that difficulty, by rendering closing on the Sunday oblioatory. a great blessine would be conferred on the community. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in proposing the resolution. They all knew Mr. Beamont would be ever first and foremost in every good work, and that whenever he was asked to preside over a meeting he was ready to do so, and whenever he did so the meeting was always a success. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN GRRENING, who was received with loud ap- plause, said that it gave him great pleasure to second the resolution. It was not often that he stood upon a platform to speak upon any public matter, but on this subject he felt that ha was only doing his duty in being there that even- ing. (Hear, hear.) He cone idered that a Sunday Closing of Public Houses Act was one of the most itnnortant pieces of legislation that could be enacted in this land. They had heard it urged eta meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil recently that such was not the case. He must say that he was astonished at the course which some gentlemen took at that Council meeting. lle was sorry to say that they lost the vote at the Town Council, but they had got it there that night by a very large majority, and in another place the next day he hoped they should get it again. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. J. H. Risme said that at that late hour be would only detain the meeting for a moment or two. He had Very much pleasure in supporting the resolution. He hoped that 87 years of age they might all be able to quote Milton as their chairman had done that evening. Ti,ey were all devoutly thankful that for so long a time they had been spared the services of their esteemed chairman—ser- vices which he had rendered, not only to the temperance movement, but to every other good cause. (Applause.) He hoped the day was not far distant when it would be quite impossible for a man to get into either a Town Council or a Board of Guardians unless it was well known that he would vote square on that drink question. (Hear, hear.) Were it in his power. as it was in the power of the working men to enforce his views, he was quite sure that at the next Town Council meeting a resolution would ba passed in favour of closing public-houses on Sunday, and also in ',your of Local Option, and the same upon the Board of Guardians. The working-men in Warrington had the matter in their own hands, and he exhorted them the next time they used their votes, either for the Town Council or the Board of Guardians, to see that the man for whom they recorded their votes would go square upon the temperance question. (Applause.) The motion was then carried by loud acclamation. The CHAIRMIaciII tesponding, said he had long entertained his present views upon the temperance question—(hear, hear)—and he hoped the present system would not long exist in Warrington. (Applause.) Three cheese for the deputation brought the meeting to a close.

A &MANOR DISAPPIDIRANCE.—NOticA have been issued stating that John Cardwell, of 33, Elistt-street, St Helens, left home on the 19th ult and has not yet returned. He iv 64 years of age, and as his mind had of late been somewhat deranged, it was feared some ill bed befallen him. He had in his possession about Ha Bd, and was wearing a blue flannel jacket, black cloth trousers, and a grey wool- len shirt.

ALLEGED LONG FIRM SWINDLER AT ST. HELENS.— Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, at the County Court. on Wednesday, John Henry Nixon, a fish salesman, of St. Helens, who did not appear, was sued for the recovery of £l5 19s 2d, by Messrs Ressick. McLaren, and Co, wholc• sale fish dealers' Leith. The firm was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, who stated that the defendant was a fish salesman, but had no place of business, and so far as he could learn, he was a lone firm swindler, never pay- ing anybody for what he got. He was continually receiv- ing goods from fishdealers at Leitb, Grimsby, and Hull, and never paid for them. Ho received the goods and sold ther4 at the station, but had or used to have a shop which only contained a pair of scales. He paid the carriage on the goods at the station, but there was no chance for any of his creditors to seize hold of anything in payment for the good I. On being spoken to about the matter the defendant said he would not pay, as he had been to prison' before and would go again. At Liverpool he had been convicted for a long firm swindle and got two years' imprisonment, and in scot- and he had also been committed for two years. In one week, ending March 23rd, he received about 30 cotrige,• ments of fish, and the carriage alone amounted to £ll 18s 3d. Mr. Thomas Garner, clerk to Mr. Swift, then dc. posed that he had seen the defendant's signature in the re- ceiving books at the railway station.—His Honour made an Order for the committal of the defendant for the full term of 40 days.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Ou Seurday the 3rd Lanark beat Port Glasgow Athletic by three to one; in the fiaal tie of the Dumbartonshire Cup competition, Dumbarton beat Vale of Leven by three to one, at Renton ; Ayr beat Battlefield at Ayr by six to four; in the final tie of the Birmingham and District cup competition, Aston Villa beat Walsall Swifts by two to none; at Kennington Oval the Old Harrovians beat 0:d Etonians by three to one; in the final tie of the Wharneffe Charity Cup competition, Sheffield Wednesday and Sheffield Heeley for the second time played a drawn game, one goal each; the third meeting of Park Grange and Mexbro', in the semi-final of the Sheffield cup competition, resulted in favour of the former by one to none; in the final tie of the Cheshire cup competition, Northwich Victoria beat Davenham by two to one, and for the sixth time won the cup. For the second time the Queen's Park have this season competed for the Football Association Challenge Cup, and for the second time they have reached the final stage, and have as opponents the Blackburn Revers. the only team pit- ted against them four times without suffering defeat. On Monday afternoon Preston North End played an ex- hibition game on the ground of the Wigan club. The Asso- ciation game has only been introduced into Wigan this season, and its exponents are having an uphill fight. They are, however, making headway and gaining converts fast. On Monday they had the assistance of several well-known players, but notwithstanding this were ".not in it " against the North End, who, by the by, were witohut four of their first team. One man, however, created quite a sensation among the Prestonians present, we mean Holmes. His tack- ling and prompt returns, with either foot, were good in the extreme, and he promises to take a leading place amongst the backs of that district.
