Prominent " Public " Man.—John Barleycorn. Invariably Beasonable.—Salt, mustard, pepper, vinegar.

WOMAN'S BEST FRIEND IN THE WEiR'LED Tsin: OF LIFE.—A pin. Many Onprons.—Mistress : "Mary, I don't like to see this dust on the furniture." Mary: "All right, mum. I'll pull down the blinds !" Fasurow.—Fashion has been cleverly hit off as "an arbi- trary disease which leads all geese to follow in single file the one goose that sets the style.' The following advertisement appears la a French paper.— " Wanted—a distinguished and healthy looking man to be cured patient' in a doctor's waiting-room. Address," Ste. A mute in Yorkshire, at the funeral of a late local mag- nate, when requested by the deceaaed's brother to tell a gentleman to take a glass of wine with hint, said, "Please. sir, the corpse's brother would like to tek a glass o' wine wi' ye." A wealthy Irish farmer, intending to "send his eon to college," recently wrote a short letter to "the heads of Ox- ford University," in which he said, "Please say what are your terms for a year; and will it coat anything extra if my son learns to write a good hand and spell proper, as well as to row a boat ?" DATUM DEVELOPMENT.—Mother : "And now tell me what you meant by introducing me to Mr. Brown as your aunt." Devoted daughter: "Forgive me, mother; but Mr.klarown appears to be en the point of proposing, and it woulernot do -to run any risks just now, you know. He has a strong pre- jadice against mothers-in-law." RECEIVED WITH WARMTH —Daring a dismission about the value of the cuirass the Doke of Wellington expressed an opinion adverse to it; thereupon someone asked whether the French Cuirassiers had not come up well at Waterloo. " Yes " he said; and they went down well too." "Can you give me the definition of nothing r inquired a number seventeen school teacher. "Yes, mum. It's a bunghole without a barrel around it," shouted little Ted Saunders, whose papa is a cooper.—Brooklyn The newspaper man who could not have improved upon Lord Wolseley's generalship, have saved Gardon's life, defeated the hiandi, and subjugated the Saadan, may be on deck; but, if so, he is hiding away in one of the scupper holes.—Fall River Advance. A man in a train was heard to groan so frightfully that the passengers took pity on him, and one of them gave him a drink out of a whisky flask. "Do you feel any better ? " asked the giver. "I do," said he who had groaned. "What ailed yen ? " "Ailed me?" "Yes; what made you groan so?" "Groan! Great land of freedom. I was singing !" A woman's affection for her husband is one of those things which are too sublime to be grappled with by common, every-day, prosaio description; and a man can never appre- ciate it is its full intensity until he reflects that, in her de- sire to show her solicitude for his comfort and pride in his appearance, she has begun to starch his stookings.—Fall River Advance. In a family where there are two boys, one of them brought home a worthless cur, to the disgust of the rest of the mem- bers. At last the eldest sister offered him half-a-crown if he would give the dog away. He assented, and pocketed the coin. When night came, prompted by curiosity, she asked the little fellow to whom he had given his dog, and was told with charming naivete," Oh, I've given him to Jack !"—his younger brother. WHY Sax LEFT.—Mistress: "What, going to leave already? Why, you have not been here a week !" Maid: "I know it, mum; but I can't stand it here. Things ran too smooth-like, mum." Mistress: "Why, what can you mean ?" Maid: "You see, mum, I has always been in places where they kept three servants." Mistress: "Oh, you are lonesome then?" Maid: "No, mum, not lone- some ; but, you see, I misses the confusion!" DONALD'S INC/CIRY.—The late Mr. W. Bromley Daven- port used to tell an amusing story of a guest at some High- land lodge who overheard this dialogue between his ducal host and the head-keeper. The Duke: "Donald, young Lord Dash will go on the hill to-day." Donald: "Yes, your Grace." The Duke: "Where will you take him ?" Donald: "Well, your Grace, i 3 he to kill a stag, or have a shot, or only see deer, or just go for a wa-a-lk ?' Long and terrible was the pause, and painfully excited the interest of the listener before, In grave measured tones, the evidently well- weighed and thought out decision hailed his ear, Well, Donald, you may just take him for a walk !" SCOTCH WHISKY AND IMAGINATION. The late Allan Pinkerton, the Scottish-American detective, had a company of gentlemen at his country seat near Chicago one cold winter day a few years ago. For an hour he took them about his place, showing them what there was to be seen; and, when at length they returned to the house they were thoroughly chilled. "Now, gentlemen," said he, "I want you to try some of this old Scotch whisky;" and his guests partook freely of theprofferred liquor. Then he invited them into the library where there was a large gas burner stove apparently glowing with heat. They seated themselves round it, holding out their benumbed hands to catch the warmth. Here they chatted for a time, when suddenly Mr. Pinkerton remarked," It strikes me that stove doesn't send out nanch heat. How do you feel? They all replied that they felt delightfully warm, and suggested that the stove door should be opened. Mr. Pinkerton acted on the sugges- tion, and, to the astonishment of the guests, revealed two lighted candles resting upon a large block of ice as the only contents of the stove. "See, gentlemen," said be, "what a vivid imagination and a little good Scotch whisky will do."
AT THE GREAT FEIGHTIN' BAZAAR.

BY AB-O'Tlf-YATE. " Come on, owd ticket," I said to eur Sal o' Monday morning, "thou says thou's seen nowt lately nobbut a garden hedge, an' an owd gate. Thou shall see a bit o' France without crossin' th' sea." "How con I do that?' hoo wanted to know. "Well," I said, "they'n sent us a town, as a sample o'th' country. If we liken it we con have o'th' job lot at a price. We're gettin' short o' lond ; an' we mit as weel have a bit o' France as anybody else. Owd Bismark has had a slice or two put to Germany, wi' feightin' for It; but we Con afford to buy what we want." "An' wheere are th' French gooin' to live?" th' owd tut said, I darsay wonderin' how this town had bin sent o'er. "I' China, if th' Chinese 'lt let 'ens," I said. "They're like another nation I could name, they're never at rest. But oome, thon'd better get thy duds on, an' let us be gooin'; this Is th' last day but one." "1 con be ready as soon as thou con," an' th' owd lass'a apron flew across th' heouse as if hoo meant it. It war a race which could be ready th' feet; but through breakin' a shoe-tee th' owd blossom licked me by a miait; then off we set. When we geet into Oxford-road I thowt everybody an' hie gronmother war theere, it war so crowded. Talk about owd England bein' done up! Not while folk con afford to pay a six times a year, to see a hossrace. Icon remember a time when leas than that had to do for a whnl day's ex- pense. But now, look at th' crowds ut go'en to theaytres, singin' shops, an' bazaars. An' see how they dress! Done up! not yet. We paid our shillins, an' th' trumpet sounded. "What's that for, Ab ?" th' owd ticket said, when th' music had bin throttled off. " Thev'n sin us come in, and sounded welcome," I said. "An' dun they do it for everybody ?" " Nawe,nobbut sich en' Rich; an' we're sich. We stood awhile lookin' at th' walls o' this French town ; an' it struck me ut some on um war th' wrong side out. Therm showing th' back o'th' picture. I could ha' takken that town mysel, if I'd had a good pair o' scithers. After we'd looked it o'er, an' seen wheere a stone had been stitched in wi' a needle anAhread, we moved down toward what they co'd th' " Barbican." • "What are o' these folk starin' at, Ab ?" th' owd rib said; an' just then I seed a lot o' chaps ut had "set " us. "I conno' tell, unless it's one of us two." "It's thee, I believe. Thou'rt takken for somebody else than thyser, like thou war at tie Tabonical Gardens." AR' just as Fre looking o'er th' top of a glass o' whiskey, ut somehow fell i' my hoot at th' "canteen," I yerd eornbody say, ut stood no' far off us,— "I didn't think aristocratic people were so good looking as they are; and I was led to understand that the Countess was rather a slim person." "Well, you see what she is like," I yerd another say. "The nobility are not such bad looking people, after all." "Is that the Earl that's got his nose in a glass?" t'other mon said. "I suppose it is; he cocks his finger like one." An' they passed on, suckin' th' knobs o' their sticks, an' starin back at our Sal an' me. "Come on, owd crater; if we stop here anether minit we'se be takken for a duke an' a duchess.' We passed through th' gateway o'th' Barbican, an' into th' town, wheere we'rn saluted i' military style, an' axt to put in a raffle. Hoo're a little she so'dier at axt me, wi' a red sash on; an' a natty little cap at fitted on a " bang" so nicely ut one mit ha bin made for th' tother, as no doubt it wur. 800 geet howd of a button, an' coaxed me, as women will when they wanten summat ; an' I felt by th' hakin o' my arm ut ther a storm brewin'. So I tom] her l're feart o' winnin' stimmat, an' it would be so mich bother gettin it away. I'd won six payannons i' my time, and I'd no place to put another in. 800 gan me sich an innocent look, an' turned away. I daresay hoo'd never yeard a gradely sproanger before. "What wur that little minx after?' ear Sal wanted to know when th' tother had ta'en hersel away. "800 wanted to know if her ladyship, meanin' thee, would like to tak a stall, as th'countess was getting quite fatigued," I said. Up went th' owd blossom's pecker; an' boo marched off wi' th' stateliness of a queen. But we kept tumblin o'er so mony o' these women soldiers, ut boo wanted to know if ther no sort else i' France. " Nawe," I 'said, " th' bulk o'th' men war killed i'th' last war; an' what wur left they'n sent to China. They'n nowt nobbut women feighters now, an' they winno ha' mony thoose if they letten 'em come o'er here. These'll go noane back, thou'll see." "It's come to summat at last ;" th' owd rib said, after tryin to swallow what I'd towd her. "Woman so'diers ! they'n tried to be men a good while,—wearin' men's clooas, an drinkin' like men. They owt t' have their 'rights,' now, an' tak' men's places. It wur but th' tother Sunday I seed what I took to be a young chap sittin' i'th' front o me at th' church, wi' a hat on like thy bobbin-nudger ; an' becose I axt him how he could think at slain' i'th' church with his hat on, he gan me sich a look, an' pointed to her ear- rings. I could see then I'd made a mistake. If her yore had bin platted at back I should ha' known th' difference. Bat it war as short as thine."

After hoo'd delivered hersel' o' this sermon, th' owd rib said hoo thowt heo could do wi' a cap o' coffee, an' hoo'd quite as mich right to it as I had to my whisky. I thowt same; so took her to "Wilton Arms," an' aid for one. A young lady honded it to me as nicely as if I'd bin a lord ; an' just then a men tapped me on th' shoother. " Don't you put a sovereign down," he said; " if you do you'll get no change." "No danger," I said, as I forked out fourpence. "1 eel lected • th' copper I could afore I coome ; an' I've nowt be.. side. It's a weight fort' carry, but I'm no' gooin to part with it o." When I turned round I found th' owd ticket i' Glees con- fab wi one o'th' waiters,—the one ut had carved her wi' th'

coffee. I yerd her sayin,— " Ay, I knew th' owd lady very wed. Hoo're a good woman; an' used to go a good deeal among th' poor. I didno' know th' last Lady Wilton; bat they say'n hoore a very nice lady. This present countess I expected to see here. But they say'n boo's tired out, peor thing, an' gone whoam. Abram, thou hasno' paid tor tie' eoffee, an' I've supped it." "Well, Icon pay now," I said. "I dar'say I'm th' fast mon nt's had strap at this public-house," an' th' waitress leafed as I stamped my fonrpence down. "Well, good day, Miss," th' owd rib said, as we ',some away. "I should like t' ha' seen th' countess." "She served you with coffee." An' I could see a smile vanish at back o'th' coffee urn, an' war seen no more till we'd gone away. "An' I've bin talkin to her o' this time; an' tellin her my ailments like a foo'! Ab, it's like a bit o' thy wark ; thou'd ha' done th' same," an' th' owd ticket sailed away. After this we'd a general stare round. Th' stalls war one blaze o' colour ; an' we'd as mich as we could de to ran th' pig market [run the gauntlet] i' those women warriors, at war bent on sena' me summat. I fund it war best parten- i din to be deeaf, an' showin"em tuppence for an article hap- pen wo'th a hauve-a-creawn, an' if they made any bother showin 'em a penny would droive 'em. Bet as th' bazaar wiar for a good cause, I thowt I ewt to do summat for it ncoore than I had done. Sp I looked round for t' see what I could invest in. Bobby clooas wur never offered me. 1 dar'say thoose ut had 'em could see it war no use. They nait as wed lo' offered me a feedin-bottle. Ther a little wench I should tak to be about fifteen,—no moors, at any- rate —coome up to us wi' a chiolt in her arms; an' th' owd rib looked at her as if hoore shocked past owt. "Is that thiae, thou little snicket ?" hoo said. " Yes ; will you boy it? Cry all night if you'll wind it up. Doesn't require any milk warming, and never ails any- thing." Just then it set up a " at drove our Sal into a corner, wonderin' what th' next would be. "Thou're properly sowd wi' that, owd crayther," I said. " Thou're gooin' to ha' fitted her ears up wi' a sarmon on forradness, if hoo hadno' spoilt it." "Well, I thorn it war awful, one so young; but I'm fain it isno' so," an' we went on. "I'll tell thee what, Sarah," I said as I looked round, "this licks Walmsley Fowt Banat. If thou'd had a stall here thou'd ha' had summat on it beside a red senglet, an' two bobbins o' cotton." "It would cost thee more, too," hoo ssid, lookin' quite nettled. An' just then hoo stopt at a table wi' a twellin booart on it, like they han at a wakes. "Now thou's a chance o' dooin' summat," / said, "Invest thy money, if t' has any. There's a nice little box there I'd like thee to win. Put thy penny on it."

Hoo did so. "Now twell it a time an' a hauve round, an' it'll just win. Donno strike it as if thou're sons'in one o'th' childer. Now for it; th' countess is watclain' thy performance." Hoo did as I towd her. Th' finger swung near round, an' stopt afacin' that little box ut I wanted her to win. Ther a shout set up ut caused everybody's "attention," an' th' prize wur borne off i' triumph. When th' box wur oppeot, lo and toehold, o that wur in it wur two bobbins o' cotton. " Theigher, owd wench," I said, " thou'rt set up now for another Walmsley Fowt Bazaar. Thou isobbnt wants a red singlet. Thou shall have a pair o' red breeches next. Come on, owd lass, it's gettin' too throng here. Everybody's fol- lowin' us about. They dunno see th' Duchess o Eiszlewo'th every day." We'd just a "smile" between 113, an' then we coome out. It war gat& too warm for us.—Frons Ben Brierley's Journal.
THE EXAMINER, SATUR )AY, APRIL 4, 1885.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. Tar',lament has adjourned for the E ester recess, the short- of which testifies to the strain upon the legislature. In be House of Cu:amens the last few hours of tee sitting were marked by an act of petty perfidy, over which it is possible Mr. Biggar is even at this moment chuckling. It • bad been arranged for some time that there should be a morning sitting on Tuesday, and that at seven o'clock the House should adjourn for the recess. This is an arrange- anent habitually made, as it gives members an opportuirty of taking part in the sitting of the House and yet getting off by train the same night. So sacred was the obligation regarded by the Conservative Opposition that their eager desire to master the papers on the Egyptian Convention had to be checked. There then remained the Irish members to deal with, and infinite pains were taken to satisfy their just aspirations. Monday should, in the ordieary course of eveuts, have been taken for the Seats Bill. But it being understood that the 'Parnellites had some grievances to air, this natural and convenient arrangement was set on one side and Civil Serviee Estimates were put down as the order of the day to give them an opportunity to bring on any subject they bad at heart. Of this opportunity they fully availed themselves. The Farnellites had claimed a sitting in order to hurl fresh as- 'persams at Lord Spencer from the back of Mr Inspector Murphy. They had enjoyed it to the full, and if they wanted any more there was Tuesday's morning sitting in which to disport themselves. Of this also they fully availed themselves, though something near their wits' end for subject matter. In the end they had to go abroad, and found in one Mr John Boyle O'Reilly a new stick where- with to beat the Government. But even John Iberia Okßeilly did not last beyond ka o'clock, and there reinained an hour in which to carry the adjournment. This was, in part, in- nocently filled up by Mr W Fowler. Mr Ashmead Bartlett also found an opportunity to orate, after which, it now being half-past six and English members tailing off, the Farnellitee again appeared on the scene and talked out the sitting, necessitating the resumption at nine o'clock. The Irish members want, or say they want, to be transferred to a Parliament on College Green. Evidently nothing is better calculated to further such a desire than thus to make themeelves intolerable in the society of gentlemen accus- tomed to keep honourable understandings. Affairs with Russia in connection with the Afghan Fron- tier have suddenly taken a favourable turn. The long- expected answer to the demands of England has been re- ceived, its tenor snaking it possible to regard a peaceable solution almost as a certainty. The demands of the Eng- lish Government in this case have been as reasonable as they are implacable. All that is asked of Russia is that she shall without unreasonable delay refer to the Delimitatiou Commission the question of tne boundary. At the.same time Russia has been given to understand, in that polished hut unmistakeable language of which Earl Granville is master, that it would be impossible to leave the matter un- determined, drifting along whilst Russia made each arrange- ments as seemed to recommend themselves to her. Russia has practically acceded to this request, and the general im- pressinn here is that peace is assured. Nevertheless the Government, with whose action in this matter it has been difficult even for the restless Conservative Opposition to dad faille, are going forward uninterruptedly with the pre- parations for war. In India as in the colonies the approach of danger has in striking degree drawn England and her dependencies nearer together, and has enabled the mother 0000f17, even whilst engaged in a great struggle in the Soudan, to make in India a military demonstration sufficient to cow Russia. The troubles through which the Government and :the country are now passing are light in comparison with those that afflict France. The French arms have met with an un- mistakable check irs China, and, after their manner, the French people have turned and rent their rulers. The lack of dignity which the French people show in the presence of a reverse, and the personal ferocity with which they pursue the unfortunate men who chance to be in power at the mo- ment has once more been demonstrated. M. Ferry, lately an all powerful Minister, who only on Saturday carried by a considerable rnejority a vote of confidence, dare not now appear in the streets of Paris. He has to enter the legisla- tive assembly ley a back door, and his house is guarded by a troop of oevalry. We are not quite so bad as that, but we must not crow over our virtues. It cannot be forgotten how, eight years ago, Mr. Gladstouens windows were broken by a street mob, and he himself was howled at in the divi- sion lobby of the House of Cemmoes by a better dressed mob of gentlemen leaving seats in the House. There is another little incident in the fall of M. Ferry that finds a striking parallel with us. When M. Clemenceau fumed and writhed in the Tribune on Monday, it seems that the French Premier, though standing on the brink of the precipice over which he was within the next hour to fall, could not refrain from smiling. Whereupon he was howled at from the extreme Lett. A little later, at some fresh ex- travagance he seems to have smiled again when a hot Gamete member jumped up and solemnly announced that he was "able to declare that M. Ferry was smiling again! " This is vary absurd, but everybody knows how Sir at Cross a session or two ago made it a matter of complaint that he, as he said, "heard an hon. rneinher smile.' Only on Mon- day week Sir Henry Wolff jumped up and denounced Mr Gl.dsron because, as he said, the right hon. gentleman was lagghing and talking whilst Lord tiartlngton was reading the record of losses in Sunday week's surprise of General McNeilPs forces in the Soudan. There is a great deal of human nature in both Parliaments. There has been much talk of the Queen's departure for the Continent at the present juncture, one of the gravest of recent times, when the country is actually engaged in one desperate war and is faced by the possibility of another. The coincidence is a little unfortunate, and it might perhaps have been well if in deference to public opinion the Queen could have seen her way to postpone her holiday for a week or two. But actually the consequences have no bear- ' ing upon the conduct of public affairs. Ministers, already overworked, will fiad some addition to their labours, and there would be some herd riding to and fro on the part of Queen's messengers. Bet of Coarse the direction of policy is in the hands of the Cabinet, subject to the ultimate con- trol of Parliament. The mischief in the circumstances which have now arisen it hat her Majesty, in even increas- ing degree, exacts the rigorous fulfilment of the Ministerial parts in the constitutional comedy which maintains the old Plantagenet autocracy of the Sovereign. Whilst queetions of broad policy are actually settled in the House of Commons and put in shape in Cabinet Coun- cil, the fiction is kept up that all national acts are initia- ted by the sovereign. This is seen in such documents as the proclemation ceiling out the reserves, or in references made in communications from the Queen to " My troops" and "My ships," as if the army and navy were, as WAS the Case up to the time of Charles the first, a kind of personal appannage of the sovereign. To the Queen all these little ways of putting things are very real, and the slightest lapse of the ceremony of obtaining the Royal consent for Minis- terial acts is visited with severe displeasure. Thus it be- came necessary before the Queen left on her holiday trip that her signature should be obtained to the proclamation calling out the reserves, and it will be the same in whatever contingencies may arise during her absence. No step, how- ever imperative may he its necessity, or however perilous delay, may be undertaken till the Queen's ceasent has been obtained. As it is at topmost speed a three days' journey to Aix-le-Bains and back, this may cause some inconve- nience. But as matters are now shaping there is not likely Is be any real danger to the public service. The itinerant propagator of the arts, whose barrow is full of Peony cartes-de-visite of the leading characters of the day, is becoming an increasingly well- known personage in the London streets. His wares are not as unsatisfactory in point of likenees as their extreme cheapness would seem to promise, and the heroes of the hour (and some of the heroines also, if ballet girls and bur- lesque actresses can be counted as such), find a rapid sale at his hands. The agents of the great photographic firms are alway on the look out for a chance to catch the barrow- merchant tripping over the law of copyright, but a few con- victions at the police courts have made the gentlemen of the street as wary in this particular as their brethren of the shops. If internal evidence goes for anything the penny photographs are imported mainly from Germany, and the manner in which the names of some of the char- acters is printed is deliciously un-English. Lord Wolseley, who is a favourite figure just now en the stalls, has te be content with being called plain '' Sir Garnet," but the brother-in-arms with whom he is just now returning from Dongola to Cairo receives a good many steps in promotion, being boldly labelled "Admiral Lord Charles Bereeford." But what better can be expected from people who give us namee like "Major Wardrof " and ." The late Colonel Eyere," to say nothing of each an astounding title as "Sir General Fr. Roberts " ? Byron, the poet-peer, not the burlesque writer, is respOnsi• ble for a great deal, but even his many sins scarcely deserved that one of his masterpieces should have been so travestied as has "Don Juan " by " Glenaveril." Lord Lytton has never been accused, even by his worst enemies, of being possessed of a sense of humour, bat the first part of the new poem, which is " to be continued in our next " for some six months to cones, ha l provoked more smiles than have rewarded the labours of many a professional humour- -Ist. The severest critic of Lord Salisbury as a public man can hardly help sympathising with him .under the heavy burden of his henchman's flattery in several verses, and rumour may not be far wrong in declaring that "CeelliuS" has expressed a hope that his noble friend will "never do it again."

Mr Caleb Wright, cotton spinner, Tyldetley, was on Wed- nesday night select as Liberal candidate for the Leigh Division of South-West Lancashire. Whittaker presided over an attendance representing twenty-two trades, a discussion took place upon labour re- presentation. Mr. Judge, the secretary, proposed :—"That the Council at once communicate with Mr. Henry Broad- hurst with a view to his becoming a candid ite for one of the divisions of this borough."—Mr. John Warrington (corn miller) seconded the motion—AlLer some discussion) She re solutiOn was carried with only one dissentient.

------- - _ _-------- THE BRADLAUGH ,DtFFICULTY. Sir,—Constitutional representative government is en- dangered by the veto of Parliament, in not allowing a law fully elected member to sneak and vote. If Mr.Bradlaugh's exclusion from Parliament becomesm precedent, the right of all electors in every constituency in the kingdom is vio- lated, and their votes may be made void an of no effect. 1 here is not the least practical good gained by excluding Mr. Bradlaugh, and no harm could come from admitting him. His exclusion from Parliament, and nothing else, has been the cause of all the notoriety that has so immense- ly increased the circulation of his publications and views. The very clever and interesting novel;' We Two," by Edna Lyall, is an illustration of the impolicy of persecuting Atheists. If Mr. Bradlaugh affirmed and sat now, he might not be returned for more than one place at a general elec- tion and made a hero; but he would probably sink into oblivion and the spread of erroneous opinions be checked. The passing of Mr. Hopwood's Affirmation Bill would enable Mr. Bradlaugh to affirm, and would also relieve all those persons who feel bound to obey Christ's command," Swear not at all." (See Matthew, v.-34) By excluding Mr. Bradlaugh from Parliament, his opponents are playing into ' his hands. A CHRIiTIAN.

THE DOGS OF WAR. is jest possible that ere these remarks see the light in your paper, England may be launched into a still more deadly struggle than the one she already has on hand in the Soudan. There is a class of people termed in deri- sion "Peace at-any-price men." Of these, I think the taunt thrown at them is scarcely deserving. Desirous as they are of helping on every movement tending to bring , nxtions more in harmony with each other, they will cer- tainly not view with satisfaction the already too rapid 1 strides made by Russia in her efforts to reduce Asia to her autocratic control. The despicable, and blundering, yet blood-guilty carnage now going on in the Soudan is at last being seen in its true light, and nearly all "men of light and leading" are agreed, that from the day when, the great shout ascended about" Peace with honour," and when the Dual Control was supposed to be an established fact, the whole of our pro- ceedings in the East have been a woeful and miserable raise take. The sickening reports of the war in the Soudan must convince every one of the great and almost universal enthusiasm pervading the Arab tribes. Women dressed as soldiers, children of ten fighting with the tenacity of grim warriors, crippled Arabs hobbling into our ranks, and hail- ing with their last death-struggle the fatal spear, must ' surely convince our people that at least the Soudanese are fighting for their homes and country. We are fighting in the Soudan to prop up a bankrupt State.: to defend usury in its worst form, our troops are now shedding blood. Our capitalists lend .V 3,000,000 to a spendthrift Khedive and call it £90,000,000, and charge for use from 12i- to 26 per cent.! Their whole capital is returned to them, but they are not content, and a Liberal Government, with a "great Christian Statesman" at its head, sends cut our fleet and troops to defend the capitalists' vested intereste. Surely "Christian heroes" and "Christian Statesmen " will make the people understand soon what is meant by" operations of war. In Afghanistan the case is altogether different. Should the Ameer remain true to his premises our work there should have a speedy ending; but should he listen to the voice of the charmer our work will become difficult and complex. Russia, we are told, in her wily and insidious fashion is holding out bribes to Turkey, and intends to gain her as ally if possible. Should she be successful in this, the I permanence of such an alliance may still be doubtful. What we have in any case to hope for, is that our recent diplo- matic relations with Afghanistan may have inspired its people with confidence in our civilising influence. If this is the case we have nothing to fear. Bussia, with all her hordes, will meet more than her match. In her attempt to stride to India she will find her path contested by the results of Western civilisation. In what poeition does Russia at present stand ? Look at Poland and Hungary, the history of whose patriots is a standing curse, and a warning against allowing the spread of autocratic and irresponsible rule. In Russia itself, the ranks of Nihilism are swelled by her best and most patriotic sons and daugh- ters. Literature itself is so made subject to a stupid and ignorant censorship that such a thing as public opinion is impossible. Her best novelists are exiled at once if they dare to speak outside the rigid lines laid down for them by this Ca Lr of all the Russias. Historians she has none, for what do people want with history who are not allowed to think ? Students there are, and should any of them betray the least sympathy for their down-trodden fellow-country- men, a long and weary journey is before them, with Siberia

at the end. One of her writers, " Stephniak," has in glow- ing pages given us a thousand reassns why the pestilential course of Russia should be stayed. Incapable of governing Russia proper, how can she be expected to benefit further acquisitions ? England has her duty before her. With firmly planted foot we must assert our right to stay the further progress of the Asiatic barbarian, and it is to be h Ted this will be done without encouraging any of that jingo, or Russopbobist feeling, that reminds one of the Irishman who is always challenging some one to "tread on the tail of my coat." Another, and very important, nay, the most important feature in ourquarrel with Russia is the welfare of India. Not for its trade benefits should I call upon the Govern- ment to defend India. There is a higher and a grander argument in favour of our keeping a friendly and close re- lationship with that gem of the British crown. India has a past history the grandest in the world's records; her po- tential power is such that her history in the future may contain all the civilising features so eagerly sought after at present, to enable a just harmony of classes to be brought about. Indian youths are receiving the best of educations in English Universities, carrying back with them Western influences ; we know its benefits are now permeating the , native Indian circles.

Why, sir, it is clear that should Russia by. any of her numerous tricks ever manage to plant her foot in India, it would be but the presage of her.owu downfall. Yet our rule in India has not been, is not, all that could be deeired. ;The short-sighted policy that recently led certain Englishmen and Anglo-Indians to oppose the Ilbert Bill was but the outcome of a system dating back to the days of Warren Hastings. We must govern India by making her see that our rule is not for sel flsh trading purposes. She mast see that we are but carrying out the great harmonising theory whereby the peoples of the world may ba led to lay down the sword mad cease to slay each other at the bidding of Monarchs and statesmen." March 30, 1881 CLIFFORD DIX.

div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday. Present: Lieut.-Col Ashton (in the chair), the Rev. J W N Tanner, J Lockwood, Messrs. R Ashton iirghfield, A tron, Lewis, Stokes, Midwood, Wallington, Pickering, Smith, Jackson, C It;gby, NV Whitlow, H Linaker (clerk), IV H Linaker (detruty clerk), Adams (medical officer). THE CLERK'S SILARY.—The Deouty C:erk said the clerk's salary last year was £B5. The Clerk said there were now two Parochial Committees which had employed a lot of his time. From May 9th, 1884, to Mty 13th there were 154 folios of minutes for these committees. —The Chairman: And saved work to this authority to that extent.—The Clerk: Every meeting has had to be attended ' and the minutes taken.—The Deputy Clerk said the work had increased considerably since the formation of the Authority.—The Clerk remarked upon the number of loans he had to attend to. The clerkship of the Authority was no sinecure.—A Member suggested that Frodsham should pay for the clerk's services to the Parochial Committees.— The Chairman said he had no doubt Frodsham would be glad to do so if they could, because the committees were a great advantage.—The Clerk observed that Frodeham could not do so.—A committee, consisting of Messrs Aaron, NVeir, and R Ashton, was appointed to confer with the clerk upon the matter.—The Committee retired, and on returning, Mr R Ashton said the cemmittee disc tvered that the clerk had had a great deal of extra work, and recommended that the salary be fixed at £B5, and that he be given a gratuity of £25 for his extra services.—Mr Aaron seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. FRODSHASI DRAINACIE.—Tbere were 14 tenders opened for the carrying out of the Frodsham sewerage. The amounts ranged from £495 to £1,239. It was unanimously decided that the tender of Mr H Beotb, of Bacup, be ac- cepted. This contractor's was the lowest tender. TILE EXPECTED VISITATION OF CHOLERA.—The Clerk reported that since the last meeting of the Authority he ha 4 met Dr. Airy, one of the medical inspectors of health to the Local Government Board, with Dr. Adams anti the nuisance inspector at his office. Dr. Airy inquired generally as to what was being done by the Authority, but particularly with reference to what was being done or could be done in the case of a visitation of cholera. All information possi- ble was given to the inspector, and he (the clerk) told Dr. Airy that if structural works for water supply and drainage works were made on the owners and not on the occupiers, the Sanitary Authority would more freely take up the neces- sary works of that description. (Elear, hear.) THE MEASLES ENDE‘IIC.—RUNCORN DEFEN DED.

The Medical Officer presented a special report, in which he said he had ascertained that there were upwards of 80 cases of measles in Halton in upwards of 40 houses, extend- ing to Asttnoor and Stockharn. The schools had been closed, and every precaution taken to prevent extension. He desired to specially acknowledge the able and strenuous efforts made by the Rev Mr Lockwood, vicar and guardian of Halton, with the view of arresting and stamping out this disease in his parish. Acting upon his suggestion, and his promise of circulation and distribution of printed instruc- tions, he (the medical officer) had drawn up a short code of rules and instructions which, be believed, had been printed and circulated through the township. Disinfectants were obtained and distributed gratis to all applicints at the vicarage with full directions for using them. Such zeal for the public welfare deserved acknowledgment wherever met with, and he was sure the Authority would approve of the public recognition of it which he hod felt compelled to make. A local medical gentleman had also supplied him with valuable information, and to him the Authority's thanks were due in view of the eminently unsatisfactory status of notification of infectious diseases. As to the origin of this outbreak, he was afraid the Authority must acknowledge its indebtedness to Runcorn. The propinquity of this urban district to the rural district rendered it almost impossible for highly infectious diseases to appear in Runcorn without their deeming it obligatory upon them to make excursions into the adjoining country districts; and in this respect they appear to possess an intelligent appreciation of the fact that for these districts, and so Runcorn is the "market town"

A SLEEPY CARTER, ktc.—Abrah Andrews, of Culcheth, was fined 5s at the Police Court, Strangsways, before Mr Flateley and Mr Cook for being asleep while in charge of a korse and cart on Monday, March 23rd, on Liverpool-road, Lower Irlam —Thomas Priestman, of Cadishead, was fined 5s at the Police Court, before Mr Flately and Mr Cook, for being drunk and disorderly on Liverpool-road, Warn, on Monday, March the 23rd. ENTERTAIRMENT.—Tbe Cadishead Tonic Sol-Fa Class gave their last entertainment for the season in the Wesleyan Diy School on Tuesday evening. The programme, which was a full one and gave great satisfaction, was as follows: Glee, " See our oars ;" part song," Male voices ;" song, "The better. land," Miss Chadwick ; glee, " The seasons ;" song, with. vocal acc)mpaniments, " Corns where my love lies dreaming ;" humeurous, " Pro phundo basso ;" part song, with humming accompaniment, " Look aloft ;" duet, " L aboard watch," Messrs Bowden and West ;" " Bells *of freedom," choir ; quartette, "Ye banks and braes," Misses Dodd and Owen and Messrs F Taylor and J Hea- ton ; glee, ', The friar of orders grey ;" quartette, " Hymn of the Moravian Nuns," Misses Davies and Chad- wick and Messrs Bovrns and Davies (encored) : part song, " The wanderer's farewell ;" song, with vocal accompani- ment,' Oh, gently breathe," Miss NI Taylor ; glee, " Once upon my cheek ;'.' part song. "The hunter's farewell," male voices ; part song, " Good speed the plough ;" hurnourous, "The burlesque band" (enured) ; song, " Sleep well," choir. - _ THE BIRTH Ail) -.DEATH —RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending Saturday, March 28th, 1885.—The mean , temperature was 396 Fahrenheit, and therefore about the sAree as the preceding week. The maximum temperature, 50 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 27th nlt., and the minimum temperature' 28 Fahrenheit, on the 23rd ult. The rainfal! measured 2 inches. The general direction of the wind was N.W. During the week, which was the 13th of the current year, 29 births and 15 deaths were registered. The death, rate from all causes was equal to 17.1 per 1,000, agaisst 17.1 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 23 6 the corresponding week of last yea. The deaths included 1 from whooping cough, 1 from old age, 4 from tsbercular disease, 4 from lung disease, and 2 from brain disease. JOHN GORNALL. Medical ()Inner of Health.
WARRINGTON. WARRINGTON INFIRMARY.—Mr Ziba Artnitige begs to acknowledge receipt of £1 50 4d from the ernployoi f Mr Henry Hoult, King-street, towards the funds of the above institution.
WICLIPFEI CHIIRCH.—On Sunday evening,. another of

the special people's services was hei'd in Wycliffe Church. when the Rev. J. Yonge spoke on " The Fatherhood of God" to a large congregation. In the course of the service Mrs. R. H. Pearson sang in an excellent manner "The , Prodigal Child." ORATORIO AT EIOLY TRINITY —Farmer's oratorio," Christ

and His Soldiers," was given in Holy Trinity Church on Monday evening by the combined choirs of Holy Trinity, Warrington, and Christ Church, Latchford. The solos were taken by Misi Parkinson, Mr Edward Rose (headmaster of the Blue boat School), Mr H Y Westbrook, and Master Edward Smith. Mr W Johnson officiated at the organ. EASTEIIi Exctrusiorrs.—li will be seen from our advertis- ing columns that the long-wished for revision of We holiday rates of the railway fares horn Warrington to Liverpool has at last been adopted by the two C3mptnies interested. Both the Cheshire Lines and the London and North-Western Railway now announce return and single tickets from War- rington to Liverpool proportionate in price to the tempting rate hitherto held out to passengers starting from Man- chester only. At ds 63 the holiday third-class return to the popular seaport cannot, but result in a large increase of traffic on both routes.

ROBBERY BY Grnr.s.—At the Borough Court, on Thurs- day, three young women named Catherine Connolley, Annie Barrow, and Jane Flynn, were charged, the former with be- ing drunk on the previous night in Tanner's-lane, and with assaulting a young man named James Eligham, and the three with stealing, or receiving knowing to have been stolen, the sum of 63, the property of James Higham.— Chief Constable Hunt said that the prosecutor was a labourer on the London and North-Western Railway, who resided at Stamford-street. Annie Barrow (18), Jane Flynn (21), and Catherine Connolly (25), were all fustian cutters; they were women of loose character. For some few nights they had been lodging in Berry's-yard, off Tanner's-lane. On Wednesday they met the complainant in Winwick-street, land took him to a house in Berry's-yard. Shortly after go. tog there he missed his purse, containing 63 in silver. He gccused the girls of stealing it, whereupon Connolly broke a hlass bottle on his head, and the three put him out of the touse and ill-used him. They were then given into cue- ; ody.—The Bench serit the prisoners to hard labour for a I month.

THEFTS OF CLOTHING —At the Borough Court on Mon- day a middle-aged woman named Margaret Frances Lindock and anither woman named Mary Farrell, were charged with having stolen on Saturday, a dress skirt, value ss, the property of Ann Farrell, janr., Cloth Hall-yard, Bank-st. ; they were also charged with receiving the property, know- ing it to have been stolen. The evidence showed that the skirt was pawned by Lindock, who hod been staying at, rxrrell's, and she was sent to gaol for a month, but Mary Farrell was dismissed; the evidence against her not being such as to warrant a conviction. -- On Tuesday, at the same court, a young man named James Towey, who lives in lodgings at 3, Vernon's-yard, pleaded guilty to stealing on Monday afternoon, a dress skirt and an ulster, value 4s, the property of Winifred Hail, from the house of that per- son's husband, which is situated in Vernon's-yard, next door to the one in which prisoner was lodging. The key of the one house fitted both, and prisoner appeared to have en- tered Mrs Hall's house during her absence. He sold the ar- ticles for threepence to a second-hand clothes dealer. When apprehended he replied, "It is a dear 43 worth." He had been previously sent to jail for theft, and was now commit- ted to prison for three months, with hard labour. THE New BOROUGH MAGISTRATES. At the Borough _ _ . .

_ The COTTON TR4DE.—As will have been seen from the reports we have given from week to week, the cotton trade , has gradully been getting from bad to worse. On inquiry at the office of Messrs. Armitage and Ri4by, cotton spinners and-manufacturers, Cockhedge Mills, on Thursday, we were informed that notice had been given that the workpeople would be put on three days a week, to commence on Tues- day next. A fortnight's notice has also been given to the weavers of a redaction of 5 per cent, in their wages. Up- wards of 1,000 hands are affected by the short time, and about 800 of tbem are weavers who will be affected by the 5 per cent. reduction. I CHILD BURNED TO DEATH : THE lequesr.—On Tuesday afternoon Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street, touching the death of a little bey named Thomas Cummings, aged two and a half years, the son of a labaurer living at 2, Friar's-lane, Friar's-green, which occurred on Sunday. On Saturday afternoon the child was put to bed by its mother, who left the house for a short time, and the father was at the time asleep. Soon afterwards he was awakened by hearing screams, and found the child on the top of the stairs, its clothing being in filmes. It was at once wrapped in a shawl and taken to the Infirmary, where its injuries—severe burns about the thighs, arms, and breast—were atteaded to. It died, however, on the followinz day. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," the supposition being that deceased had got out of bed, gone downstairs, and its clothes had become ignited by its playing near the fire. Ihe Coro- ner afterwards remarked on the large number of cases of death from burns that came before him, and said that many might be prevented by the use of an ordinary fire gurrd as a precaution. PRESENTATION TO SERGEANT BLEASE.—On Saturday the 9th Lancashire (Warrington) Rifle Volunteers paraded for drill uuder Colonel Greenall, the commanding officer. The Martini-Henri rifles that have recently been obtained were handed to the men by Colonel Greenall, who expressed the hope that each member would endeavour to make himself a good shot. Referring to the Russian crisis, he said that several commanding officers of rifle corps had volunteered, but bethought the proper time for such a step had not ar- rived. Notwithstanding that, however, he had privately notified to the War Office that when the time did come the 9th ware at their disposal. (Applause.) There was a ' rumour that men might be asked for from the volunteers to fill up gaps in the Line, but he did not believe in splitting up regiments and separating coinrades.—Sergeant-Instruc- tor Blease was then called to the front, and Colonel Green- all, on behalf of the officers and members of the corps pre- sented him with a timepiece on his retirement, after a period of 37 yeers in her Majesty's service.—Sergeant Blease replied, and the band played "Auld Lang Syne."— A letter was subsequently read from Mr T H Lyon, thank- ing the volunteers for their strong muster at Stretten on the occasion of the funeral of the late Colonel Lyon. WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB—On Wednesday after- noon the first meeting of the siewly-formed Warrington Farmer's Club was held at the White Bull Hotel, Horse- market-street. The chair was occupied by the president, Mr John Marsh, of Bradley Hall, and there was a large attend- ance. Officers for the ensuing year were appointed and tales adopted, the subscription for membership being fixed at ss. a year. The Chairman referring to the benefits of a club such as the one they had formed, said that many times their complaints as individuals were unheeded, but those complaints would be listened to if they came from an influential body like a strong club. He was of opinion also that if proper information was given to them on the subject farmers might make artificial manures at a much cheaper rate than they could buy them. Some of the dealers in manures, he said, they knew to be honest and reliable, but there were others who were not so conscientious.—Mr J L Stelfox read an interesting paper on " Agriceltural depres- sion: its causes and remedies," for which he was awarded a cordial vote of thanks.—A resolution was also unanimously passed calling upon the Government to oppose the Railway Rates Bill as being likely to injure the interests of farmers. HIGHWAY PARISH OF WARRINGTON.— On Thursday evening a meeting of inhabitants contributing to the high- way rates of the Highway Parish of Warrington, was held at the King and Queen Inn, Padgate-lane, for the transac- tion of the usual yearly business. Mr John Grounds was voted to the chair, and there were also present Messrs Isaac Ashcroft, Samuel Clare, Jonathan Caldwell, and J L Tunstall (collector.)—fle annual statement of accounts was read by Mr Tunstall, who said that a rate was made in June, 1.884. The amount collected was £502 19a 61, and other receipts make a total of £532 25 6d. The total amount of the rate was £539 153 11d, of which £502 19s 6d was col- lected, £29 10e Ild aelowed to owners, and £7 5s 61 irre- coverable, The sum of £6O 19s had been paid over to the treasurer towards the next precept. The accounts were passed without discussion, on the motion ef the Chairman, seconded by Mr Ashcroft.—The Chairman was asked to act as waywarden for the ensuing year. but he said that as he had occupied that position for four years he should prefer that it should now be taken by some one else. Finally, after consideratle pressure, he consented to again take office.—The proposition that he be re-elected was moved by Mr Caldwell, and seconded by Mr Ashcroft.—On the motion of Mr Grounds, seconded by Mr Clare, Mr J L Tun- stall was re-appointed collector.—This was all the busi- ness. WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. —A meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, at which there were present the Rev G F Roberts (chairman), and Messrs Derbyshire, Brown, Bonnell, Jolley, and Mackie; and S Sutton (assistant clerk.) The annual reports of the school attendance officers were read, and showed that educational matters in the district were in a satisfactory condition, the average attendance having in- ereased since last year.—lt was reported that since the last meeting the assistant clerk had written to the Local Govern- ment Chronicle upon the subject of prosecutions in cases of negligence te send children to school to ascertain whether prosecutions entered upon by the School Attendance Com- mittee could be heard by any bench of magistrates sitting within the Union, or whether the committee were bound to take all cases before the magistrates acting for the division of the county in which the committee's district is situate. The answer to this query was that it appeared to the editors of the above-named journal that, inasmuch as it was provided by 30 and 31, V. C. 106, s. 27, that "where a Union extends into several district jurisdictions every matter, act, charge, or complaint by which the Guardians thereof are affected or in which they have any interest shall, for the purpose of jurisdiction, be deemed to arise or exist equally throughout the Union," the same principle applied to Union school at- tenOance committees, and therefore it was competent for the committee to take proceedings if they thought fit before the borough justices instead of the county. After some con- versation the committee instructed the officers to apply in the future to the borough magistrates for summonses. RETURN Or MR. T. B. WITHINGTON TO CULCHETH Meet. --Culcheth was gaily decorated on Tuesday, in honour of the return of Mr. Thomas Ellarnes Withington to the Hall, from Oxford, near which place he has resided for the last thirteen years. Mr. Withington travelled from Oxford to Warrington by train, and arrived at Cuicheth by carriage. He was met near the Rowe Farm by a procession of the Sunday and day scholars of the school, as well as the Glazebrook Brass Band, and the Croft Drum and Fife Band. The tenantry of his estate were present in large numbers, and friends from Croft, Kenyon, Glazebury and the surrounding district were also present, making a tottl in all of about 4,000 persons. The procession of scholars numbered about 200. On Mr. Withington's carriage cominz into view the D:urn and Fife Band etruck up " See the conquering hero comes," and was followed by loud cheers from the tenant y. 'When the car- riage approached, Mr. Withington was loudly applauded, and cheers were given for Mrs. and Miss Withiugtou, who occupied seats in the conveyance. These uninistakeable signs of kind affection Mr. Wallington aCknowledged by raising his hat. The Rev. Dr. Black, rector, then read an address, and Mr Withington, who -was loud y applauded, said : Friends and neighbours, it is very pleasant indeed for me to come back, and to be received in this manner. This recep- tion is almost unexpected, although I had a note of warn- ing ; and I can only thank you' all from the bottom of my heart for this very kind reception in the name of my- self and Mrs and Miss Withington. I am very glad to come amongst you—(applause)—and I am sorry that 1 htve been away so long. But I hope to make up for that by living the remainder of my life amongst you. (Loud and con- tinued applause.) —The horse was then taken out of the shafts, and the carriage was run to the Hall by the tenants. —The assembly then dispersed, the scholars having been regaled with buns, oranges, dtc. The bells of the Parish Church wane rung at intervals, and flags were displayed from the tower, as well as from many other parts of the village.

Police Court on Monday, shortly after the cemmencement of business, Mr John Greening and Mr E J Guest, two of the gentlemen recently appointed to the commission of jus- tices of the peace, took their seats for the first time on the borough bench. Having made the usual declaration, they were addressed by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who said : " Gentlemen,—l am very happy to congratulate you on your advent to an office that is as honourable as it is ancient. and I think it dates back from the time of William the First, about the eleventh century. I have no doubt you will frequently experience, as I have experienced some- times, very painful incidents in this c nut, but the recollec- tion that you are acting in vindication of the majesty of the law, will, I am quite sure, always help to soften down that feeling, whenever it may arise. I very sincerely congratu• late you on your elevation to the borough bench, and I hope you will live to be magisterial patriarchs." The busi- ness of the court was then proceeded with, and the next prisoner brought forward, who happened to be an old offen- der, was discharged, the Bench thinking the opportunity a fitting one for clemency. —On Wednesday Councillor Platt I was duly sworn in as a magistrate at the Borough Court. I There was no other business before the court.

div.head: CIVIL AND MILITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: CIVIL AND MILITARY AUTHORITY.
EJECTION OF A BAILIFF. • EXTRAORDINARY CASE.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, a case was heard in which Jno Thomas, a bailiff of the court, claimed damages from Sergeant-Major Bailey and Private Grany, stationed at Orford Barracks, for an assault alleged to have been com- mitted under peculiar circumstances at the barracks on the 2nd of last month. Mr. A. Browne (solicitor) Warringtoe, appeared on behalf of the high bailiff (Mr. J. Harrison), and Mr. Pickford, banister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington) was for the defence.—Mr. Browne, in opening the case' said that two bailiffs of the court, named Waterhouse and Thomas, were given an exe- cution upon the goods of Sergeant Thomas Skinner, at the barracks, Orford-lape. On the 2nd ult„ they went to the barracks, obtained admission, and were taken across the square by one of the privates. They told Skinner that the sum they wanted was £1 4s sd, and asked him if he could get the money. Owing to not receiving it they went to the men's quarters and saw the wife of Skinner closing the door. They rushed up to it and pushed it baek. Skinner haying beard the warrant read, sent for the defendant Bailey, who told them they had no right there, and could not take anything out. He also said that if they did not go out he would fetch someone to put them out. Bailey then struck his cane on the table in rather a threatening manner, and demanded whether the bailiffs did not know that a soldier was exempt from execution for any sum under £3O. Thomas replied that his duty was simply to execute the warrant. The other bailiff (Waterhouse) then went downstairs, and was escorted across the square. He also heard orders given that he was net to be allowed in the barracks again. Thomas was left in possession, and Bailey demanded that he should leave, but he refused. The de- fendant Grany was fetched, and took hold of the sofa upon which Thomas was sitting and dragged it into the centre of the room. He next dragged Thomas to the landing, and I he was there seized by two or three soldiers and forced step I by step dawn the stairs, notwithstanding that he tried to bold on by the rails. His coat was tons, his hat was I knocked off his head, his papers were scattered about the premises, and he was hauled out of the barracks by the neck. The high bailiff was afterwards told what had hap- pened, and wrote to the barracks asking for an apology, and saving that if it were tendered nothing more would be beard of the matter. None, however, was made, and no reply was sent to the letter. The bailiff Waterhouse was first called, and proved going to the barracks and taking possession of Skinner's quandrs. Sergeant-Major Bailey cams, and said if he and Thomas did not leave he would fetch those who would put them out, at the same time striking his cane on the table. The goods in the house were household furniture, and not things belong- ing to the army. Witness then detailed how he left the barracks, Thomas remaining in possession, went to the polica station, and was returning with an officer, when he met Thomas coming from the barracks. The latter said that his coat had been torn, and be had been assault-d.—By Mr Pickford: Did net think it requisite to tell the man at the gate that they had a warrant to execute, as they did not want to expose Skinner, and tell everyone their business. They did not want to get into barracks by a trick. Did not speak to Skinner when he was drilling. Told him in the square that they had a warrant against him. Went with a man named Dickinson and some friends to the canteen. Did not remain there long. Had some porter. Did not say anything to Sergeant-Major Bailey about the warrant, and did not know that the sergeantonajor was responsible for discipline in the barracks.—lf you see a woman by hereelf shutting a door, do you think it right to push that door open, is that in your opinion the way to execute a war- rant? Sometimes it is.—You thought it was in this case? Yes.—Did it never occur to you that if any opposition was offered to you in making the execution your proper course was to go to the commanding officer or the person in charge ? We did not think so. No one laid a finger on him, and the assault happened when he was away —Was not Thomas smoking in Skinner's quarters ? I think he smoked after- wards.—He was sitting or lying on Skinner's sofa smoking? He was sitting on it—ls that a right thing to do? Certain- ly. (Laughter).—ls it your opinion that a bailiff may do anything he likes to get into a house, and do anything he likes when he is in ? No.—He can smoke ? Yes.—Can be spit on the floor? Not very nice to do it. (Laughter.) Thomas did not do that to hie knowledge. The warrant was afterwards shown to Bailey.—By the Judge: The dup- licate was ehown to Bailey.—By Mr. Pickford He told the high bailiff about it the following morning. Was not ex- amined on oath by the high bailiff, and did not tell him that both of them were turned out of the house. He was not turned out In a violent manner. Was sober when he left the barracks. Skinner said the debt was his wife's, and he knew nothing of it, but would pay it. He did so the same evening. John Thomas, bailiff, corroborated, and stated the assault he complained of.—By Mr Pickford: We had a can of beer each, bet did not drink all of it as it was not fit for drink- ing —Not fit for a bailiff, only for a soldier !—How much did you drink of it ?—I do not think we drunk half of it. 4 Continuing, witness said that Sergeant-Major Bailey ceme four times to the house and said that witness had no right there, and would be 'put out. Grany got hold of him " anyhow "by the front of his coat. He was leaned out of the house, his hat and stick flying about, and eventually he was dragged down the steps and escorted out of bar- racks like a thief. (Laughtor.)—Mr Browne : Who escor- ted you out ? Grany.— How? By the coat collar. (Laughter.)—Cross-examined, witness said he did not think it necessary to say they had come to levy an execution.— How long were you in the canteen ? Ten minutes or a quarter of an kour.—You did not drink anything? We had a small drop.—But could net drink any more? I would not give Gd for a barrel ; it is tight enough for soldiers, you know.—You do not consider it is good enough for a bailiff, an impudent fellow like you, but if it is good enough for a soldier who has to do his duty to his country.—ln further cross-examination, witness said he smoked by Mrs Skinner's permission in Skinner's quarters, but denied cleaning his pipe with her knitting needle, or being drunk.—Evidence having been called as to the bailiffs' being sober at the time in question, Mr. Pickford spoke for the defence. He contended that by the evidence of the bailiffs it was distinctly proved that Sergeant-Major Bailey had not commhted any assault, and said that if Grany had done so it was not through any order from the Sergeant-Major. He commented atrongly on the manner in which the bailiffs had entered the barracks, and said that in serving a civil process the proper course was to state their errand, which would be communicated to the commanding officer, and every assistance would be given

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Lord Randolph Churchill left Alexandria on Thursday for England, (site well. Franz Abt, the celebrated musical csmposer, died at Wiesbaden on Thursday morning. Mr Chamberlain has accepted an invitation to dine with the members of the Eighty Club en the 28th inst. Sir Charles Dilke, has gone to E iinburgh, where sittings of the Royal Commission on the Housing of the Working- classes will be held during the Easter recess. Prince George of Wales will join the "Excellent " gunnery ship at Portsmouth on the 11th inst., to go through a course of training in torpedo gunnery and pilotage. The Madagascar, a new paper published in Mauritius, advocates the colonization of Madagascar by Mauritian creoles. The paper is distinctly anti-English in tone. The transport Conway Castle arrived at Portsmouth on Friday evening with 233 officers and men invalided from Egypt. Colonel Chichester, sth Lancers, recalled by Duke of Cambridge, is amongst the passengers. Lord Derby has promised to receive, after the Easter re- cess, a deputation from the Straits Settlements on the subject of the defences of that important possession. It is hoped that Lord Hartington will be present at the later- view.

. . FRIGHTFUL TRAMCAR ACCIDENT AT BURY. A steam tramcar, crowded with holiday-makers, ran off the line whilst rounding a curve in King•street, Bury, and, turning completely over all the passengers were more or less badly bruised, and about 20 were seriously injured. Dasmvcrivs FIRE.—The great fire which occurred about midnight on Thursilay in the hosiery warehouse of Messrs Thornton and Mawby, Leicester, was still smouldering at noon yesterday, but there is no danger of its spreading. The damage is roughly estimated between £30,000 and £40,000. GOOD FRIDAY AND VOLUNTEERS.—Last year SOM43 ob- jection was made in Episcopal circles to the Volunteers ta.ting part in military movements on Feod Friday. An arrangement made this year by which religious services ware specially provided last evening for the Volunteers who are quartered in the villages near Brighton,
THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN.
THE MAHDI'S FORCES.

DONGOLZ TuunsnAV.—The Arabs state that it is impos- sible for the Mandl to move a large force from Khartoum by the desert route to Debbeh or Dongola, as the season is ex- ceptionally dry, there being barely sufficient water to supply 100 men on the march. A large gathering of rebels is reported at Gubra Wells, situated 218 miles from Debbeh and 50 from Khartoum, where water is always plentiful. ADVANCE OF GENERAL GRAHAM.. -OCCUPATION AND BURNING -OF TAMAL-RETREAT OF THE ARABS SIJAILIM FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—GeneraI Graham; with the bulk of his force, advanced from Teselah Hill early this morning to Tama', which was occupied after a smart skirmish, the enemy having retreated apparently to Tamanieb. ur troops set fire to Tamil-which was soon destroyed, and are now returning to M`Dieill's Zereba. Our total losses are one killed and twelve wounded, including Lieutenant Lallor' of the Royal Marines. The colonial troops behaved well and had several wounded. OFFICIAL TELEGRAMS.
We have received the following from the War Office ---• . . - •

Telegram from Lieutenant General Gmham to the Secre- tary of State for War (despatched from Suakim 8 a.m.), Tesellah Hill, 3rd April, 1885. Hills around ztreba occu- pied last night by chain pickets and strong reserve. At 1 a.m, there was firing from Tamai side about 800 yardq from the camp. It was silenced by a volley from the advanced picket of the Grenadiers, followed by shell from 13-pounder on the hill. The remainder of the night was quiet. I re- gret that one man of the Surrey Regiment was killed, and that two men of the Berkshire Regiment were wounded. The morning was cool and the troops in good condition; only seven fell out during the march yesterday although 15 hours on the march and having to form zareba at the end; the number on the sick list not exceeding 8. I shall move and occupy the Springs this morning, and do not expect serious resistance. I Am leaving this position and the trans- port. Telegram from Lieutenant-General Sir G Graham to the Secretary ef State for War (despatched from SuAkim at 8-30 a.m.), Teselah Hill, 3rd April, 1885 :—Killed, let Bat- talion East Surrey Regiment, 1,479, Private H Bradley ; wounded severely, Ist Battalion Becks Regiment, 179, Pri- vate C Barden ; 1768, Private J Colborne. From Lieutenant-General Sir G Graham to the Secretary of State for War (despatched from Suakim at 11-40 a.m ) : —Tamai Springs, 3rd April, 1835. The force advanced at 8 a.m. this morning and occupied village and Khor with slight opposition ; found very little water, and that of very bad quality. lam returning the whole force on to the first zareba. Two privates of the Scots Guards and twe privates of the Australians were wounded.
GENERAL GRANT'S ILLNESS. NEW YORIC, FRIDAY AFFEENOON.—GeneraI Grant's con- dition is unchanged. He is slowly sinking. SHOOTING A JAPANESE DIPLOMATIST.

div.head: REVOLT IN ZASEIGAR.
div.p: REVOLT IN ZASEIGAR.

- VIENNA, THURSDAY NIGHT —We learn from a Russian source that the news of a revolt having broken out in the Chinese Mohammedan province cf Kashg tr is confirmel. The population sent two notables to their neighbour, the Khan of 136khara, and also communicated with the Khans of Khiva and Afghanistan, the Indian Government, and the Czar. They ask for aid to en able the Mohamme lens of Kashgar to form an independent State such as existed before 1878. _

div.head: RISING IN CANADA.
div.p: THE RISING IN CANADA.

OTTAWA, TIMRSDAY.—The latest news from Battleford, dated yesterday, says the Indians, on their way to the Reserve, killed an old man who was repairing the telegraph lines, and continued plundering. Battleford news states the place is provisioned for three months, and that there are 300 women and children, b -sides 200 armed men, insiie the town. The rebel Indians were shelled out of the vicinity yesterday. The ice is clearing out of the South Saskatchewan river, and part of the troops will therefore be conveyed to Prin :e Albert by stetmer, the remainder going by train. Al- together 4000 men are srei en route for the scene of the rebellion.

OTTAWA, THURSDAY, 3 P.M.—Sir John Macdonald, the Dominion Premier, has received a telegram from the Lieutenant-Governor of the North-west Territory, stat- ing that the powerful Indian chief Piapot, whose loyally has been considered more than doubtful, has agreed to go south with his band, and refrain from all participation in the rising,

MANTLES.—Some Mantle Shope have a disreputable system of ticketing Mantles in the window met under value, and this is often observed by ladles who purchase at the Mantle Co.'s Whol4sale Warehouse, which necessitates an ex- planation of this bad system. Ladies should know that Mantles prominently displayed, apparently under value, if secured might be bargains, but when marked under cost it is not intended they should be sold. These are made specially for the window as a draw, and prbably so made as to fit no one, or are artfully changed for inferior copies hanging in readiness at the back of the window, of commoner materials and trimmings, in imitation of the one ticketed. This system is carried on with Black Costumes also. The Mantle Co. chal- lenge competition ; but this false window display neeils ex- posure.
